fields.name: Andrew Murray
fields.bio: Andrew Murray Jr., born in 1828 in South Africa, served as a minister and theologian, influencing many through his teachings on prayer. He established educational institutions, authored over 240 works, and profoundly impacted Christian thought until his death in 1917. His books on deeper spiritual life continue to guide believers worldwide. Murray emphasized humility, absolute surrender to God, and the indwelling Christ. His classic works remain essential reading for Christians seeking deeper spiritual maturity.
fields.bio_html:
Andrew Murray was born on 9 May 1828 in Graaff-Reinet, a dusty frontier town in the Cape Colony, into a home already saturated with prayer. His father, a Scottish minister sent out by the Church of Scotland, kept a standing habit of reading revival accounts to his family and pleading, week after week, that God would pour out His Spirit upon South Africa. Andrew grew up hearing those petitions at the family altar, and though the answer would be long in coming, it would come through the son who knelt beside that father. His mother, Maria Susanna Stegmann, traced her blood to French Huguenot refugees and German Lutherans, so that in the boy's veins ran the memory of two peoples who had suffered for their faith.

A Boy Sent Across the Sea

At ten years old, in July 1838, Andrew and his elder brother John were sent across the ocean to Scotland to be schooled in Aberdeen, making the long voyage under the care of the Rev. and Mrs James Archbell and lodging with their uncle, the Rev. John Murray, who oversaw their training. It was a formidable thing to place two small boys on a ship for another hemisphere and not see them again for years, and the separation pressed on them. But Scotland gave as well as took. In the spring of 1840 the revivalist William C. Burns came to Aberdeen, and the boys saw at close range a man whose preaching and whole manner of life were given over to God; the impression Burns left on young Andrew became one of the shaping influences of his life. The brothers were caught up in the wake of the evangelical awakenings then stirring the land, breathing the same air as men like Robert Murray M'Cheyne and Horatius Bonar, and both took their degrees at Marischal College in Aberdeen in 1845. From there they went on to the University of Utrecht in the Netherlands to read theology, and fell in with Het Réveil, a Protestant revival movement that set itself against the cold rationalism of the Dutch church and prized conversion, inward piety, and experiential religion.

For all his devout upbringing, Murray did not presume upon his own religion. By his own account he had first aimed at the ministry as a respectable career rather than as an act of faith. It was during the Utrecht years that his own faith came to a settled assurance, and he wrote home of the change with the plainness of a man who knew the difference between inherited creed and personal surrender.

Your son has been born again… I have cast myself on Christ.

— Andrew Murray, in a letter to his parents from Utrecht

The change went deeper than a single decision; it became a lifelong thirst for the presence of God, caught in his own prayer that not a single moment of my life be spent outside the light, love, and joy of God's presence. On 9 May 1848, his twentieth birthday, he and his brother were ordained by the Hague Committee of the Dutch Reformed Church, and set their faces homeward to Africa.

A Ministry of the Saddle

His first charge was Bloemfontein, a parish that was less a town than a territory — some hundred thousand square miles of it, stretching beyond the Orange and Vaal Rivers. Installed in 1849 at barely twenty-one, he became the first settled minister north of the Orange River, responsible for scattered Voortrekker communities spread across immense and roadless distances. He rode for weeks at a stretch to reach lonely farms, baptising, catechising, marrying, burying, and preaching to people who might not see a minister again for a year; in one stretch of two consecutive years he baptised more than six hundred children. The trekkers came to trust the young minister with more than their souls, and he stood beside them as a friend and go-between in their negotiations for freedom from British rule. It was a ministry of the saddle and the open veld, and it taught him early that the work was God's and not his own.

On 2 July 1856 he married Emma Rutherford in Cape Town, a marriage of deep and durable affection that would give them eleven children, nine of whom lived to adulthood. Then, in 1860, came the hinge of his life. Murray accepted a call to Worcester, and there walked straight into the answer to his father's decades of prayer.

The Revival of 1860

The revival of 1860 did not begin with Murray. On a farm near Worcester, a handful of believers had been meeting weekly for months, pleading for an outpouring of the Spirit; one woman among them grew so burdened that she prayed almost without ceasing for a week. When the Spirit fell, it fell with a force that overturned all the ordinary decencies of a Dutch Reformed service. Murray himself, presiding at one such gathering, gave his careful instructions and invited the people to pray one at a time — and instead the whole assembly broke at once into simultaneous, weeping prayer for mercy. When Murray tried to restore order, one of the farmers told him plainly to stand back: no man could throw a dam wall around what God was doing. It was a lesson the ordered, cautious young minister took to heart. He learned to loosen his grip on the reins, and God used him to shepherd an awakening he could not have manufactured and dared not quench.

Long before Andrew Murray reached Worcester, a small band of believers on a nearby farm had been meeting weekly for months to plead for revival, and one woman among them prayed almost without ceasing for a week. Their prayers were answered in the awakening of 1860: the Spirit fell in a prayer meeting, whole congregations broke spontaneously into prayer for mercy, and the movement spread from the village to the lonely surrounding farms — the very outpouring Murray's own father had been praying for across decades of family worship.

Out of that revival came Murray the writer. His pastoral care for the flood of new converts, his anxiety that their first love not cool into formality, drove him to write Abide in Christ — first in Dutch as Blijf in Jezus — and with it he found the vein he would work for the rest of his life. From Worcester he moved to Cape Town's Groote Kerk in 1864, standing there against the rising tide of theological liberalism, and in 1871 to Wellington, where he settled for the longest and most fruitful season of his ministry, thirty-five years in one pulpit.

Wellington and a Widening Vision

Wellington became the seedbed of his wider vision. His church knew his worth: six times over the years the Dutch Reformed Church in South Africa called him to serve as moderator of its Synod, and few men did more to turn that inward-looking body into a missionary church. Convinced that the church must turn outward, he laboured to found institutions that would outlast him. In 1874, inspired by the pioneering work of the American educator Mary Lyon, he established the Huguenot Seminary for the Christian education of women, recruiting its teachers from America; rooted in prayer, the school grew into the Huguenot University College and lives on today as Huguenot College, still training Christian workers and social leaders. As a member of his church's foreign missions committee he raised the funds to found three societies at Wellington in 1877 — the Ministers' Missionary Union, the Bible and Prayer Union, and the Layman's Mission League — and in 1889, with Martha Osborn and Spencer Walton, he helped form the South African General Mission, a work that outlived them all, becoming the Africa Evangelical Fellowship in 1965 and folding into SIM International in 1998.

His pen never rested. By the end he had produced more than 240 books, testimonies, and sermons — on prayer above every other theme, but also on the confession of sin, on knowing the will of God, on daily fellowship with God, on Christian victory — written in English and Dutch and translated into more than fifteen languages, until his quiet Afrikaans devotion was being read on every continent. His best writing grew out of the preacher's eye for a living illustration. In the summer of 1898 he acquired a brown vine stump, and out of long meditation on it wrote The Mystery of the True Vine, dedicating it to struggling Christians the world over; by the time it was published the old stump had taught him another lesson, and he wrote The Fruit of the Vine after it.

Humility, the place of entire dependence on God, is, from the very nature of things, the first duty and the highest virtue of the creature, and the root of every virtue.

— Andrew Murray, Humility

Trials and the Silent Years

His faith was not spared its trials, and he did not pretend otherwise. In 1879 his throat failed him; he lost his voice and entered what he called his “silent years,” two years in which the preacher could not preach. Even writing became a labour, so he dictated his meditations to his wife and daughter — and at the close of each one he would fold his hands, shut his eyes, and pray the final lines aloud before they were set down, so that his books ended where his heart did, in prayer. He sought out those who taught the theology of divine healing, and in 1882 travelled to a faith home in London, from which he returned convinced that healing belonged within Christ's redemptive work and restored to his pulpit. Yet he never made his healing a stick to beat the sick with, nor a rejection of ordinary care. Later, in 1893, a carriage accident in Natal left him with a permanently injured back and a bent frame; in his last decades he often preached seated, an old man folded over his infirmity but not silenced by it.

It was out of one such season of pain that he left the church its most beloved word of counsel. In 1895, resting in a friend's home in Wimbledon, in physical pain and stung the night before by a sharp letter attacking his teaching, he took up a pen and wrote a note not for publication but for his own soul.

First, He brought me here; it is by His will I am in this strait place: in that fact I will rest. Next, He will keep me here in His love, and give me grace to behave as His child. Then, He will make the trial a blessing, teaching me the lessons He intends me to learn, and working in me the grace He means to bestow. Last, In His good time He can bring me out again — how and when He knows.

— Andrew Murray, “In Time of Trouble Say,” written at Wimbledon, 1895

The Inner Chamber

The habit beneath all of it was prayer. Murray — called by some the leading student of Christ's school of prayer — taught that prayer is at once the simplest thing a child can do and the highest work to which a man can rise, and he practised what he taught, guarding the “inner chamber” of secret prayer as the source from which everything else flowed. He rose to meet God before he met men, and counselled others that to know how to speak to God is a greater thing than to know how to speak to man.

Prayer was the discipline at the root of Murray's whole life and the subject he returned to more than any other in his writing. He held that the secret place of prayer — the “inner chamber” — is where the Christian's strength is drawn, and that though prayer is simple enough for a feeble child, it is at the same time the holiest work to which anyone can rise: a real fellowship with the unseen and most holy God, entered in full surrender to His will and in the name of Jesus.

Though in its beginnings prayer is so simple that the feeble child can pray, it is at the same time the highest and holiest work to which man can rise.

— Andrew Murray, Lord, Teach Us To Pray

Legacy

Andrew Murray died at Wellington on 18 January 1917, in his eighty-ninth year, having outlived by more than half a century the revival that made him and having given the church a shelf of books that still teach believers to abide, to humble themselves, and to pray. His influence ran far beyond his own communion: readers as different as Watchman Nee in China and Jessie Penn-Lewis in Wales drew deeply from his teaching and carried it on into movements of their own. He never asked to be remembered as a great man; his own writing pressed relentlessly the opposite point — that the creature's glory is its nothingness, and that only the soul emptied of self leaves God free to be all. Statues stand to him in Wellington and outside the Groote Kerk in Cape Town, but the truer monument is the man on his knees, anywhere in the world, who opens one of Murray's little books and learns again to say, “Lord, teach us to pray.”

fields.name: Watchman Nee
fields.bio: Watchman Nee, born in 1903 in Foochow, China, was a prominent figure in 20th-century Christianity and Chinese church leadership. He embraced Christianity at 17, dedicated his life to ministry, and authored numerous influential works like "The Normal Christian Life." Persecuted for his faith, he died in 1972 while imprisoned at 69. His legacy continues through the Local Church movement worldwide. Nee's teachings emphasized the spiritual realities of the church and the believer's position in Christ.
fields.bio_html:
Watchman Nee was born Ni Tuosheng in Shantou on 4 November 1903, into a family from Fuzhou already touched by the Christian faith. His grandfather had been among the first Chinese ministers ordained by the Congregational missions in Fujian province, and his mother, Lin Heping, was a woman of strong will and deep devotion. Nee was the first son among nine children, and his mother received his birth as the answer to her longing for a son — and dedicated the child to God in gratitude for it, a consecration made over him before he could speak a word. The Chinese name the family came to use for him, Tuosheng, evokes the sound of the night-watchman's wooden gong struck through the dark hours of a Chinese town — the watchman who stays awake while others sleep, calling out the passing of the night. It became, in English, simply Watchman: a name he would spend his life living up to, as one who watched and warned and kept vigil for the coming of the morning.

As a boy Nee was clever, ambitious, and by his own later admission proud. At thirteen he entered the Church Missionary Society's Vernacular Middle School in Fuzhou, beginning a Western-style education, and went on to excel at the Anglican-run Trinity College there, placing near the top of his class. A bright worldly future seemed assured, and for years he resisted the faith of his household, set on advancement. Grace reached him first through his mother. Under the preaching of the itinerant evangelist Dora Yu — herself a former medical student who had forfeited a lucrative career for the gospel — Lin Heping was so convicted that she came home and did something almost unheard of in that culture: she apologised to her own son for a wrong she had done him. The humbling of his mother pierced the pride of the boy, and he began to attend the meetings himself.

The night he could not rest

On the evening of 28 April 1920, at seventeen, Nee was alone in his room and could find no peace. His first inclination was not to believe, not to become a Christian — and yet that resolve left him more restless still. There was a real struggle within him. At last he knelt to pray. At first he had no words at all; then his sins rose up before him one by one, and he knew himself to be a sinner. As he made that first true prayer, joy and peace such as he had never known flooded in. He said simply to the Lord, "Oh, Lord, You have indeed been gracious to me." From that night he consecrated himself wholly to Christ and to the preaching of the gospel among his own people. The bright career for which his education had prepared him he laid down without looking back. At his baptism he declared what that surrender meant:

Lord, I leave my world behind. Your cross separates me from it forever, and I have entered into another. I stand where you have placed me in Christ!

— Watchman Nee, at his baptism

His conversion was itself an answered prayer — and not only his own. His mother had prayed for him for years before Dora Yu's meetings; her own broken repentance, and the apology she offered her proud son, were the human means by which grace at last found him. On the night of 28 April 1920, kneeling wordless in his room until his sins rose up and drove him to confession, Nee prayed his way from struggle into a peace that filled the room like light.

The new convert was eager for training, and he joined Dora Yu's Bible institute in Shanghai — only to be sent home, dismissed for undisciplined habits such as sleeping in late. The humiliation did its work. Determined that his character should be remade, he sought out the influence that would shape him most: Margaret E. Barber, an independent English missionary living near Fuzhou who had renounced her denominational ties for what she called a life of faith. Barber baptised Nee and his mother in 1921, treated him as a learner under strict, sometimes severe, discipline, and opened to him the deep well of her Holiness and Brethren library — introducing him to the writings of D. M. Panton, Robert Govett, G. H. Pember, Jessie Penn-Lewis, and T. Austin-Sparks, and to Brethren teachers such as John Nelson Darby, William Kelly, and C. H. Mackintosh. Nee devoured them, and his own library eventually grew to more than three thousand Christian volumes, reaching back to writers of the earliest centuries. When Barber died in 1930, she left everything she owned to him. From her he absorbed a conviction that would run through all his work: that the crucified and risen Christ must not merely be admired but must actually live His own life through the believer.

Ministry and the Little Flock

He did not wait for maturity to begin. With a band of like-minded students he organised independent meetings, dedicated Bible study, and street preaching through the town and its schools, and in those early years sixty-nine of his own college classmates were led to salvation. From 1922 Nee began holding church meetings in Fuzhou that grew into an indigenous Chinese movement, free of foreign denominational control, which outsiders called the Little Flock and its members called simply the church in each locality. In 1923 he launched a magazine, The Present Testimony, followed in 1925 by The Christian — the year he set aside his birth name Shu-tsu and took the name To-sheng, the watchman's gong. At twenty-one he helped establish a local church as far away as Sitiawan in Malaya, and soon afterwards the church in Shanghai that became the centre of his life's work. He lived what he preached: in those early days he is said to have kept only a third of his income for his own needs, giving a third to help others and spending the last third on spiritual books, and there were seasons in Shanghai when a little bread was all he had to eat in a day.

He held that there was only one true church in each city, and he laboured to see Chinese believers gathered on that ground rather than divided by imported labels. The work spread with remarkable speed. Beginning with a handful of members, in less than twenty years it grew to more than seven hundred assemblies and some seventy thousand believers across China, with daughter churches reaching into the Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia, and beyond — by 1949 the largest Protestant movement in the country.

All of this was carried on under the shadow of illness. From 1922 he was repeatedly struck down by tuberculosis; later came a chronic stomach disorder and a serious disease of the heart. In 1926, already weakened, Nee began his first major work, The Spiritual Man, writing much of it from a sickbed; it appeared in three volumes in 1928, the same year he convened his first Overcomer Conference in Shanghai. Recurring frailty dogged him for the rest of his life — he was healed of the heart disease, and said that his ministry was sustained not by physical strength but by resurrection life — and yet the stream of teaching never stopped. He was above all an expositor of the inner life: the crucifixion of the old self, the indwelling of Christ, the difference between the forgiveness of sins and deliverance from sin. His most enduring book, The Normal Christian Life, grew out of messages he delivered in English on a journey to Europe in 1938 and 1939 and distilled the whole of it into a single insistence: that the ordinary birthright of every Christian is not endless struggle but Christ Himself lived out from within.

God makes it quite clear in His Word that He only has one answer to every human need: His Son, Jesus Christ. In all His dealings with us He works by taking us out of the way and substituting Christ in our place. The Son of God died instead of us for our forgiveness: He lives instead of us for our deliverance.

— Watchman Nee, The Normal Christian Life

Nee taught that prayer was not a way of bending God to our wishes but of aligning ourselves with His will, and that this alignment was itself costly labour. He gathered much of this in the book Ochorus readers know as Let Us Pray, where he described prayer as the very track along which God chooses to run His work in the world.

Prayer is the rail for God's work. Indeed, prayer is to God's will as rails are to a train. Without any doubt, God is almighty and He works mightily, but He will not and cannot work if you and I do not labour together with Him in prayer.

— Watchman Nee, Let Us Pray

He was not a man who found prayer effortless or automatic. He called true prayer a real work, a self-denying work, the union of the believer's thoughts with the will of God.

True prayer is a real work. Praying according to God's will and praying only for His will is indeed a self-denying work.

— Watchman Nee, Let Us Pray

It was this understanding of prayer as costly partnership, rather than as a lever for personal comfort, that would carry him through the years no one could then foresee.

Marriage, arrest, and the long night

In 1934 Nee married Charity Chang, whose family had been friends of his for three generations; the decision had been the subject of much wrestling in prayer, for it drew public criticism at the time. The couple were never given children, and through Nee's frequent bouts of illness Charity cared for him with unwearying devotion. Together they gave themselves to the work through the turbulent 1930s and 1940s.

Those years held a humbling of another kind. In 1939, under family pressure and seeing in it a way to provide for co-workers suffering through the war, Nee took over his brother's struggling pharmaceutical firm, the China Biological and Chemical Laboratory, restructured it, and staffed it with members of the Shanghai church. But the elders were troubled that a minister of the gospel should be running a business, and in 1942 Nee laid down his public ministry; for a time the church in Shanghai ceased meeting altogether. He managed the factory quietly, even relocating to Chongqing in 1945, while continuing to give messages that would later be published as The Orthodoxy of the Church and his studies on the Song of Songs. In 1946 co-workers Peace Wang and Witness Lee began labouring to restore the church in Shanghai and Nee's ministry with it, and by April 1948 revival had swept the congregation and Nee stood before them again. He marked his restoration by giving the pharmaceutical factory itself to God for the work — an offering that moved many others to lay their own possessions on the altar. The Shanghai church swelled past a thousand members, and Nee acquired twelve bungalows at Kuliang, outside Fuzhou, as a training centre for his co-workers.

Then came the Communist victory of 1949 and, with it, a hardening hostility toward independent Christian movements that would not submit to state control. It was through the business that the authorities built their case. On 10 April 1952 he was arrested in Shanghai — accused of espionage and counter-revolutionary activity alongside charges of bribery, theft of state property, tax evasion, and moral irregularities. He was held for four years while an indictment running to 2,296 pages was assembled. The public trial of 1956 announced that he had been excommunicated by the Shanghai church and found him guilty on every count; he was sentenced to fifteen years of imprisonment with reform through labour. That same January a nationwide sweep took the co-workers and elders of the local churches: some died in labour camps, others served long sentences, congregations were shut, and the Shanghai assembly hall was in due course turned into a factory. When Nee's own sentence was complete in 1967 he was not released, for he was judged "unreformed." He would never again be free.

The suffering was not his alone. His wife Charity was arrested, released for failing health, then seized again during the Cultural Revolution, interrogated and beaten by Red Guards, paraded through the streets in a dunce's cap with a heavy board hung about her neck — and she refused to deny Christ. She was the only person permitted to visit him. Charity died in 1971, and Nee outlived her by barely a year.

"I maintain my joy"

Through twenty years of imprisonment, cut off from the movement he had raised up, in failing health from a diseased heart and a chronic stomach ailment, Nee's inner testimony did not break. In one of his last letters, written to his sister-in-law only thirty-eight days before his death, he set down four plain words: "I maintain my joy." He had written elsewhere that though his body was worn, the inward joy surpassed everything.

The regime and the state-controlled church spread word that Nee had renounced his faith in prison. After he died alone in a labour camp in Anhui on 30 May 1972, his surviving relatives came to gather his few belongings, and beneath his pillow they found a scrap of paper on which he had written his final confession: "Christ is the Son of God who died for the redemption of sinners and was resurrected after three days. This is the greatest truth in the universe. I die because of my belief in Christ. Watchman Nee." The slander was undone by his own hand. The prayer of a lifetime — that Christ would prove faithful in him to the very end — had been answered under the pillow of a prison cot.

He died on 30 May 1972, at sixty-eight, and was cremated two days later. He never saw the earthly vindication of his labour, for the churches he founded had been suppressed, his books banned, and his name slandered. Yet the seed did not die. His writings — more than forty volumes of devotional, sermonic, and theological work, most of them drawn from notes of his spoken messages — were carried out of China and translated into languages East and West, from Japanese, Korean, Indonesian, and Tagalog to English, French, and Spanish, and went on to shape hundreds of thousands of believers who never met him. Today assemblies tracing their spiritual descent to his ministry number in the thousands worldwide, and The Normal Christian Life remains one of the most widely read devotional works to come out of the modern Chinese church.

Watchman Nee was a real man, not a plaster saint: proud in his youth, sharp in controversy, dogged by illness, and by no means beyond the criticism of his contemporaries. But the note under the pillow says what the whole life was reaching toward. He had spent himself calling the church awake through the long night, and when his own night came he kept the watch he was named for — believing, to the last breath, in the Son of God.

fields.name: R. A. Torrey
fields.bio: Reuben Archer Torrey (1856–1928) was an American evangelist, pastor and teacher who came to faith at Yale on a night he had resolved to take his own life. D. L. Moody made him the first superintendent of the Moody Bible Institute and he pastored the Chicago Avenue Church, later serving as first dean of the Bible Institute of Los Angeles. With Charles Alexander he preached to millions across Australia, Asia and the British Isles between 1902 and 1905 — a tour he attributed to a Saturday-night prayer meeting. He wrote more than forty books, chiefly on prayer and the Holy Spirit.
fields.bio_html:
On a spring night in 1875, a Yale undergraduate sat alone in his room and decided to end his life. Reuben Archer Torrey was nineteen — born on 28 January 1856 into a wealthy Hoboken, New Jersey family — and by his own account thoroughly done with the faith he had been raised in. It was a faith with a face: his mother was a woman of deep and persistent prayer, who had asked God for years for her son's salvation and for his service, and who was not shy about reminding him what a life given to Christ might be. He had shrugged it off. He had come to New Haven at fifteen, and the years since had been given to the theatre, the racetrack, the card table, and a good deal of drink. He had also given them to argument: he was, he said later, "the leader of the new theology and destructive criticism wing of the seminary" — a young man who could dismantle a doctrine and enjoyed doing it.

What happened that night he told plainly, without embroidery. He had settled on suicide and had the means to hand. Instead he found himself praying — and in the dark of it remembering his mother, her faith, and the long years of her prayers for him. That memory became the turning point. In the praying he made a promise — that if God would deliver him, he would do whatever God asked. "I'll even preach!" he said, as though naming the last thing on earth he wanted to do. He rose from that prayer a different man, made his profession of faith publicly in the Yale chapel, and never went back on the bargain.

The apprenticeship of a doubter

Torrey took his degree and stayed on at the divinity school, finishing in 1878, and was ordained to the Congregational ministry the same year. He married Clara Smith in 1879 and went to a country pulpit in Garrettsville, Ohio. In 1882 he took his questions to their source, studying at Leipzig and Erlangen under Franz Delitzsch and Theodor Zahn — the very citadel of the higher criticism that had once been his stock-in-trade. He came home holding the opposite of what he had gone to confirm. Having examined the case against the Scriptures at first hand, he spent the rest of his life defending them, and he never lost the debater's habit of stating an argument fairly before answering it. Nor did he forget what honest doubt felt like from the inside. Having wrestled with unbelief to the edge of despair, he could speak to people caught in the same struggle without a trace of condescension — not as a man who had never doubted, but as one who had doubted and been answered.

Then came Minneapolis, and the making of the man. He pastored there and served as superintendent of the city's Congregational mission work, and in 1888 he did something that decided the shape of everything after: he gave up his salary in order to work among the poor, and threw his family's living entirely upon prayer. He had four children at the time.

From that day on, every mouthful came directly from my Heavenly Father — not a meal on our tables, not a coat that went on my back, not a dress on my wife's back, nor the clothing on the backs of the four children, that was not an answer to prayer.

— R. A. Torrey

Reading George Müller's autobiography had given Torrey his lifelong motto — pray through. In Minneapolis he tested it against the grocer's bill, and found it held. The lesson he drew was not that God is obliged to answer, but that most of us stop asking too soon.

Moody's man in Chicago

Years earlier, during an evangelistic campaign in New Haven, D. L. Moody had looked at the young Torrey and said, "Young man, you'd better get to work for God!" In 1889 Moody sent for him. Torrey was thirty-three when he became superintendent of the Chicago Evangelization Society — the school the world would come to know as the Moody Bible Institute — and he held the post until 1908. He built its curriculum around a simple conviction: that ordinary believers, grounded in Scripture and empowered by the Holy Spirit, could be trained for effective ministry. And, characteristically, he refused to let the school become an academy of talkers: students were sent out to street meetings, to hospitals, to jails, to the doors of the tenements. Book learning that produced no evangelists did not interest him. In 1894 he added the pastorate of the Chicago Avenue Church, now the Moody Church, and preached there for twelve years.

He was not an easy man to caricature. The scholar who had read Delitzsch in German ran a school for working people; the polished New Englander preached on Chicago street corners; the debater who could take an argument apart insisted that the church's real weakness was not intellectual at all.

Prayer is God's appointed way for obtaining things, and the great secret of all lack in our experience, in our life and in our work is neglect of prayer.

— R. A. Torrey, How to Pray

The Saturday-night room

In 1898 Torrey began a prayer meeting at the Institute on Saturday nights, from nine until ten. It was not a service and it was not advertised as an attraction; it was an hour of asking. As many as three hundred people came week after week, and what they asked for was a worldwide outpouring of the Spirit — not revival in Chicago merely, but revival in the earth.

Every Saturday from nine to ten, for years, three hundred people knelt in a room at the Bible Institute and prayed for a revival they could not organise, in countries most of them would never see.

Torrey prayed there for something else too, and more privately: that God would send him around the world preaching the gospel. He had no invitation, no committee, no money, and no reason to expect one. Within a week of laying that burden down in prayer, representatives of the churches of Australia — who knew nothing of it — wrote asking him to come.

He asked to be sent around the world. Within a week, and entirely unsolicited, the invitation came from Australia. Torrey told the story for the rest of his life, and never as a technique — only as evidence that the God who commands the asking intends the answering.

Around the world

From 1902 to 1905, with the song leader Charles M. Alexander beside him, Torrey preached in Australia and New Zealand, in China and Japan and India, and through the British Isles. The scale is hard to take in at this distance. At Bingley Hall in Birmingham in January 1904, some seven thousand people professed conversion in thirty days. The London campaign of 1905 ran from February to June: two hundred and two meetings, an aggregate attendance of more than 1,114,000, and over seventeen thousand who professed faith. Across the whole tour the figure usually given is around one hundred and two thousand conversions.

Torrey distrusted the arithmetic even as he reported it. He had written before he left that revival is not manufactured, and he refused to let the meetings be described as his achievement. The Saturday-night room in Chicago, he maintained, had done the work; the platform merely collected it.

When we learn to come to God with an intensity of desire that wrings the soul, then shall we know a power in prayer that most of us do not know now.

— R. A. Torrey, How to Pray

Los Angeles, and the long finishing

He came home to America for good in December 1905 and spent the next six years in campaigns across the country. In 1908 he founded the Montrose Bible Conference in Pennsylvania, a place of summer teaching that outlived him. In 1912 he went west to become the first dean of the Bible Institute of Los Angeles, and from 1915 the first pastor of the Church of the Open Door — holding both until 1924, and shaping a generation of students, among them Charles E. Fuller.

The public years had their private griefs. He and Clara lost children, and the sorrow of it cut deep — those who knew the family said the losses left their mark on them both. But grief did not embitter him. It enlarged his compassion for the suffering, and it drove him harder upon the God he had trusted for the grocer's bill in Minneapolis. The man who stood before crowds of thousands kept the disciplines of a much smaller room: significant time every day in prayer and in the Bible, in the settled conviction that a preacher's effectiveness depended not on his platform but on his personal fellowship with God.

These were also the years of The Fundamentals, the twelve-volume series he helped edit, which gave a name to a movement he would have described more simply as believing what the Bible says. He wrote constantly — more than forty books, and for thirty years a Sunday-school commentary read across the country. How to Bring Men to Christ became a plain, practical handbook for ordinary believers who wanted to lead someone to faith, for he held that sharing the gospel was every Christian's work and not a specialist's. But the titles that lasted are the ones about prayer and about the Holy Spirit, because those were the subjects on which he was not merely instructing others.

The Spirit and the ordinary Christian

Of everything Torrey taught, the doctrine he pressed hardest was that the Holy Spirit is a Person to be known and not a force to be used. He wrote about it at length and returned to it in every campaign: that the Spirit convicts, regenerates, indwells, and — this was the emphasis his contemporaries argued about — that there is an enduement of power for service which the believer may and should definitely seek and definitely receive. He was careful about what he was not saying. It was not a second salvation, and it was not a badge of superior sanctity. It was equipment for work, offered to ordinary Christians, and in his view the reason so many of them laboured without visible fruit was simply that they had never asked for it — that they lived defeated because they leaned on their own strength instead of trusting the power of God.

He argued the point the way he argued everything, by piling up texts and daring the reader to check them. But the force of it came from somewhere else. A man who had renounced his salary and watched the meals arrive, who had asked to be sent around the world and been sent, was not speculating about the availability of God. He was reporting.

He resigned his Los Angeles posts in 1924 to return to evangelism, still travelling, still preaching, and lectured again at Moody in 1927. He died at his home in Asheville, North Carolina, on 26 October 1928, at seventy-two, and was buried on the grounds of the Montrose conference he had founded. Will Houghton, who knew him, put the epitaph better than any summary of the campaigns could: those who knew Dr. Torrey more intimately, he said, knew him as a man of regular and uninterrupted prayer.

It is worth remembering how the whole of it began — not in a pulpit or a lecture hall, but in a room at Yale where a young agnostic who had decided to die remembered his mother's prayers and found himself praying instead, and promised God he would go wherever he was sent. He was sent a very long way.

fields.name: Gareth Evans
fields.bio: Gareth Evans, born in 1938 in Merthyr Tydfil, is an itinerant pastor, teacher, and author. He studied physics, taught globally, authored devotionals, and now ministers to the hurting church through his website. Gareth, married to Anne, has three daughters, eight grand children, and fourteen great-grand children. His teachings emphasize practical faith and biblical wisdom. With a unique blend of scientific background and spiritual insight, Evans brings clarity to complex theological concepts.
fields.bio_html:
Gareth Evans was born in 1938 in Merthyr Tydfil, among the coal valleys of South Wales, and it is hard to think of a life that has ranged farther from that starting point. Physics teacher and pastor, chaplain on a mercy ship off West Africa and Bible teacher on five continents, he has spent more than six decades walking out a single conviction — that the Lord who saved a Welsh schoolboy also holds every one of his tomorrows. He describes himself simply as a worshipper, and his life, in his own telling, as a series of stepping stones laid down by God one at a time.

I see so many stations or ‘stepping stones’ in my life that have led on to deeper experiences with the Lord, and, without which, I would not have the story I want to relate. Each stepping stone led on to the next, each one being a direct intervention of the Lord in my plans.

— Gareth Evans

A Childhood in the Welsh Valleys

Gareth was born to Cyril Evans, an RAF man of the Second World War remembered for his singing voice and his love of cricket, and Ethel Evans, a gifted pianist who gave herself to the making of a home. Music, sport, and story ran in the family, as they run through Wales itself — a land famous for its eloquent orators and impassioned preachers. At eight, Gareth moved to his grandfather's home in Bonvilston, near Cardiff, and at eleven he entered Cowbridge Grammar School, the second oldest school in Wales, a community of some three hundred boys. There the boy who loved cycling, soccer, storytelling, and music also proved to have an exceptional head for mathematics. He shared those years with a younger sister, Barbara, who today lives in Australia.

Then, when Gareth was thirteen, sorrow entered the house: his mother died of a prolapsed heart, leaving a void in a close-knit family. His father, who never remarried, admirably shouldered the burden of providing for his children, and entrusted his son with responsibilities beyond his years. Grief pressed the boy into an early independence — and, quietly, into the shape of the man to come: an introvert, as he discovered, yet one with a surprising gift for meaningful conversation with all kinds of people.

“What Will You Do with the Lord Jesus Christ?”

Gareth grew up in an Anglican household, at home with the Christian ethos but not yet possessed by it. The turning came at sixteen, through the Friday-night youth meetings of Betty Bishop, a devout Christian and founder of a children's ministry — lively evenings of choruses, Bible quizzes, and visiting speakers. One night Ms. Bishop put a question to him directly: “Tell me Gareth, what will you do with the Lord Jesus Christ?” For five weeks he evaded it, all the while watching the authentic devotion of the young people around him and feeling the living presence of Christ pressing in. Then a friend named David brought news that a young preacher called Austin — a familiar face from their school days — was to speak at a nearby chapel. Twenty young people went, Gareth among them. Afterwards Austin fixed him with a determined gaze and asked the very question he had been running from: “Tell me Gareth, what will you do with the Lord Jesus Christ?”

That night Gareth knelt in prayer for the first time since his mother's death. Opening his heart to Jesus, he asked forgiveness and invited Christ into his life — and the answer came unmistakably. During a Thursday morning school assembly soon after, he was flooded with the assurance of forgiveness and the presence of the Holy Spirit.

The Spirit of God came upon me and at that moment I knew that Jesus loved me, and I was a child of God. At that moment something was birthed within me.

— Gareth Evans

The new faith became the bedrock of his identity, and he embraced it boldly among friends and at school. Sunday school under Mr. Collins, the local postmaster, laid his foundations; his first pastor, Wynne Lewis — a man with, as Gareth put it, “a fire burning in his belly” — ignited his zeal; and the Elim church at Bridgend, with its young adults' group, the Elim Crusaders, grounded him in the Word. “I was blessed by having some good teachers who loved the Lord and His Word,” he recalls. “I was beginning to discover the riches of our inheritance in Christ and discovered the fruit of His Spirit.” While at university he lodged in the home of Donald Evans, who went from Bible college and pastoral ministry to become one of the world's leading authorities in medical ethics — living proof that faith and rigorous scholarship could walk together. And it was Donald's father, Mr. Aubrey Evans of Swansea, who gave Gareth the counsel that has stayed with him ever since: that those who follow afar off can still see the Lord, but those who go one step ahead of the Light of the World can no longer see Him, and find themselves walking in their own shadow. From that word came the motto of his life: “I will walk with Jesus, not ahead of Him nor lag behind.”

The Scientist in the Classroom

From Cowbridge Grammar School, where he took pure mathematics, applied mathematics, and physics at Advanced Level, Gareth went up to the University of Swansea to read for an Honours degree in Physics, adding a Diploma of Education. Swansea gave him something better than a degree: there he met Anne, a dedicated young secretary whose mother belonged to the Rees Howells Prayer Band, and whose profound Christian character he came to cherish. They were engaged on the day of his graduation and married a year later, on 15 July 1961. Anne's father, a dedicated Norwegian minister of the Gospel, became another wellspring in Gareth's life; the two men shared a love for the devotional writings of A. W. Tozer and Watchman Nee that kept the fire of the Spirit burning.

For the next two decades Gareth's pulpit was a classroom, and the disciplines of the laboratory — precision, patience, a refusal to rest in vague answers — would later lend his Bible teaching its characteristic clarity. He began at Kenfig Comprehensive School, teaching physics to Advanced Level. “I never understood how I obtained that position,” he says. “It must have been another of the Lord's appointments because it was an opportunity I never sought.” In his third year came an invitation to the Windsor Boys School in Germany, a school of more than five hundred children of military personnel — making Gareth, remarkably, the youngest teacher ever hired by the Ministry of Defence, despite lacking the National Service and five years' experience such posts normally required. “God can even override army regulations!” he laughs. Postings followed to Hamm in West Germany and then to Hong Kong with the British Army education service; and everywhere he taught, he also witnessed, founding Christian Unions or similar gatherings in each school. In Hong Kong he partnered with Jackie Pullinger in her work among drug addicts, venturing into the walled city of Kowloon to join a Bible class in ‘the dragon's den’; he and Anne visited a countryside orphanage each month to tell the children about Jesus; he led weekly Bible studies hosted by the veteran missionary John Bechtel for up to thirty British soldiers, including Nepalese Gurkhas; and he even joined a Chinese choir, daring solo parts in an Easter cantata sung in Cantonese.

Back in Wales in 1969, Gareth became Head of Physics at Ogmore Grammar School, led its Christian union, and conducted school assemblies, while serving on a select team of physics teachers at Cardiff University devising a new advanced-level curriculum. At home, Anne started a teenagers' fellowship that spread across churches throughout the Bridgend area; from it grew a youth newspaper, a thirty-voice choir singing Easter and Christmas cantatas in halls, chapels, and prisons, summer camps, weekend youth nights, community outreaches, and YMCA programmes. In August 1975 the family emigrated to Canada, where Gareth headed the physics department at Toronto French School and then the science department at the Toronto Hebrew Academy — an Orthodox Jewish school where he coached the soccer team to its first winning season and shared the Gospel with students and the senior Rabbi alike.

A Teacher Turned Shepherd

The Hebrew Academy proved the last stepping stone of his teaching career. When the pastor of his church resigned, Gareth was invited to speak at the farewell, and two former pastors told him plainly that he belonged in ministry. After prayer, and with Anne's wholehearted support, he left teaching to become a pastor with the Christian and Missionary Alliance. At Hazelglen Fellowship in Kitchener, Ontario, he shepherded the congregation, led the youth, served as chaplain to Malaysian Christian students at a local university, conducted seminars, and ran summer camps in Toronto. In March 1983 came an invitation to Vancouver Island, and by September 1984 he was installed as pastor of Victoria Alliance Church, where he served for eight years — and where he and Anne have made their home ever since. All of it, be it noted, without a day at theological college: the Lord had trained His teacher in classrooms, choir lofts, and army bases instead.

Out onto the Sea

In September 1990 an unforeseen turn arrived: a sudden illness that placed Gareth in the care of a sleep clinic at the University of British Columbia and forced him from the rhythm of ministry for two years. Undeterred, he prescribed himself exercise and voracious reading to keep spirit and mind alive — and then the telephone rang again. He was invited to serve aboard the Mercy Ship M/V Anastasis, working in West Africa. Not yet fully restored, Gareth and Anne sailed anyway, joining the ship at Rotterdam in May 1991 as chaplains. With their fellow missionaries they became builders of hope — schools, hospital wings, clinics, freshwater sources, hygienic latrines raised against deadly disease — but Gareth's deepest joy lay in the souls they touched. He ministered to missionaries and pastors in weekly seminars and conferences, instructed over 150 church leaders in Sierra Leone, carried his teaching into French-speaking Guinea, Côte d'Ivoire, and Senegal, and taught a week-long pastors' conference in Nigeria.

To the Ends of the Earth

When Gareth and Anne left the Anastasis at the end of 1994, they did not leave the itinerant life it had opened. January 1995 found Gareth leading the summer school at Capernwray Bible School in Moss Vale, near Sydney, Australia, its students drawn from around the world. Invitations multiplied, many from YWAM leaders eager for his help with their Discipleship Training Schools: Mexico in February 1996, with a two-day pastors' conference and a marriage seminar besides; YWAM Fortaleza in north-eastern Brazil that August, and again in 1997 and 1998; a men's retreat with some seventy men from a Baptist church in Kelowna; Baja California, the UK, India, Nepal, and Brazil in 1998; a year of speaking across the churches of Victoria in 1999. The new millennium brought an invitation from Ade Ajala to a new ministry in Nigeria, a second trip to India in 2001 — to Chennai in the south — and, in 2002, ministry at home and abroad spanning Haiti, Manitoba, the UK, Portland, Fortaleza, and Australia. Looking back, he can trace the decades like chapters: Gurkha soldiers in Hong Kong in the sixties, the young people of Bridgend in the seventies, the Jewish Academy in Toronto in the eighties, pastors' conferences in West Africa in the nineties. Three times in that long walk, he recalls, he has audibly heard the Holy Spirit speak to him.

In September 2003 trial visited again, as a routine hiatus hernia operation left him in prolonged weakness. Once more he refused to waste the wilderness.

Through more than a year of recovery, until the close of 2004, Gareth kept to his study — reading deeply, writing poetry, and deliberately deepening his prayer life, turning a season of enforced stillness into a season of communion.

The Storyteller at His Desk

Out of all that teaching came his books. Gareth wears the mantle of a storyteller, and his writing is unhurried, plain, and pastoral, aimed at the hurting church — believers worn down by suffering or disappointment who need to be reminded that God holds their tomorrows. Titles such as He Holds My Tomorrows, The Key in My Hand, Stepping Stones, Soar Like the Eagle, and Feasting at the Table lead the reader slowly through Scripture, pairing careful exposition with the encouragement of a man who has pastored real congregations through real trouble.

Some would even title Hebrews 11 as “Heroes of Faith.” I see no heroes there.

— Gareth Evans, He Holds My Tomorrows

That single sentence opens a window onto his whole approach. For Gareth the great examples of faith are not spiritual giants to be admired from a safe distance but ordinary, flawed people who simply took God at His word — which means theirs is a faith the reader can actually share. It is the note he returns to again and again: faith is practical, faith is for the weak as much as the strong, and it is walked out one obedient step at a time.

Family remains a cornerstone of it all. The Lord blessed Gareth and Anne with three daughters — Corinne, born in Wales, and Andrea and Lynette, born in Hamm, West Germany — and in time with eight grandchildren and fourteen great-grandchildren, alongside the countless children and young people they have parented in the faith. Today, no longer tied to a single pulpit, Gareth ministers largely through his website, where his devotionals, books, and poems gather the wisdom of an expansive journey for the scattered and the isolated. He continues to carry a particular burden for the young — to disciple and equip them to maturity in Christ — and to walk, still, by the motto given him long ago in Swansea: not ahead of Jesus, not lagging behind, but with Him, one stepping stone at a time.

fields.name: Hannah Whitall Smith
fields.bio: Hannah Whitall Smith, born in 1832 in Philadelphia, was a prominent Quaker speaker and writer during the Holiness movement. Her influential book "The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life" became a classic of Christian devotional literature. Despite personal tragedies, she maintained a vibrant faith that influenced generations of believers until her death in 1911. Her teachings emphasized the victorious Christian life through faith. Smith's message of consecration revolutionized Christian thinking, presenting sanctification as resting in Christ's completed work.
fields.bio_html:
Hannah Whitall Smith spent her life insisting on one plain thing: that God is good, and that God is enough. She wrote it in seventy years of diaries, argued it across two continents, and clung to it through griefs that would have hardened a less generous heart. To hundreds of thousands of readers she remains the quiet Quaker voice behind The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life, a woman who taught that the burden-bearing labour of holiness belongs to God, and that ours is only to trust Him and let go.

She was born Hannah Tatum Whitall on 7 February 1832 in Philadelphia, into a prominent and devout Quaker family. Her father, John Mickle Whitall, and her mother, Mary Tatum Whitall, raised her a "birthright" Friend within the evangelical Gurneyite tradition, and the shaping was total. "Every word, thought, and action of our lives was steeped in Quakerism," she remembered. "Never for a single moment did we escape from it." She did not resent it; looking back at seventy she gave daily thanks for "such a righteous and ennobling influence." Nor was it a faith of the parlour only. The Whitall home was Quaker conscience in action: the family threw itself into the reform causes of the day, opposing slavery and supporting the movements for social betterment, and through her father's business and reform circles a stream of influential thinkers and activists passed through the house — company that encouraged in Hannah an independence of thought she never lost, and a lifelong conviction that genuine Christianity must transform both personal character and social life. By her own testimony the childhood was radiantly happy — she called it "one fairy scene of sunshine and of flowers" — and yet, tellingly, even as a girl of seventeen she wondered aloud in her diary why no affliction ever came "to wean me from the joys of this life."

Like most women of her generation, Hannah never followed a formal academic path — the universities of her day were largely closed to women — but she received at home the strong intellectual and moral education that well-taught Quaker families prized. It was, above all, a spiritual and reflective schooling: the Quaker emphasis on meditation and attentiveness to the "Inner Light," the guidance of God within, formed in her a lifelong habit of contemplation and thoughtful writing. She would never hold a degree, yet many readers later remarked that her ability to explain profound spiritual truths in simple language was one of the chief reasons her books became so widely loved. Her true education came not through institutions but through life experience, Scripture study, and spiritual struggle.

The Long Search

Smith's awakening came not through fear of sin but through wonder. Around sixteen and a half she caught, in her reading, a glimpse of the sheer magnificence of God, and "then and there, my search began." It was, by her own frank account, "a blind, ignorant search." Reared to look only for "the light within," she turned relentlessly inward and found there nothing but wrestling. Her early religious diary, she confessed, "is one long record of wrestlings and agonies, with scarcely a ray of light." The candour is characteristic: she refused ever to gild her own experience.

As a young woman she wrote in her diary of the one thing she could not do for herself: "I know not how to pray. Oh, what shall I do? Where shall I go? … It is said, 'Ask, and ye shall receive.' … But I cannot become really righteous until I repent, and I cannot repent." It was a cry from the very edge of her own strength — the honest prayer of someone who has discovered she cannot save herself.

In 1851, at nineteen, she married Robert Pearsall Smith, a businessman from another notable Quaker family who would later become an evangelist in his own right. Marriage widened her world and, mercifully, drew her out of the "morbid self-introspection" that had made religion a misery. The couple settled near Philadelphia and later moved through New Jersey, and in the 1850s both came into a warmer evangelical faith. But the decisive turn was still to come.

The Secret Discovered

"It was in 1865," she wrote, "that the fourth, and by far the most captivating, epoch of my spiritual journey dawned upon my soul." She had been a Christian for nine happy years, yet she remained, by her own reckoning, "continually disappointed in myself." She knew God to be trustworthy but found her own inner life "full of failure — not so much outward sin, but inward sins: coldness, spiritual deadness, lack of Christian love." What she discovered, and would spend the rest of her life proclaiming, was that deliverance from sin's power — not merely its penalty — was God's work to accomplish in those who surrendered to Him. She reduced the whole matter to four words: "Not I, but Christ."

In brief, I would say that man's part is to trust and God's part is to work.

— Hannah Whitall Smith

This became the heart of The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life, published in 1875. She called it a "secret," she explained, only because it had so long been hidden from her — "not a secret because God hid it, but because I had not yet discovered it." Its most famous image is the wagon and the burden: the traveller who accepts a ride but keeps the heavy load on his own shoulders, "for I could not think of letting you carry my burden too." The Christian life, she taught, means at last laying the whole weight down.

The greatest burden we have to carry in life is self. The most difficult thing we have to manage is self.

— Hannah Whitall Smith

The little book struck a nerve across the English-speaking Protestant world; it sold more than two million copies in her lifetime, was translated into numerous languages, and has never gone out of print. Her public ministry had begun quietly — in personal conversations and small gatherings where she shared her experience of renewal — but the message of trust and surrender answered so exactly the discouragement and sense of spiritual failure that so many Christians carried that interest grew rapidly. In 1873 and 1874 the Smiths crossed to England, where Hannah's calm, reasoned Bible readings won her wide affection — she was dubbed the "angel of the churches" — and their meetings, including the influential conferences at Broadlands hosted by Lord and Lady Mount Temple, helped give rise in 1875 to the Keswick Convention. For a season the Smiths were the most prominent figures of the interdenominational Higher Life movement, and Hannah became one of its most recognisable voices, especially among women. Her manner on the platform was warm, practical, and deeply pastoral: rather than mounting complex theological arguments, she spoke of the everyday struggles of the Christian life and of how believers could find peace through trust in God.

Trials Named Honestly

Then came the collapse. In 1875 Robert Pearsall Smith's public ministry ended abruptly amid accusations of misconduct, and the movement that had carried them recoiled from the scandal. Over the following years Robert drifted from the faith they had shared into agnosticism, and Hannah bore the private grief of a marriage that never recovered its early joy. She was also a bereaved mother many times over: of her seven children, four died in youth, and she buried them across the span of her middle years. The sorrows were compounded later, when the three children who survived to adulthood — Mary, Logan, and Alys — grew away from the Christian faith she had given everything to commend. Mary and Logan each became notable literary figures in their own right; Alys married the philosopher Bertrand Russell, perhaps the most famous unbeliever of the age.

Smith met these griefs not with denial but with the very theology she preached. She refused to build faith on feeling. "You may feel good or you may feel bad," she wrote, "but neither the good feeling nor the bad feeling affects the real thing... If God loves you, it is of no account, as far as the fact goes, whether you feel that He loves you or do not feel it." She loved to quote Luther, who, when the devil demanded whether he felt himself a child of God, answered: "No, I do not feel it at all, but I know it. Get thee behind me, Satan." That distinction — between the fact of God's love and one's fluctuating sense of it — was the ground she stood on when the ground shook.

The fruit of her long, agonized search was a settled and answered peace. "After I had learned that the facts of religion were far more important than my feelings about these facts," she wrote, "and had consequently given up looking at my feelings, and sought only to discover the facts, I became always happy in my religious life." The girl who once wept that she did not know how to pray came, through surrender, into a rest she never afterward lost — the very "secret of a happy life" she spent her remaining decades pressing upon others.

The God of All Comfort

Out of these years came her mature conviction: that the God she had once, like so many, imagined as "one of the most selfish, self-absorbed beings in the universe" was in truth "exactly the opposite." Her spiritual autobiography, The Unselfishness of God and How I Discovered It (1903), traces her life as a sequence of religious "epochs," and its whole burden is summed up in a sentence she found on the flyleaf of her Bible: "This generation has rediscovered the unselfishness of God." In The God of All Comfort (1906) she pressed the same tender vision of a Father whose love, she believed, must exceed even a mother's. Alongside her writing she gave herself to reform: she helped found the Woman's Christian Temperance Union in 1874, served as superintendent of its Evangelistic Department, championed women's right to public religious voice, and spoke for the suffrage cause.

In her last years arthritis confined her to a wheelchair and to considerable pain, yet her outlook only brightened. Old age, she wrote, need not be "a sad and wearisome time"; with "our beautiful, unselfish God, behind it all, old age becomes a delightful resting-place." Knowing "that God is, and that God is enough," she said, made "death a delicious prospect for the future."

Secure in the knowledge that God is, and that He is enough, I find old age delightful in the present, and death a delicious prospect for the future.

— Hannah Whitall Smith, The Unselfishness of God

Hannah Whitall Smith died in England on 1 May 1911, at the age of seventy-nine. She had named her sorrows plainly — a wounded marriage, four small graves, children who walked away from her faith — and had not been defeated by any of them. Her influence can still be traced in the many devotional writers who echo her themes of rest, trust, and abiding in Christ; more than a century after her death, her message remains piercingly relevant in a world where believers still struggle with anxiety, spiritual performance, and uncertainty. Her legacy is not a system but a single, steadying conviction, handed down through books still read a century later: that the burden of our own transformation was never ours to carry, that man's part is only to trust and God's part is to work, and that the God who does the work is unfailingly, unselfishly good.

fields.name: Hannah Buyinza
fields.bio: Hannah Buyinza is a contemporary contributor to the Ochorus library. She is the author of Prayer – The Pulse of Life, a devotional reflection on the place of prayer in the everyday Christian life.

fields.name: Charles H. Spurgeon
fields.bio: Charles Haddon Spurgeon, born in 1834 in Kelvedon, Essex, England, became known as the "Prince of Preachers." Converted at age 15, he began preaching at 16 and by age 20 became pastor of London's New Park Street Chapel, later the Metropolitan Tabernacle. Spurgeon authored over 3,500 sermons, numerous books, and founded a pastors' college, orphanage, and various Christian ministries. Despite battling depression and illness, he maintained a prolific ministry until his death in 1892. His biblical expository preaching and literary works continue to influence Christians worldwide.
fields.bio_html:
Charles Haddon Spurgeon has been called the “Prince of Preachers,” and for once the title is not an exaggeration. For nearly forty years he stood before congregations of five and six thousand in the heart of London, without a microphone, and held them still with the plain preaching of Christ crucified. His sermons were taken down in shorthand, printed every week, and carried by the shipload to every continent; by the end of his life he had preached to perhaps ten million people and published more words than any other Christian author in the English language. Yet the man behind the fame was often a suffering, praying, tender-hearted pastor who insisted that the real power of his ministry was not his own voice at all, but the people on their knees beneath the pulpit.

A Boy in the Snow

He was born on 19 June 1834 in Kelvedon, Essex, into a family already rich in gospel ministry — both his father, John Spurgeon, and his grandfather, James Spurgeon, were Congregational preachers who faithfully served rural England. Because his father’s ministry often kept him from home, much of the boy’s childhood was spent in his grandfather’s manse at Stambourne, a house filled with old Puritan books. There the child spent countless hours with John Bunyan, Richard Baxter, John Owen, and Thomas Watson, and those writers shaped his mind for life. He grew up knowing the doctrines of grace by heart. What he did not yet know was the Saviour himself. For months, as a teenager, he was under deep conviction of sin, longing to know that he was truly forgiven and finding no peace.

The turning point came on a snowy Sunday morning, 6 January 1850, when he was fifteen. A blizzard drove him off his intended road and into a tiny Primitive Methodist chapel in Artillery Street, Colchester. The appointed preacher never arrived through the snow, so a thin, unlettered layman — a shoemaker or tailor by trade — climbed into the pulpit with nothing to say but his single text: “Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 45:22). Fixing his eyes on the miserable-looking boy under the gallery, he cried out, “Young man, look to Jesus Christ. Look! Look! Look!” In that instant Spurgeon looked, and was saved.

There and then the cloud was gone, the darkness had rolled away, and that moment I saw the sun.

— Charles Spurgeon, on his conversion

He was baptized that spring in the river Lark, having become, by his own glad conviction, a Baptist. The transformation was immediate and total: the boy who had wrestled so long in the dark now could not keep silent about the light, and from that day he burned to proclaim the message that had saved him — that salvation comes not through human striving but through faith in Jesus Christ alone.

The Boy Preacher

It is one of the wonders of his story that this future prince of the Victorian pulpit never attended university or theological seminary. His schooling was modest — local schools in Essex and a season at Newmarket — while the celebrated clergy of his day were polished at Oxford and Cambridge. What Spurgeon possessed instead was an extraordinary memory, an insatiable appetite for books, and the Puritan library of his boyhood; by his teens he had devoured more theology, history, and literature than many ordained men. Personal study, spiritual discipline, and a rare gift for putting deep truth into vivid, practical language did the rest.

Within months of his conversion he was teaching, distributing tracts, and — by the age of sixteen — preaching in the village churches around Cambridge. Still in his teens he became pastor of the little chapel at Waterbeach, where his fervent preaching soon filled the building and the congregation grew rapidly. His gifts could not stay hidden long. In 1854, at just nineteen years old, he was called to the historic but declining New Park Street Chapel in London. The congregation that met to hear the untried country boy was small; within weeks it could not hold the crowds. They enlarged the building, then hired Exeter Hall, then the vast Surrey Gardens Music Hall, and still thousands were turned away. London had never seen anything like it: a teenager preaching old-fashioned Calvinistic doctrine to overflowing multitudes, in language a servant girl could follow and a scholar could not fault.

In 1856, amid the whirlwind, he married Susannah, whose love and steady support would anchor him for the rest of his life. The couple had twin sons, Thomas and Charles junior, and both would one day follow their father into Christian ministry.

Fire and Darkness

The fame brought bitter trials. On the evening of 19 October 1856, as Spurgeon led some ten thousand people in prayer at the Surrey Gardens Music Hall, malicious troublemakers shouted “Fire! The galleries are giving way!” There was no fire, but in the stampede for the doors seven people were crushed to death and many more injured. Spurgeon, only twenty-two, was carried from the pulpit “more dead than alive” and sank into a grief so heavy it nearly ended his ministry. For the rest of his life he battled recurring depression, and he never pretended otherwise.

That honesty became one of his great gifts to the church. He spoke openly of the “causeless depression” that would fall on him, and he comforted thousands of fellow sufferers by refusing to hide his own. His theology of suffering was not glib; it was hammered out in the furnace. He came to believe that his afflictions — the disaster, the slander, the gout that later racked his body — were the very things that drove him again and again to cling to Christ, and made his preaching tender toward the broken.

The Powerhouse

In 1861 the congregation moved into the newly built Metropolitan Tabernacle at Newington, seating around five thousand, where Spurgeon would preach for the next thirty years. Visitors came from around the world to study his methods, expecting to find the secret in his oratory. Spurgeon knew better. He would take them down to the basement before a service and open a door on several hundred members of his church, kneeling and pleading with God for the preaching about to begin.

“Would you like to see the powerhouse of this church?” Spurgeon would ask visitors — and lead them not to the pulpit but to the basement prayer meeting, where hundreds interceded before every service. He called that room the boiler-house of the Tabernacle, and never doubted it was the true engine of all he did.

He believed prayer to be real work with real results, and he pressed his people to labour at it with all their strength.

Prayer pulls the rope below, and the great bell rings above in the ears of God. Some scarcely stir the bell, for they pray so languidly; others give but an occasional pluck at the rope; but he who wins with heaven is the man who grasps the rope boldly and pulls continuously with all his might.

— Charles Spurgeon

So bound was he to the prayers of his congregation that he told them plainly he could not go on without them.

May God help me, if you cease to pray for me! Let me know the day, and I must cease to preach.

— Charles Spurgeon

Faith That Builds

Spurgeon’s ministry was never confined to the pulpit. In 1856 he founded the Pastors’ College to train preachers who, like himself, lacked the money for a formal education, personally teaching and supporting scores of men who went out to plant churches. He launched a Colportage Association to carry Christian books to the poor, published the monthly magazine The Sword and the Trowel, and gave himself away in a hundred works of mercy. He was convinced that the gospel must transform both souls and society, and he refused to preach a grace he would not practise.

The Stockwell Orphanage was born of exactly this praying, believing spirit. Grieved by the plight of fatherless children, Spurgeon had asked God to let him help them — and the answer came in a way he could never have engineered.

A widow named Anne Hillyard, moved by Spurgeon’s appeal, offered him £20,000 — a fortune — to build a home for orphan boys. When a financial panic meant her railway shares could not at first be turned into cash, Spurgeon prayed on, and gift after gift arrived from others until the land was bought and the houses raised. The orphanage opened in 1867, cared for hundreds of children, and continues its work to this day.

He would not separate the preaching of grace from the doing of it. The same faith that filled the Tabernacle built the college, the orphanage, and the almshouses, and it did so, again and again, in answer to prayer.

The Down Grade

Spurgeon’s last great battle was for the truth of Scripture itself. He had always held the Bible to be the inspired Word of God and the final authority for faith and life, and every sermon he preached was rooted in it. So in 1887, alarmed by a drift toward doubt about the Bible, the atonement, and the reality of judgment among some Baptist ministers, he sounded the alarm in a series of articles known as the “Down-Grade” controversy. Rather than compromise, he withdrew from the Baptist Union, which then formally censured him. The conflict cost him friendships and, many believed, hastened his decline. But he counted the authority of God’s Word worth any price, and he would not be moved.

Home

His body, worn by gout, rheumatism, and Bright’s disease, gave way under the strain of a lifetime’s labour. Nursed faithfully by his beloved Susannah — herself an invalid, who from her sickroom ran a Book Fund that placed thousands of theological volumes into the hands of pastors too poor to buy them — he sought relief in the milder air of Menton, on the French Riviera. There, on 31 January 1892, at the age of fifty-seven, he died. London mourned as for a prince; tens of thousands filed past his coffin, and his open Bible lay upon it.

He left behind more than three thousand five hundred published sermons — still the largest body of work by any Christian author — along with beloved books like Morning and Evening, The Treasury of David, All of Grace, and Lectures to My Students. More than a century later they are read as eagerly as ever, translated into scores of languages, because the man who wrote them never preached himself. He preached Christ, and he did it on his knees. The Prince of Preachers would have wanted it remembered that his crown was borrowed, and that the secret of the powerhouse was open to anyone who would take hold of the rope and pull.

fields.name: William Booth
fields.bio: William Booth, born in 1829 in Nottingham, England, was the founder of The Salvation Army. Originally a Methodist minister, he felt called to serve the urban poor and began his ministry in London's East End. In 1865, he established the Christian Mission, which later became The Salvation Army in 1878. Booth and his wife Catherine pioneered innovative approaches to evangelism and social welfare, establishing shelters, rehabilitation centers, and soup kitchens.
fields.bio_html:
William Booth was born on 10 April 1829 in Sneinton, on the edge of Nottingham, the second child of Samuel Booth, a nailmaker and builder, and Mary Moss. His father had once known modest prosperity, but the trade collapsed around him, and the boy grew up watching a household slide steadily into want. When William was thirteen, his father—unable to keep him in school—apprenticed him to a pawnbroker. Samuel Booth died soon after, in September 1842, and the teenaged William spent his days behind a counter where the poor came to trade the last of what they owned for a few shillings. He learned early, and never forgot, what poverty does to a person. The pawnshop was, in its way, his first mission field.

Conversion and Call

Two years into that apprenticeship, in 1844, Booth was converted. He had been attending Wesley Chapel, and one night, walking home through the Nottingham streets from a meeting, he came to a settled conviction that he could no longer belong half to God and half to himself. By his own account, the turning point was a restitution: he had gained a small dishonest advantage in a boyhood transaction, and he could not rest until he had made it right. Out of that reckoning came a resolve he carried for the rest of his life—that God should have not part of him but the whole.

God shall have all there is of William Booth.

— William Booth, at his conversion, aged fifteen

That single sentence became the seed of everything that followed. Booth was fifteen years old and had almost nothing to give but himself; he gave that entirely. The fire was fanned soon afterward when the American Methodist evangelist James Caughey came to Nottingham. Caughey's revival meetings left a profound mark on the young convert, awakening in him a burden for the salvation of souls that he would later call the great burden of his life. Booth began at once to act on it. With a band of young believers he went through the poor neighbourhoods distributing tracts and inviting people to revival meetings, and he soon began to preach.
