In 1873 he accepted the pulpit of Chestnut Street Presbyterian Church in Louisville, Kentucky. There, in a city still wounded and divided by the Civil War, he persuaded rival congregations into united evangelistic campaigns and learned to preach for a verdict. And there a deeper crisis found him: outwardly successful and inwardly exhausted by his own striving, he read of the higher Christian life and yielded himself wholly to Christ — discovering, as he later put it, that sanctification is not an attainment to be struggled toward but an indwelling Person to be received.

New York and the Neglected Masses

In 1879 Simpson came to Thirteenth Street Presbyterian Church in New York City. He was soon burdened beyond bearing by the crowds outside his church’s doors — Italian immigrants, dock workers, the unchurched poor — who could never feel at home among rented pews and formal society. When it became plain that his congregation did not share the burden, he resigned, in November 1881, with no salary, no society behind him, and a wife and six children to feed. Margaret Simpson later confessed she thought the decision madness; she came to share the work with her whole heart. Beginning with a handful of followers in a rented hall, he formed an independent Gospel Tabernacle where every seat was free and every class of person welcome.

Healed and Wholly His

Behind that resignation lay another transaction. Simpson had been sickly for years — a heart condition so serious that physicians gave him little hope of continued labour. In the summer of 1881, at Old Orchard Beach in Maine, he heard the scriptures opened on Christ’s ministry to the body, and alone among the pines he made a solemn covenant: he took the Lord Jesus as his healer, promised to use whatever strength was given for God alone, and asked never to be released from the bargain. The chronic trouble lifted; the man whom doctors had written off carried one of the heaviest workloads in American church history for nearly forty more years. From this grew his best-known formulation, the Fourfold Gospel: Jesus Christ our Saviour, Sanctifier, Healer, and Coming King.

Friday afternoons at the Gospel Tabernacle were given to a meeting for healing — but those who came looking for a wonder-worker were gently redirected. Simpson would pray with the sick only after pointing them past the gift to the Giver; the meetings were, before anything else, hours of worship and waiting on God.

The Alliance

Simpson could never see a need without founding something to meet it. In 1883 he opened the Missionary Training Institute — the first Bible college in North America, later settled at Nyack on the Hudson — to prepare ordinary, consecrated men and women for the fields no one else would fill: not scholars only, but clerks and carpenters and widows who had heard the call of God. The same year he sent his first missionary party toward the Congo. In 1887, at Old Orchard, he formed two societies, one for the deeper spiritual life at home and one for the evangelization of the world, which united in 1897 as the Christian and Missionary Alliance. He meant it as a fellowship across the churches, not a new denomination; it became, in time, both a denomination and a missionary force on every continent, from China and India to South America and the Congo basin. The unreached world lay on him like a private grief. His missionary hymn mourns the “hundred thousand souls a day” passing into eternity without the gospel, and answers with Christ’s own commission: all power is given unto Me — go.

Pen and Hymnbook

Out of the same tireless heart flowed the writing: weekly editorials in the magazine he founded (today’s Alliance Life), devotional classics such as Days of Heaven Upon Earth, A Larger Christian Life, and The Fourfold Gospel, Christ-centred expositions spanning the whole Bible, and hymns still sung wherever the deeper life is prized. The best window into the man is the testimony he gave at Bethshan, London, in 1885, published ever since as Himself — the story of how he stopped seeking experiences and found everything in the Person of Jesus. He set it to verse:

Once it was the blessing, now it is the Lord;
Once it was the feeling, now it is His Word;
Once His gift I wanted, now the Giver own;
Once I sought for healing, now Himself alone.

— A. B. Simpson, “Himself”

Those who lived with Simpson said the engine of it all was the early morning — hours kept jealously for the Bible and unhurried communion with God. He wrote that the secret of the deeper life was “a little sanctuary within,” carried through the busiest day, where the soul steals away to Christ between duties.

Rest at Nyack

Simpson preached, travelled, wrote, and administered at full stretch into his seventies, and when his strength finally failed he grieved most that he could no longer carry the missionary burden in prayer as before. He died at Nyack, New York, on 29 October 1919, and was buried on the hillside campus of the institute he founded. The societies he began now number their churches in the thousands and their missionaries around the globe; but his truest monument is smaller and nearer: the reader who, somewhere in his pages, stops chasing the blessing and finds the Blesser — Himself.

fields.name: Amanda Berry Smith
fields.bio: Amanda Berry Smith (1837–1915) was an African-American holiness evangelist who was born into slavery in Maryland and freed when her father bought his family's liberty. A washerwoman by trade, she became one of the most widely traveled preachers of the Wesleyan-Holiness movement, ministering across the United States, Britain, India, and for eight years in West Africa as an independent missionary. Widowed twice and having buried four of her five children, she later founded one of Illinois's first orphanages for Black children and died in Sebring, Florida.
fields.bio_html:
Amanda Berry Smith liked to say that she had been set free twice. The first freedom was bought with a father's sweat; the second was given at the foot of the cross. She was born into slavery on 23 January 1837, in Long Green, a farming settlement in Baltimore County, Maryland, one of thirteen children of Samuel Berry and Miriam Matthews. Her father was an enterprising, tireless man who, after his own long day's labour, worked deep into the nights making brooms and husk mats to earn the price of his family's liberty. One by one he bought them out of bondage. Amanda grew up knowing, in her own flesh, what a costly thing freedom is, and how it can be won by a love that refuses to sleep.

Her schooling amounted to only a few scattered months. What she learned of letters she largely taught herself, spelling out words by lamplight after the housework was done. At thirteen she went into domestic service, and for much of her life she supported herself as a washerwoman, cook, and cleaner in white households across Maryland and Pennsylvania. The world would later call her "the Singing Pilgrim" and print her name in mission reports from three continents; but she never lost the plain speech and worn hands of the laundry tub. It gave her preaching a particular authority. She spoke to the poor as one of them.

Grief, and a heart made clean

Sorrow came early and stayed long. In 1854 she married Calvin Devine; her conversion followed about two years later, during a grave illness in which, near despair, she cried out to God and found herself lifted into peace. Devine went to fight in the Civil War and did not return. In 1863 she married James Smith, a deacon in the African Methodist Episcopal Church, hoping for a settled home and a partner in the work she felt stirring within her. That hope was disappointed; the marriage was hard and often lonely, and he died in 1869. Of the five children born to her across both marriages, four died young. Only her daughter Mazie lived to grow up. By the age of thirty-two, Amanda Berry Smith had buried two husbands and four children. She knew, as few do, the particular silence of a house emptied by death.

It was into this grief that the deepest experience of her life came. In September 1868, at Green Street Methodist Episcopal Church in New York City, she sat under the preaching of John S. Inskip and felt God offering her what the holiness people called "a clean heart" — entire sanctification, the love of God filling every dark corner as sunlight fills a room. She longed to shout for joy, and three times the impulse rose in her; but she was the only Black woman in the crowded church, and fear held her back. A voice whispered that the white worshippers would put her out. At last the fear broke. She rose and shouted "Glory to Jesus!" and from the front Brother Inskip answered, "Amen, Glory to God." Something settled in her that never afterward moved. Out of that night came the sentence she would repeat all her life:

I often say to people that I have a right to shout more than some folks; I have been bought twice, and set free twice, and so I feel I have a good right to shout.

— Amanda Berry Smith

Before she could shout, she had to wrestle. In that Green Street pew she sat gripped by the old fear of what the white congregation might do, the impulse to praise rising and being pressed down, three times over, until at last she surrendered it to God and stood. Her whole ministry was born in that small, hidden act of yielding — the private battle in a crowded room where no one else could see what it cost her to obey.

The washerwoman evangelist

The year after her sanctification, Amanda became convinced that God was calling her to preach. It was an audacious thing. Women preachers were scarcely tolerated in that generation, and a Black woman preaching to mixed and often white congregations was, to many, unthinkable. She had no ordination, no salary, no denomination behind her, and no formal training. What she had was a clear call and an unusual voice. Dressed in a plain Quaker-style gown and poke bonnet — partly from conviction, partly because it was all she could afford — she began to speak and sing at African Methodist Episcopal churches and at the great holiness camp meetings that were sweeping the country.

Her singing disarmed crowds before her preaching convicted them. Camp meetings that might have turned a Black woman away found themselves weeping and shouting under her ministry. She supported herself by taking in washing between engagements, folding the gospel and the laundry into the same long days. She never pretended that the prejudice she met did not wound her; she named it plainly. But she refused to let it define her, and one of the most quietly defiant passages she ever wrote turns the whole question inside out:

Now, to say that being black did not make it inconvenient for us often, would not be true; but belonging to royal stock, as we do, we propose braving this inconvenience for the present, and pass on into the great big future where all these little things will be lost because of their absolute smallness! May the Lord send the future to meet us!

— Amanda Berry Smith

There is no self-pity in that. There is a woman who knows exactly who she is because she knows whose she is. The insults of a segregated church become, in her telling, "little things" measured against the vast inheritance of a child of God.

Across the sea

In 1878 she sailed for England, and what began as a visit stretched into twelve years of travel that carried her farther than almost any American evangelist of her day. She preached across Britain, Ireland, and Scotland, and arranged for Mazie to study in England. From there she went on to India for some eighteen months, at the encouragement of Bishop James M. Thoburn, whose respect for her would later be printed in the introduction to her autobiography. Then came the longest chapter of her overseas work: eight years in West Africa, mainly in Liberia and Sierra Leone, where she preached, championed temperance against the ruinous liquor trade, and took needy African children into her care as her own.

She went as an "independent missionary" — which is a dignified way of saying she went without a society to pay her way or promise her a passage home. She simply prayed, and trusted God to provide the fare and the bread. Again and again in her story, provision arrives at the last hour: a gift pressed into her hand, a sum sent by a stranger, exactly the amount needed and not a day early. Long before, when one of her free-born sisters was seized and sold back into slavery while visiting relatives in Maryland, Amanda had scraped and borrowed the fifty dollars to buy her out. She had learned young that God answers the prayers of those who have run clean out of options.

Facing a task that terrified her, she carried a single verse like a coin in her pocket: "Fear thou not, I will help thee." She had no missionary board, no guaranteed income, no ticket home — only that promise. And the record of her voyages is a record of it being kept: on more than one occasion the exact money for her passage arrived just as it was needed, from hands she had never asked. She went out with empty pockets and a full assurance, and the assurance never failed her.

Obedience, for Amanda Berry Smith, was never abstract. It cost her comfort, safety, and the settled home she had always wanted. But she reckoned the cost of disobedience higher still. Of the pull between staying safe and going where God sent her, she left a line as blunt as her faith:

To stay here and disobey God — I can't afford to take the consequence.

— Amanda Berry Smith

The orphanage, and the long fire of trial

She returned to the United States about 1890, worn down in health, and friends urged her to write her life story. She prayed much over it, unsure whether it was God's will, and at last set to work. An Autobiography: The Story of the Lord's Dealings with Mrs. Amanda Smith, the Colored Evangelist appeared in 1893 — a plain, vivid, five-hundred-page account of privation, hunger, faith, and travel that became a classic of American religious testimony. She wrote it not for fame but for children. The proceeds, together with her savings and a small newspaper she published, went toward a dream she had carried for years.

On 28 June 1899, in Harvey, Illinois, just south of Chicago, she opened the Amanda Smith Orphanage and Industrial Home for Abandoned and Destitute Colored Children — one of the first institutions of its kind for Black children in the state. It was the work of her old age and the object of her deepest anxieties. Money was always short. There were quarrels with staff, complaints from neighbours, failed inspections, and at least one fire. She poured into it the last of her strength and much of her peace. It is honest to say that the orphanage brought her as much heartache as joy; the woman who had trusted God for passage across oceans found the daily grind of feeding and housing destitute children a heavier and less romantic burden. Yet she would not abandon them. She had been a child that the world counted worthless, and she could not bear to let another be.

Sebring, and a long-awaited rest

In 1912, aged seventy-five and unable to carry the work any longer, she handed the home over and retired to Sebring, Florida, where a benefactor had provided a house for her. The institution passed to the state and was later chartered as the Amanda Smith Industrial School for Girls; it burned down in 1918, three years after her death. She did not live to see that loss, and perhaps it was mercy that she did not.

Amanda Berry Smith died in Sebring on 24 February 1915. She had been born a slave in a Maryland cabin and had preached the gospel on four continents; she had lost nearly everyone she loved and had gathered up the abandoned children of strangers; she had been paid in insults and had answered with joy. The holiness movement remembered her as one of its brightest lights, and later generations rediscovered her as a pioneer of Black women's preaching and social reform. But she would have wanted a simpler epitaph — the one her whole life kept spelling out, that a poor washerwoman with a clean heart and an obedient will is richer than she looks, and that the God who set her free the first time by a father's love had set her free forever by His own.

She had spent her life on the road, singing. It seems right to imagine her, at the last, laying down the burden she had carried so far, and finding that the future she prayed for had at last come out to meet her.

fields.name: Samuel Ajayi Crowther
fields.bio: Samuel Ajayi Crowther (c. 1809–1891) was a Yoruba boy from Osogun captured in a slave raid in 1821, rescued by the Royal Navy from a slave ship and landed at Freetown, Sierra Leone, where he was baptized in 1825. Educated by the Church Missionary Society, he became the first African ordained in the Anglican Church (priest, 1843) and, in 1864, its first African bishop. He translated the entire Bible and the Book of Common Prayer into Yoruba, and bore with humility the undermining of his mission by younger European missionaries in his last years. He died at Lagos on 31 December 1891.
fields.bio_html:
Samuel Ajayi Crowther is remembered by two names, and both of them are true. The first, Àjàyí, was given to him in a Yoruba town called Osogun around the year 1809 — the name a family gives a child born face-down, a child marked, they believed, for an unusual destiny. The second, Samuel Crowther, was given to him at a font in Sierra Leone in 1825, a borrowed English name laid over an African boy who had already lost almost everything a person can lose and had somehow not lost his faith in life. Between those two names lies one of the most astonishing journeys in the history of the Church: from a slave coffle to a cathedral, from a boy bartered for a horse to the first African bishop in the Anglican communion, from a captive who could not read to the man who first gave the whole Bible to the Yoruba people in their own tongue.

A childhood broken open

He was born into the Oyo country of what is now south-western Nigeria, into a household that farmed and wove and worshipped the old gods. It was a settled, ordinary boyhood — until it wasn't. In 1821 the wars that were feeding the Atlantic slave trade reached Osogun. Fulani and Oyo raiders fell on the town, burned it, and drove its people away in ropes. Àjàyí, about twelve years old, was taken with his mother and his baby brother and marched off among grandmothers and cousins and strangers, all of them now merchandise.

Years later, at the request of the Church Missionary Society, he set down what happened in a long, extraordinarily calm letter — one of the very few first-person accounts of the Middle Passage written by a man who survived it. He does not rage. He measures. He remembers the exact texture of the day his world ended, and he had by then learned to read it two ways at once.

From this period I must date the unhappy, but which I am now taught, in other respects, to call blessed day, which I shall never forget in my life. I call it unhappy day, because it was the day in which I was violently turned out of my father's house, and separated from relations.

— Samuel Ajayi Crowther

What followed was a slow selling-down. He was passed from owner to owner along the trade roads, his price falling as he was carried toward the coast. In one town, he records without self-pity, it was agreed that he should be bartered for a horse; later he was exchanged again for tobacco and rum. He was a boy watching himself become a currency. The despair of it nearly killed him — by his own hand. In the darkness of one of those holding places he tried more than once to strangle himself and could not do it, and afterward he understood that failure as a mercy he had not asked for.

Rescued from the sea

At the coast he was sold to Portuguese traders and packed into a slave ship. He had been aboard only a matter of hours, bound for a lifetime in Brazil or Cuba, when the vessel was intercepted by the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron — the ship HMS Myrmidon — which was hunting slavers under Britain's ban on the trade. The captives were taken off, and instead of a plantation the boy was carried to Freetown in Sierra Leone, a colony founded as a home for the liberated. He stepped ashore in 1822 into a strange kindness: not chains, but a school.

The Church Missionary Society took him in, fed him, and taught him his letters. He learned English quickly and then hungrily, and he began to read the Scriptures — first as a curiosity, then as a claim upon his life. Somewhere in those Freetown years the boy who had survived one slavery came to believe he had been rescued from a deeper one.

About the third year of my liberation from the slavery of man, I was convinced of another worse state of slavery, namely, that of sin and Satan. It pleased the Lord to open my heart.

— Samuel Ajayi Crowther

On 11 December 1825 he was baptized by the CMS missionary John Raban and took the name of an English clergyman he had never met, Samuel Crowther. When the CMS opened Fourah Bay College two years later to train African teachers and pastors, he was its very first student.

He had prayed, in effect, to be made free twice over — freed from men, and then freed from himself. The answer, when it came, he refused to credit to his own searching. "It pleased the Lord to open my heart," he wrote, and the whole grammar of the sentence is grace: the door opened from the inside, but not by him.

A pastor, a husband, a scholar

In 1829 he married Asano, a fellow liberated captive who at her own baptism took the name Susan Thompson; their marriage would last more than half a century. Crowther became a schoolmaster and catechist, and everyone who worked beside him noticed the same thing: a mind of unusual patience and reach, especially for language. He began to take his own mother tongue apart and write it down — sounds, grammar, proverbs — work almost no one had attempted before.

In 1841 the CMS attached him to the ill-fated Niger Expedition, a venture up the great river to plant commerce and Christianity in place of the slave trade. Fever devastated the European members; many died. Crowther survived, and the journal he kept was so observant and so clear that it made his reputation in London. The Society brought him to England, trained him further, and on Trinity Sunday, 11 June 1843, he was ordained a priest — the first African clergyman of the Anglican Church.

The word made Yoruba

Ordained, he turned homeward. In 1846 the Yoruba Mission established itself at Abeokuta, and there the long arc of Crowther's life bent back on itself in a way no novelist would dare invent. Among the townspeople he found his own mother, Afala, from whom he had been torn twenty-five years before. Neither of them, at first, could speak.

We could not say much, but sat still, casting many an affectionate look towards each other, an affection which twenty-five years had not extinguished.

— Samuel Ajayi Crowther

He called the reunion the greatest gift the Lord had ever given him. In time his mother was baptized Hannah, and his sister with her — the captive son become the means of his own mother's salvation.

For twenty-five years a family had been scattered across an ocean of loss, and a boy had grown into a bishop-to-be with an ache no achievement could reach. That God should set his mother down again in front of him, alive, in the town where he had come to preach — Crowther could only sit in the wonder of it. He had learned long before not to name a day unhappy too quickly.

Then came the work that would outlast everything else he did. Crowther gave himself to translating the Scriptures and the Book of Common Prayer into Yoruba, building the grammar and dictionary the task required almost from nothing. Word by word, proverb by proverb, he carried the Bible across into the language his mother had sung to him — the whole of it, the Bibeli Mímọ́, completed under his oversight in his last years. A tongue that had been written in the ledgers of slavers as a price was now made able to carry the words of God. Once, brought before Queen Victoria, he read her the Lord's Prayer in Yoruba, and she is said to have called its sound soft and melodious. The boy sold for a horse now prayed, in his mother's language, before the Queen of the empire whose navy had freed him.

Made a bishop

On St Peter's Day, 29 June 1864, in Canterbury Cathedral, Samuel Ajayi Crowther was consecrated Bishop of the Niger Territories — the first African bishop of the Anglican communion. Oxford gave him a doctorate of divinity. It was a summit of honour, and he wore it as he wore everything, quietly. He gathered African clergy around him, ordained African pastors, and built a mission that was, by design, to be led by Africans for Africa — the very thing the missionary societies had once said they wanted.

The long humbling

It is here that his story darkens, and honesty requires that it be told. As Crowther aged, a new generation of young European missionaries arrived on the Niger, men shaped by the harder racial confidence of the later nineteenth century. They did not believe an African should lead. Through the 1880s they moved against his mission — audits, accusations of mismanagement and corruption levelled at his African staff, dismissals and suspensions, one by one, until the men he had trained were pushed out and replaced with Europeans. The work of a lifetime was taken apart in front of him.

He might have fought it with the weapons of grievance, and no one would have blamed him. He did not. A retiring, soft-spoken man, he made little effort to answer the charges heaped on his people, and in 1890, his own reputation still unbroken, he resigned his authority with a dignity his accusers never matched. There is a particular pain in being undermined by those who owe their very presence to the ground you cleared, and Crowther felt it fully. But he had been made a slave and had not become bitter; he had been made a bishop and had not become proud; and he would not now, at the end, let smaller men make him small. He kept praying, kept serving, kept his eyes on the God who had opened his heart in Freetown sixty years before.

Lord, You who turned an unhappy day into a blessed one, and gave back a mother thought lost forever, and set Your word in our mouths in our own tongue — teach us, when our work is torn from our hands and our names are made low, to hold our peace as Your servant held his, trusting the One who freed us twice to be faithful still.

On the last day of the year 1891 — 31 December — Samuel Ajayi Crowther died of a stroke in Lagos, about eighty-two years old. The men who had displaced his mission gave the bishopric, next, to a European. But the deeper verdict of history has gone the other way. The Yoruba Bible he made is still read; the African church he insisted could stand on its own feet is now vast beyond his imagining; and the boy bartered for a horse is honoured across a continent as a father of its faith. He had been right about the day he was captured all along. It was, in every respect that finally mattered, a blessed one.

fields.name: Richard Allen
fields.bio: Richard Allen (1760–1831) was born into slavery in Philadelphia, sold as a boy to a Delaware farmer, and converted to Christ as a teenager under Methodist preaching. After his master was himself converted and let him buy his freedom, Allen became a pioneering itinerant preacher; the humiliation of segregated seating at St. George's Methodist Church led him to found an independent Black church, Mother Bethel, in Philadelphia. In 1816 he organized and was consecrated first bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church, the first fully independent Black denomination in America.
fields.bio_html:
Richard Allen was born a slave on the fourteenth of February, 1760, in the city of Philadelphia. His first owner was Benjamin Chew, a prominent Quaker lawyer; and while Allen was still a boy his whole family — mother, father, and children — was sold away to a farmer named Stokeley Sturgis, near Dover in the Delaware country. There, on a modest plantation among the fields and marshes, the future founder of the first independent Black church in America grew up under the plainest and hardest of schools. He learned early what it was to belong to another man, to be counted as property, to watch a family divided at a stranger's convenience. Yet Allen would remember Sturgis, in the end, as a kind master. The bitterness he never forgot was not the man but the thing itself.

I had it often impressed upon my mind that I should one day enjoy my freedom; for slavery is a bitter pill, notwithstanding we had a good master.

— Richard Allen

Awakened in the Fields

When Allen was about seventeen, a Methodist preacher came into the neighbourhood, and the young slave went to hear him. The Methodists in those years were a fervent, unpolished, wandering people who preached to anyone who would listen — the poor, the enslaved, the outcast — and their message went straight to Allen's heart. He came under deep conviction of sin. He describes himself in his memoir as brought low and desperate, certain that unless God had mercy on him he was lost.

I was awakened and brought to see myself, poor, wretched and undone, and without the mercy of God must be lost.

— Richard Allen

For weeks he cried to God day and night, working the fields by day and wrestling in prayer by night, until one evening, alone, the burden broke. The language he chose to describe that moment is the language of a man who had worn literal chains — and now felt spiritual ones fall.

As a young man still in bondage, Allen prayed to God both day and night under conviction of sin, crying out for mercy while he laboured on another man's farm. His conversion did not come in a church or a school, but in the fields, on his knees, where no one could sell his soul.

The deliverance, when it came, was total and joyful. He never forgot it, and he set it down plainly in his own account of his life: all of a sudden my dungeon shook, my chains flew off, and glory to God, I cried. My soul was filled. I cried, enough for me — the Saviour died. From that hour Richard Allen was, by his own reckoning, a free man in the deepest sense long before he was free in the eyes of the law.

Praying His Master Into the Kingdom

The new convert did not keep his joy to himself. He and his brother reasoned that the surest way to honour Christ — and to disarm the slander that religion made slaves lazy — was to work harder and more faithfully than ever, so that no one could say Methodism had ruined a good servant. Allen even worried aloud that his master might think faith had spoiled him, and so he laboured all the more diligently. In time he won Sturgis's permission to hold Methodist meetings in the farmhouse itself.

Preachers came and prayed under that roof, among them the great Methodist itinerant Freeborn Garrettson. One day Garrettson preached from the book of Daniel on the words, weighed in the balances, and found wanting — and applied them without flinching to men who held their fellow creatures in bondage. The word went home. Stokeley Sturgis became convinced that slaveholding was a sin against God, and that he could not meet his Maker with slaves in his fields. He offered Allen and his brother the chance to purchase themselves.

Allen had prayed and laboured for the soul of the very man who owned him. The answer came through a sermon in his master's own house: Sturgis was converted, concluded that slavery was wrong, and opened to Allen the door to freedom. The one who had prayed as a slave would walk out a free man because his prayers had reached his master first.

The terms were set: the brothers were to pay sixty pounds in gold and silver — two thousand dollars in the depreciated continental currency of the Revolution — buying back their own time by their own sweat. Allen agreed, and through years of hired-out labour, sawing wood, hauling bricks, and driving a wagon of salt for the army, he made the payments. By 1783 the debt was cleared and Richard Allen was, at last, legally free. He was twenty-three years old.

The Wandering Preacher

Freedom for Allen meant not ease but errand. He took to the roads as an itinerant preacher, walking and working his way through Delaware, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Maryland, supporting himself with day-labour and preaching wherever a door opened — to white congregations and Black, in barns, in forests, at camp meetings. He attended the historic 1784 Christmas Conference in Baltimore, where American Methodism organized itself as a church, and there he came to know Bishop Francis Asbury, who recognized the young man's gift and once invited him to travel with him through the slave states. Allen declined that particular journey, unwilling to be silenced about slavery, but the two men's paths would remain entwined for life.

In 1786 Allen came to Philadelphia, the city of his birth, and was invited to preach to the Black members of St. George's Methodist Episcopal Church. He preached at five in the morning so as not to disturb the regular services, and under his labours the number of Black worshippers grew quickly. That growth, meant to be a joy, became the occasion of a wound.

"They Were No More Plagued With Us"

As the Black congregation swelled, the white leadership of St. George's grew uneasy. They moved the Black worshippers from their accustomed seats to places along the wall, and then up into the gallery. One Sunday morning Allen, Absalom Jones, and others knelt to pray in the gallery — and a trustee seized Jones by the shoulders, trying to haul him up off his knees in the middle of prayer, hissing that he must not kneel there. Jones begged him to wait until the prayer was finished. He would not. When the prayer ended, the Black members rose together and walked out of the building for good. Allen recorded the moment with a dignity sharper than any protest.

By this time prayer was over, and we all went out of the church in a body, and they were no more plagued with us in the church.

— Richard Allen

They did not walk out of the faith — only out of a house that had shamed them at their prayers. Already, in 1787, Allen and Jones had formed the Free African Society, a mutual-aid and religious fellowship that cared for the widow, buried the dead, and disciplined its members toward sober and godly living. It was one of the first independent Black organizations in the nation, and out of it, and out of the walkout, would come churches.

The Fever of 1793

Before Allen could build his church, the city was visited by terror. In the summer of 1793 yellow fever swept Philadelphia; thousands died, and those who could afford to fled. Physicians, led by Dr. Benjamin Rush, appealed to the Black community to nurse the sick and bury the dead, under the mistaken belief that people of African descent were immune. They were not — many died — but Allen and Jones answered the call anyway, organizing Black Philadelphians to go house to house among the dying, to lift the sick, to carry away the corpses that no one else would touch.

When the city's own citizens fled and its churches emptied, Richard Allen and Absalom Jones rallied the Black poor of Philadelphia to nurse the fevered and bury the dead at the risk of their own lives — and then had to defend their people, in print, against the slander that they had profited from the calamity. It was the answer to their own prayers for a people who could serve Christ freely: a despised community became the city's mercy in its worst hour.

When the epidemic passed, a pamphleteer accused the Black nurses of extortion and theft. Allen and Jones answered with their own published Narrative, defending their people and turning the pen against the whole system that despised them. Allen appended an address to slaveholders that has never lost its force, grounding the cause of the enslaved not in politics but in the character of God Himself.

God himself was the first pleader of the cause of slaves.

— Richard Allen

Mother Bethel and a Church of Their Own

In 1794 Allen bought an old blacksmith's shop, had it hauled to a lot he owned on Sixth Street, and made it into a house of worship. Francis Asbury preached at its dedication, and it was named Bethel — "house of God." The people called it Mother Bethel, and it stands to this day on the oldest parcel of land continuously owned by Black Americans in the United States. That same year Allen was formally recognized in ministry, and in 1799 Bishop Asbury ordained him a deacon — the first Black man so ordained in the Methodist Episcopal Church.

But independence had to be fought for. The white conference tried again and again to bring Bethel back under its control and its property under its power. Allen and his congregation resisted through years of legal struggle, until in 1816 the Pennsylvania Supreme Court affirmed Bethel's right to govern itself. That same year Allen gathered Black Methodist congregations from Philadelphia, Baltimore, and beyond, and together they organized a wholly new denomination: the African Methodist Episcopal Church — the first fully independent Black denomination in America. On the eleventh of April, 1816, Richard Allen was consecrated its first bishop.

The Long Labour and the Rest

As bishop, Allen gave the rest of his life to a people forming themselves in freedom. He built congregations, licensed preachers, opposed the schemes to ship free Black Americans off to Africa through the Colonization Society, championed education, sheltered fugitives from slavery, and in 1830 helped convene the first National Negro Convention in the very rooms of Mother Bethel. His home was a station on the road to freedom; his pulpit was a school of self-respect for a people told daily that they had none.

Richard Allen died on the twenty-sixth of March, 1831, at seventy-one, and was buried at Mother Bethel, where his tomb remains. He had come into the world as another man's property and left it the shepherd of a church that would carry the gospel and the cause of freedom across a continent and beyond. The chains that flew off in a Delaware field had, in the end, loosed a whole people's tongue to pray and to sing in a house that no one could take from them.

He is remembered as bishop, founder, abolitionist, and statesman. But he first knew himself as a slave who had found mercy on his knees — and everything else grew from that. The man who once feared his faith would be mistaken for laziness gave the enslaved and the free alike a place to stand before God as sons and daughters, and not as anyone's property at all.

fields.name: Festo Kivengere
fields.bio: Festo Kivengere (1919–1988) was a Ugandan Anglican bishop and evangelist of the East African Revival, often called “the Billy Graham of Africa.” Converted from nominal faith during the 1941 revival, he became Bishop of Kigezi in 1972 and a leader of African Evangelistic Enterprise. After Archbishop Janani Luwum's murder in 1977 he fled Amin's Uganda over the mountains into Rwanda, then wrote the celebrated book I Love Idi Amin, a testimony to forgiving the tyrant who had driven him into exile.
fields.bio_html:
Before he was a bishop, before the crowds and the cathedrals and the title the world would fasten on him — the Billy Graham of Africa — Festo Kivengere was a small boy in the high green hills of Kigezi, in the far south-west corner of Uganda, walking behind cattle. He was born in 1919 into a proud, traditional ruling family among the semi-nomadic herders of that country, and his earliest world was one of long grass, mist on the mountains, and the slow patience of the herd. As a boy tending the calves he sometimes turned the pages of little mission picture-books that told the story of a man named Jesus. He could not have guessed that the figure in those pages would one day become the whole meaning of his life — nor how costly that meaning would prove to be.

At about ten he was taken into a mission school newly planted in his village, and because he was quick and bright he was sent away for more education. He learned to read and to reason; he learned the Christian catechism; he was, on paper, a Christian. But it was the faith of a name only. In his teens he drifted from it altogether. At high school he fell in with a crowd untouched by the revival stirring around them, slipped off after dark to the shops, and took up drinking and smoking with a will. By the time he had qualified and returned home as a young schoolteacher, expected by his missionary employers to teach the Bible to children, he taught it with a sneer, unable to resist a sarcastic remark at the sacred text he did not believe.

A flood of light

All this while, the great East African Revival — the movement of the Balokole, the "saved ones" — was moving across the region like wind through the tall grass. It reached Festo not through an argument but through a friend. One day another young man named Festo Rwamunahe came to him, changed past recognition, and said simply, "Three hours ago Jesus became a living reality to me. I know my sins are forgiven." Then he asked Festo's forgiveness for the life they had led together, and promised he would never live that way again. Kivengere had no answer for a joy he could not explain away.

What he did not know was that two small girls had been praying for him by name.

On a Sunday morning early in October 1941, Festo's fourteen-year-old niece told him that she and a twelve-year-old friend named Eva had been praying for his soul — and that God had told them their prayers would be answered that very weekend. The next day it fell to Festo to walk the schoolboys to church. It was an ordinary Anglican prayer-book service, but before ever the sermon began people were rising all over the building to confess their sins and turn to Christ. Festo went down on his knees and surrendered everything. He would say afterward that it was as though a flood of light poured into his soul, and the burdens he had carried simply vanished in the presence of love. Two children had prayed; heaven had kept the appointment.

The conversion was total, and it never wore off. The mocking schoolteacher became one of the youngest and most radiant voices of the revival that was sweeping Uganda, Rwanda, Kenya, and Tanzania. The Balokole lived by open confession, joyful singing — their great song was Tukutendereza Yesu, "We praise You, Jesus" — and a fierce insistence that a Christian must walk continually in the light of the cross, keeping short accounts with God and with every neighbour. Festo drank this in, and it became the marrow of his preaching for the rest of his days.

Called to the whole world

He taught, and he evangelised, and his gift for making the gospel vivid and personal carried him further and further afield. He would eventually serve as an interpreter for Billy Graham when Graham preached in Africa — turning the American's English into words that struck home in Luganda and beyond, and learning the crusade platform from the inside. In 1971 he joined the South African evangelist Michael Cassidy in launching African Evangelistic Enterprise in East Africa, a team of African evangelists carrying the good news into the cities of the continent. He turned down invitations to more comfortable and prominent work — including one from Billy Graham himself — to give his strength to Africa. Ordained a priest, he grew into one of the most beloved evangelists his continent had produced, and in 1972 he was consecrated Bishop of Kigezi, shepherd of the very hills where he had once herded cattle.

He came to the office at the worst possible hour. Idi Amin had seized power, and Uganda was descending into terror.

The years of the beast

Under Amin the disappearances began — the road-blocks, the arrests in the night, the bodies in the forests and the rivers. The church would not stay silent. In February 1977 the Anglican bishops, led by Archbishop Janani Luwum, delivered a protest against the regime's murders. The answer was swift. Luwum was seized, and on 16 February 1977 he was killed. Festo Kivengere was among those closest to him and one of the last to see him alive; he waited outside the building where the archbishop was held until soldiers forced him away at gunpoint. Luwum had already told him, quietly, "They are going to kill me. I am not afraid."

Now the danger closed around Festo. He was a marked man, a bishop who had signed the protest and whose voice carried across the world. On the night after Luwum's murder he and his wife Mera fled. They drove as far as the road would take them, and then, guided by church people who knew the country, they climbed on foot through forest and up the flank of the mountains that divide Uganda from Rwanda, walking through the dark toward the border. He crossed carrying almost nothing but his Bible.

Somewhere on those mountainsides, in the cold and the fear, a bishop and his wife walked and prayed — not knowing whether the next ridge held safety or a soldier, leaving behind a diocese, a home, and a murdered friend. It was the prayer of the hunted: Lord, we have only You left. Bring us over.

"I love Idi Amin"

Safe in exile, Festo could have become a prophet of denunciation. Instead he found a harder road. He discovered bitterness rising in his own heart — the natural, justified hatred of a man who had killed his archbishop and driven his people into terror — and he knew it was poisoning him. In the very year of the terror, as Uganda marked the centenary of the gospel's arrival in the land, he watched imprisoned Christians singing in their cells and men and women streaming to Christ, and he could not carry hatred into that light.

The Holy Spirit showed me that I was getting hard in my spirit, and that my hardness and bitterness toward those who were persecuting us could only bring spiritual loss… So I had to ask for forgiveness from the Lord, and for grace to love President Amin more.

— Festo Kivengere

The turning point came as he contemplated Christ on the cross, praying, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." He saw that the prayer left no one out — not even the tyrant of his own country. He knelt and forgave Amin by name, and peace flooded back into his soul as it had on that October morning long before. Out of that struggle came a small, astonishing book, published in 1977, with a title that scandalised many who saw it: I Love Idi Amin. It was not a book excusing evil. It was a testimony that the love which had saved Festo was strong enough to reach even the man who had tried to destroy him.

On the cross, Jesus said, "Father, forgive them, because they know not what they do." As evil as Idi Amin is, how can I do less toward him?

— Festo Kivengere

Asked how he could possibly love such a man, Festo did not pretend to feel warmly toward him. "I may not like Idi Amin," he said, "but if I am a Christian believer I am obliged to forgive him, love him with Christ's love, and want the highest and best for his life." The prayer he had prayed on his knees in exile — for grace to love his enemy — was answered not in a feeling but in a decision that held, and that set countless other Christians free from the acid of their own hatred.

Homeward, and home

When Amin fell in 1979, Festo went back. He returned to a broken diocese and a wounded nation and set himself to rebuild — restoring churches, caring for orphans and refugees, pouring himself into relief and reconciliation as readily as into preaching. And preach he did, all over the world: in packed African stadiums and in Western cathedrals and university halls, always with the same message he had learned as a young teacher on his knees — that the love of God is real, that it meets us at the cross, and that it is powerful enough to change not only individuals but the bitter history between peoples. He never lost the note of costliness in his gospel.

Peace is not automatic. It's a gift by the grace of God. It comes when hearts are exposed to the love of Christ. But this always costs something. For the love of Christ was demonstrated through suffering, and those who experience that love can never put it into practice without some cost.

— Festo Kivengere

The cost caught up with his body at last. Festo Kivengere died of leukemia on 18 May 1988, still preaching until near the end, still speaking of the Christ who had flooded his soul with light. He was not yet seventy. He left behind a healed man's testimony — that a cattle-herder from Kigezi, once a scoffing schoolteacher, could be so mastered by grace that he would climb a mountain in the dark rather than nurse revenge, and write a tyrant's name in a book about love. His life remains one of the clearest windows the modern church has onto the plain, staggering proposition at the centre of the faith: that on the cross, no one is beyond forgiveness, and that those who have been forgiven much are set free to forgive at any cost.

fields.name: Simeon Nsibambi
fields.bio: Simeon Nsibambi (1897–1978) was an educated, prosperous Muganda health officer in Kampala whose spiritual hunger drove a pivotal September 1929 meeting with the missionary doctor Joe Church at Namirembe. Their weekend of Bible study and prayer over the fullness of the Spirit helped ignite the East African Revival (the Balokole, “saved ones”). Nsibambi gave up his government post for a life of prayer and personal evangelism, becoming, in many accounts, a father of a movement that reshaped East African Christianity and produced leaders like Festo Kivengere and Janani Luwum.
fields.bio_html:
Some of the great awakenings of the church began in cathedrals or crowded revival tents. One of the largest began on a quiet hill in Kampala, over an open Bible, between two men who were tired of being respectable Christians and hungry to be holy ones. Simeon Nsibambi was one of those two men. He was a Muganda of standing — educated, decorated, prosperous, a leader in his people's church — and by every outward measure he had arrived. Yet he carried within him a restlessness that no promotion could quiet, a sense that there was something more of God to be had than he had yet found. When at last he found it, the fire that was lit in him spread across half a continent.

A respected man with a divided heart

Nsibambi was born in 1897 into a prominent Buganda family; his father was a chief among a people who had embraced the Christian faith with remarkable speed a generation before. He was well schooled for his day, studying at Mengo High School and at King's College, Budo, the training ground of Buganda's leaders. During the First World War he served in the African Native Medical Corps and was decorated for distinguished service. Afterward he rose into the government of the Buganda kingdom as a health officer — a sanitation inspector responsible for the wellbeing of Kampala, respected in the streets he walked, secure in salary and in name.

He was also, by the 1920s, a baptised and believing Christian, a member of the Anglican Church of Uganda that the pioneer missionaries and the Baganda martyrs had watered with their blood. But Nsibambi was not content, and his discontent was the holy kind. He looked at himself and at the church around him and saw a faith that was correct but cool, a religion of forms that lacked fire. He had the outward marks of a Christian and the inward hunger of a man who knows he is missing the heart of it. That hunger would not leave him alone.

He had everything a man could want and still knelt as a beggar, asking God for the one thing he could not earn: not more religion, but a living power he had read about in Scripture and had never yet felt in himself. His prayer, in essence, was the oldest prayer of the awakened soul — there must be something more; give it to me.

The weekend on Namirembe Hill

In September 1929 God answered that prayer through a weary Englishman. Dr. Joe Church was a medical missionary of the Ruanda Mission, running the hospital at Gahini, and he too had come to the end of himself — spiritually dry, discouraged, and taking a few days away in Kampala to recover. He was staying on Namirembe Hill, whose name means full of peace, and on the Sunday he climbed to the great cathedral. There the two men met. Nsibambi, sensing in this tired doctor a fellow seeker, pressed him with the question that had been burning in his own chest: what was missing — in the church of Uganda, and in himself?

Church knew the answer, or at least the direction of it, from the "victorious life" teaching he had drunk in at the Keswick conventions of England. He began to speak to Nsibambi of the fullness of the Holy Spirit and of a Christian life lived in victory rather than defeat. The two men could not let the conversation go. Over that weekend — the account remembers it as roughly two days — they sat together with the Bible open, poring over the Scripture and the Scofield notes on the filling of the Spirit, and they prayed. They prayed to lay down every known sin, to be filled, to hold nothing back. It was not a lecture; it was two hungry men coming empty to God together and being filled.

There can be nothing to stop a real outpouring of the Holy Spirit in Rwanda now except our own lack of sanctification.

— Dr. Joe Church, writing of the meeting with Nsibambi

Church went back to Gahini, as those who tell the story put it, in the power of Pentecost. But the deeper change was in Nsibambi, and he did not go quietly back to his old life. He had touched the thing he had ached for all along, and he could not now hold it in.

What began as two discouraged men praying over a shared Bible on a hillside did not stay on that hillside. From that single weekend of surrender the fire ran outward — into Rwanda, into Uganda, and in time across Kenya, Tanzania, Burundi, and beyond — until an awakening now remembered as the East African Revival had touched millions. Few prayer meetings in the history of the church have been so small in the moment and so vast in the answer.

The man who could not stop asking about souls

Nsibambi's transformation was total and, to his respectable neighbours, alarming. He gave up his government post and the security it carried, and gave himself wholly to prayer and to preaching. He took his stand on Namirembe Hill and on the street corners near the cathedral, calling men and women to brokenness, confession, and new life. He led his own younger brother, Blasio Kigozi, to a living faith; Kigozi joined Joe Church at Gahini and became a burning evangelist in his own right before his early death in 1936, and it was Nsibambi who buried him on Cathedral Hill.

Above all, Nsibambi became a man who could not meet a stranger without asking after his soul. He stopped people on the road, in the market, at the gate, and asked them plainly whether they were saved — the kind of buttonhole evangelism that embarrasses the polite and rescues the lost. Not everyone approved. When Joe Church returned to Kampala some months later, an indignant missionary confronted him about what his friend had unleashed:

Oh, he's gone mad and is going round everywhere asking people if they are saved. He's just left my gardener.

— A missionary in Kampala, recounted in the histories of the Revival

It was not madness. It was a man who had finally believed his own gospel. What his critics called excess, the movement he helped birth would call normal Christianity — the natural overflow of a heart that has been genuinely filled. Historians of the awakening have called him, without exaggeration, in many ways the father of the whole Balokole movement — the movement of the balokole, the "saved ones," whose watchword became the sweet Luganda hymn Tukutendereza Yesu, "We praise You, Jesus."

A hidden man of prayer

Around 1941 Nsibambi's health failed. Joe Church described the illness only as a "weakness," and from then on Nsibambi lived increasingly withdrawn, confined much of the time to his home near Namirembe Cathedral. For the leader of a great revival it might have seemed a cruel silencing. It was nothing of the kind. The man who had once stopped strangers in the street now became a fountain of intercession, receiving those who came to him, praying over the movement he had helped to start, holding up in prayer the very leaders whose names would go around the world.

There is something fitting in it. The Revival Nsibambi lit was never chiefly about platforms and crowds; it was about repentance, confession, the "walking in the light" of open honesty before God and one another, and above all prayer. That the man remembered as its father should spend his last decades largely unseen, on his knees, is not a tragedy but a parable. He had already given the movement the only thing that mattered — its hunger for holiness and its habit of prayer — and he went on giving it from the hidden place until the end. He died in 1978, an old man and, in the truest sense, a patriarch.

Lord, give us Nsibambi's holy discontent — the refusal to settle for a correct and comfortable faith when You offer a full one. Make us hungry for more of Your Spirit than we have yet known, bold enough to ask a stranger about his soul, and content, when our strength fails, to serve You unseen upon our knees.

The fire that outlived him

It is hard to overstate what came out of that weekend on Namirembe Hill. The East African Revival that Nsibambi and Church helped ignite swept through the Anglican and Protestant churches of the region for the better part of the twentieth century, breaking down barriers of tribe and race, filling churches with converts, and producing a generation of Christian leaders of extraordinary quality. Among the balokole shaped by the movement were men whose names the whole church would come to honour — Archbishop Erica Sabiti; Bishop Festo Kivengere, the evangelist who preached alongside Billy Graham and answered Idi Amin's terror with a book titled I Love Idi Amin; and Archbishop Janani Luwum, martyred in 1977 for standing against tyranny, dying, as he said, for Uganda and for Christ.

Nsibambi wrote no famous books and left few recorded words of his own. What he left instead was a fire and a family of the faithful. He was a prosperous man who chose to be poor for Christ, a respected officer who was willing to be thought mad, an educated leader who wanted nothing so much as to be holy. He teaches the church a lesson it perpetually forgets: that revival begins not in strategy but in surrender, not in crowds but in a couple of hungry believers who will not get up from their knees until God fills them. From one such surrender, on a hill called full of peace, the peace of God went out to a continent.

fields.name: George Müller
fields.bio: George Müller (1805–1898) was a Prussian-born evangelist who, after a dissolute youth that included theft and a spell in prison, was converted at a prayer meeting in Halle in 1825 and gave his life to living by faith. Settling in Bristol, he founded the Ashley Down orphanages, where he housed and fed more than ten thousand orphans over his lifetime without ever once asking a human being for money — relying on prayer alone and keeping meticulous records of the answers. His aim was to leave the world a visible proof that God still hears prayer; he preached across forty-two countries into his eighties and died at his orphanage in 1898.
fields.bio_html:
George Müller has been remembered, in the hundred and more years since his death, chiefly as the man who fed thousands of orphans without ever once asking a human being for money. But the more remarkable thing is why he did it. He wanted to leave behind him a visible answer to a question that unsettles every anxious heart: does God still hear prayer? He staked his whole life, and the lives of ten thousand children, on the belief that He does — and he kept the ledgers to prove it.

He was born on 27 September 1805 at Kroppenstedt, near Halberstadt, in the Kingdom of Prussia, the son of a tax collector. It would be pleasant to say he was a devout child. He was not. By his own unflinching account he was a liar and a thief almost as soon as he could talk, stealing even from the government money his father was charged to collect. He drank, he gambled, he squandered whatever he could lay hands on, and he was clever enough to hide most of it. At sixteen, run out of money at an inn, he was arrested for fraud and spent several weeks in prison at Wolfenbüttel before his father paid to have him released — and then whipped him, and sent him back to his studies.

The Prayer Meeting at Halle

Destined by his father for the comfortable living of a Lutheran clergyman, Müller entered the University of Halle to read divinity with no more religion in him than ambition and appetite. Then, one Saturday evening in mid-November of 1825, a friend named Beta mentioned that he was going to a small meeting in a private house where people read the Bible, sang, and prayed. Müller, curious and restless, asked to come along. What he found in that plain room undid him. A man knelt down and simply prayed. "I had never seen any one on his knees," Müller later wrote, and he had never himself knelt to pray. He went home that night a changed man, though he could scarcely have explained how. He was twenty years old, and from that evening the whole current of his life reversed.

The change was not instant perfection but a settled new direction. He began to read the Scriptures with hunger, gave up his old companions, and felt a growing pull toward missionary work. In 1828 he was accepted by the London Society for Promoting Christianity Amongst the Jews, and in March 1829 he sailed for England. Within two years he had parted from the society — not in bitterness, but because he could not in conscience keep to rules that seemed to him to bind the freedom of the Spirit. In 1830 he became the minister of a small chapel at Teignmouth in Devon, at a salary of fifty-five pounds a year.

Learning to Live by Faith

At Teignmouth, Müller made a decision that shaped everything after. He gave up his fixed salary altogether. It troubled him that a rented pew system made the gospel a transaction and left the poor ashamed; and more deeply, he wanted to depend on God directly rather than on any arrangement of men. He resolved never again to ask a fellow creature for money, nor even to let his needs be known, but to tell them only to God in prayer and wait. That same year, on 7 October 1830, he married Mary Groves, sister of the missionary Anthony Norris Groves — a woman of quiet strength who would share every privation of the venture without complaint for nearly forty years.

In 1832 the Müllers moved to Bristol, where he would remain the rest of his life, preaching at Bethesda Chapel. Two years later he founded the Scriptural Knowledge Institution for Home and Abroad — to aid schools, circulate Bibles, and support missionaries, all on the same principle of prayer and faith rather than appeals and debt. He would not go into debt for God's work; if the money was not there, he took it that God was not yet calling him to spend. It was a hard school, and he never pretended otherwise.

The only way to learn strong faith is to endure great trials. I have learned my faith by standing firm amid severe testings.

— George Müller

The Orphans of Ashley Down

The orphan work grew out of a burden and an argument. Müller had watched the fatherless children of Bristol beg and starve, and he had grown weary of hearing Christians say, in effect, that they would trust God more if only they had proof He could be trusted. So he decided to become the proof. If a poor man, asking no one but God, could house and feed and clothe and educate orphan children year after year, then the doubting believer might take heart, and the scoffer might be silenced. He was always clear that the children's welfare, dear as it was, was not the first object.

...that it may be seen that God is faithful still, and hears prayer still.

— George Müller

The first orphan house opened in a rented dwelling on Wilson Street in April 1836, taking in a few girls. It filled, and another opened, and another. In time Müller built five great houses on Ashley Down, on the northern edge of Bristol, plain and sturdy and clean, where at their fullest some two thousand children lived at once. Over the course of his life he cared for 10,024 orphans. Not once did he issue an appeal or send round a collecting plate. When money and food ran low — and they often did, sometimes to the last shilling and the last loaf — he prayed, and he waited, and he recorded in his journals, with the precision of an accountant, how the need was met. The published narratives of these dealings ran to volumes and were read across the world.

Müller had learned that he could not pray well from an anxious, empty heart. So before he asked God for anything, he would settle into the Scriptures each morning and not rise until his soul was happy in the Lord. "The first thing to be concerned about," he wrote, "was not how much I might serve the Lord, how I might glorify the Lord; but how I might get my soul into a happy state, and how my inner man might be nourished." Only then did he turn to prayer for the day's thousand needs.

Bread in the Morning

Of the countless recorded answers, one has been told and retold because it gathers up the whole spirit of the place. On a morning when there was no food in the houses and no money to buy any, the children were dressed and seated at the long tables before empty plates. Müller stood and gave thanks to God for the breakfast they were about to receive, as certain of it as if it lay before them.

As the thanksgiving ended there came a knock at the door. It was the baker: he had been unable to sleep in the night, sure that the orphans would need bread, and had risen early to bake for them. Scarcely had the bread been carried in when there was a second knock. The milkman's cart had broken down in the street directly outside the orphanage, and rather than let the milk spoil he begged Müller to take it all. The children who had bowed before empty tables ate a full breakfast of fresh bread and milk.

Such things were not, to Müller, occasional marvels but the ordinary texture of a life lived on prayer. Gifts arrived to the day and often to the exact sum needed; strangers were moved to give without knowing the need existed. He was scrupulously honest that this was no magic and no ease. There were seasons of real want, mornings of genuine dread, prayers that seemed to go unanswered for a long time. He simply refused to stop believing, or to reach for any hand but God's.

Sorrow and Steadfastness

Faith did not exempt him from grief. On 6 February 1870 Mary, his companion in every trial, died of rheumatic fever after nearly forty years of marriage. Fourteen hundred of the orphans followed her coffin. Müller, broken-hearted, insisted on preaching her funeral sermon himself, taking his text from Psalm 119, "Thou art good, and doest good." He would not let his sorrow accuse his God. "God himself has done it," he said of her death; "we are satisfied with him." A son had died in infancy years before; his beloved daughter Lydia, born in 1832, who had grown up among the orphans and married his faithful helper and successor James Wright, would die before him too, in 1890. In 1871 he married again, to Susannah Grace Sanger, who would become his fellow-traveller in the great work of his old age.

The Long Journeys

Most men would have counted the orphan houses labour enough for one life. Müller, past seventy and with the work in Wright's trusted hands, set out to preach. From 1875 to 1892 he travelled on missionary journeys that carried him, by his own reckoning, some two hundred thousand miles across forty-two countries — through Europe, America, India, China, Japan, Australia — preaching to audiences that sometimes numbered thousands, addressing millions in all. He spoke the same message everywhere, in the plain, unhurried way that was his habit: that God is real, that He keeps His word, that prayer is answered, and that a man may safely trust Him with everything.

The Last Morning

He kept working almost to the end. On the morning of 10 March 1898, in his room at the orphanage on Ashley Down, in the ninety-third year of his life, George Müller was found dead beside his bed. He had led evening devotions and retired as usual; in the night, quietly, he had gone to the God he had trusted so long. Bristol mourned him as it had mourned few men. Shops closed, flags flew at half-mast, and tens of thousands lined the streets as his body was carried to the grave, many of them men and women who had once been fed at those long tables as orphaned children.

He died, as he had lived, a poor man; the millions that had passed through his hands had all gone to the work, and he had kept almost nothing for himself. What he left instead was the thing he had set out to leave: a record, honest and enormous and impossible to explain away, of a God who hears. His own words remain the best summary of the ledger he kept for sixty years — a promise held onto until it came true, that it may be seen that God is faithful still, and hears prayer still.

fields.name: Hudson Taylor
fields.bio: James Hudson Taylor (1832–1905) was an English missionary to China and founder of the China Inland Mission. Converted at seventeen while his mother prayed for him miles away, he gave his life to reaching China's unreached inland provinces, pioneering a faith-mission that took no debt and solicited no funds but told every need to God in prayer. Through immense fruit and immense loss — the deaths of his children, both wives, and dozens of his missionaries in the 1900 Boxer Uprising — he became a byword for trusting God absolutely, and his mission continues today as OMF International.
fields.bio_html:
Before James Hudson Taylor was born, he had already been given to God. His father, a Methodist chemist in the Yorkshire town of Barnsley, had a burning interest in China and its uncounted millions who had never heard the name of Christ. Kneeling together, James and Amelia Taylor prayed over their expected child a prayer they scarcely dared speak aloud: "Grant that he may work for Thee in China." The boy, born on 21 May 1832, would not learn of that petition until he was a grown man. But heaven had heard it, and the whole of his long life would read like its slow, astonishing answer.

Childhood in a devout home did not make faith automatic. As a teenager Hudson drifted into doubt and a certain worldly coolness, troubled by his own unbelief. Then came a June afternoon in 1849. Seventeen years old and left to himself with a free half-day, he wandered into his father's library, pulled a gospel tract from a basket of pamphlets, and settled down expecting a good story and intending to skip the sermon at the end. The phrase that arrested him was simple: the finished work of Christ. Why finished? Because, as the cry from the cross declared, "It is finished" — a full and perfect atonement, the debt of sin already paid. There was nothing to add, only to receive. Alone in that quiet room, Hudson Taylor knelt and gave himself to the Saviour.

That same afternoon, seventy or eighty miles from home, his mother rose from the dinner table with an intense longing for her son's soul. She went to her room, turned the key in the door, and resolved not to leave until her prayer was answered. Hour after hour she pleaded for him — until at last a settled assurance came that the work was done, and she rose to praise God. When she returned home a fortnight later and Hudson ran to tell her his good news, she smiled: she already knew the very day and hour of his conversion.

The certainty of that shared answer marked Taylor for life. He had learned, before he owned any theology of missions, that prayer moves the hand that moves the world. The old childhood dream of China now returned as a settled call. He began, quite deliberately, to prepare his soul for a country where he would have no salary, no society behind him, and no friend at hand but God.

Learning to Move Men Through God

His training was as much spiritual as medical. Moving to the grim, ditch-side district of Drainside in Hull to work under a doctor and study medicine, he set himself a severe discipline: to live simply, give generously, and depend on God for everything. "When I get to China," he reasoned, "I shall have no claim on any one for anything. My only claim will be on God. How important, therefore, to learn, before leaving England, to move man, through God, by prayer alone." He tested the promise like a man testing ice before he trusts his weight to it.

One incident he never forgot. His employer was chronically forgetful about wages, and one evening Taylor found himself with a single half-crown to his name — no dinner in prospect for the next day. Called out to pray beside a dying woman in a wretched tenement, he was pierced by the poverty of the starving family around her bed. Something told him to give what he had. He struggled; it was his all. At last he pressed the coin into the poor man's hand, telling him that God was indeed a Father who could be trusted. He walked home with an empty pocket and a strangely full heart.

The next morning's post brought a small packet with no name attached. Inside was a pair of gloves, and folded within them, a half-sovereign — four times the coin he had given away. "Ha!" thought the young man, laughing for joy, "this is good interest. That is the bank I can put my money in." He had staked his last shilling on God, and God had settled the account.

In 1853, aged twenty-one, Taylor sailed for China with the Chinese Evangelization Society, tossed for months in a storm-battered sailing ship, arriving in a Shanghai convulsed by rebellion and war. The early years were hard and often lonely. Yet he did something that scandalised many fellow missionaries: he adopted Chinese dress, shaved his forehead and wore the queue, so as to remove every needless barrier between himself and the people he loved. To reach the Chinese, he was willing to become, as far as conscience allowed, Chinese. In 1858 he married Maria Dyer, a missionary's daughter of rare good sense and deep faith, who became the strong companion of his labours.

The China Inland Mission

Ill health forced the Taylors back to England in 1860, but rest gave Hudson no peace. Spread before him was a map of China's vast inland provinces, where whole populations — a million a month, he reckoned, dying without Christ — had no missionary at all. The burden grew unbearable. He longed for God to send workers, yet shrank from the crushing responsibility of asking men to go where he could guarantee them nothing but hardship. The struggle nearly broke his health.

The crisis broke on a Sunday, 25 June 1865. Unable to bear the pretence of worship, he walked out alone along the sands at Brighton. There, as the tide came in, he surrendered the whole weight to God: if God was calling the workers and God would keep them, then the responsibility was God's, not his. On the flyleaf of his Bible he wrote the words that founded a mission: "Prayed for 24 willing, skilful labourers at Brighton, June 25, 1865." Two for each of the eleven unreached inland provinces, and two for Mongolia. The China Inland Mission was born not in a committee room but in a prayer on a beach.

He opened a bank account for the new mission with ten pounds, and fixed its governing principles in prayer: the CIM would go to the unreached interior; it would take workers of any denomination and of ordinary background; it would never go into debt; and it would never appeal for money or solicit funds from any human being. Every need would be told to God alone. It was faith made into a method.

God's work done in God's way will never lack God's supply.

— Hudson Taylor

That principle was tested a thousand times over the following forty years, and it held. Money arrived, often unsolicited and often to the day, from people who could not have known the need. The mission's ledgers became a long, quiet argument for the faithfulness of God. Taylor was no dreamer about it; he counted every penny and kept scrupulous accounts. But he had settled it once for all that the God who calls also provides, and that a work begun and carried on in dependence on prayer would not be allowed to fail for want of funds.

Great Fruit and Great Sorrow

The fruit was immense — and so was the cost. The mission grew, stations opened across province after province, and hundreds of Chinese came to faith. But the same years were soaked in grief. Several of the Taylors' little children were laid in Chinese graves. In 1870, after burying yet another infant son, Maria herself died at the age of thirty-three, her strength spent in the work she had shared so gladly. Taylor, worn and often ill, wrestled with loneliness and with seasons of depression that he did not hide. His secret in those years was not an iron constitution but a discovered rest — the realisation, which transformed him, that the branch has only to abide in the vine, that Christ Himself would supply the strength the servant lacked.

I have not got to make myself a branch. The Lord Jesus tells me I am a branch. I am part of Him and have just to believe it and act upon it.

— Hudson Taylor

Out of that rest came his boldest ventures in prayer. In 1881, with the workers barely numbering a hundred, Taylor and his colleagues knelt and asked God for seventy new missionaries within three years. By the close of 1884, seventy-three had sailed. Emboldened, in 1886 they asked for a hundred new workers in a single year. By November 1887 the mission had accepted a hundred and two. He did not treat prayer as a formula for getting; he treated it as the natural commerce between a child and a Father who delights to give, and he was not afraid to name a number and let God answer it.

I have found that there are three stages in every great work of God: first, it is impossible, then it is difficult, then it is done.

— Hudson Taylor

The Long Shadow and the Homecoming

The deepest sorrow of Taylor's life came near its end. In the summer of 1900 the Boxer Uprising swept north China with fire and slaughter, and the China Inland Mission suffered more than any other society: fifty-eight of its missionaries and twenty-one of their children were killed. Taylor, aged and frail, was in Switzerland when the reports came, and the weight of it nearly crushed him — these were his own people, sent out by his own hand. "I cannot read; I cannot think; I cannot even pray," he confessed in the darkness of it, "but I can trust." When peace returned and the Chinese authorities offered compensation for the mission's losses, Taylor refused every penny, that the meekness of Christ might be shown to a watching nation.

His second wife, Jennie, who had married him in 1871 and stood beside him for over thirty years, died of cancer in 1904. The old missionary, now failing, set his face for one last journey to the land he had given his life to. He reached China in the spring of 1905, was carried through provinces once closed and now dotted with churches, and came at last to Changsha, the capital of Hunan — a city that had long resisted the gospel and now welcomed him. There, on the evening of 3 June 1905, quietly and without a struggle, he slipped away to be with the Christ he had served for more than half a century.
