He was buried in Chinese soil, among the people for whom his father and mother had prayed before he was born.

He left behind a mission that would grow to more than eight hundred missionaries in his lifetime and, through its successor the Overseas Missionary Fellowship (OMF International), continues to this day. But his truest legacy is not an organisation. It is a demonstration, worked out over seventy-three years and written across a whole continent, that God can be trusted absolutely — that His work, done in His way, will never lack His supply. The praying boy of Barnsley had become the answer to his parents' prayer, and a living proof that heaven still hears.

fields.name: Charles G. Finney
fields.bio: Charles Grandison Finney (1792–1875) was a lawyer turned evangelist whose preaching helped drive the Second Great Awakening across upstate New York and beyond. Convinced that revival was not a miracle to be waited for but the right use of God-given means, he pioneered the “new measures” of protracted meetings and direct appeal, saw whole towns transformed, and later became president of Oberlin College. His Lectures on Revivals of Religion has shaped how the English-speaking church has thought about revival ever since.
fields.bio_html:
Charles Grandison Finney came to the gospel late, and by an unlikely road. Born in Warren, Connecticut, in 1792, the youngest of nine, he grew up on the raw frontier of upstate New York, far from settled churches. He never went to college. Tall, striking, and formidably self-assured, he trained instead as a lawyer, reading law in the town of Adams, and he expected to make his life in the courtroom. Religion he regarded coolly — a thing the prayer meetings around him seemed to ask for endlessly and never quite receive.

But the law kept sending him back to the Bible. Blackstone's commentaries cited Scripture; the more Finney read to understand the one, the more the other pressed on him. Through the autumn of 1821 the pressure grew unbearable, until one morning he turned aside into the woods north of the village, resolved not to leave until he had settled the matter with God. There, alone among the trees, his proud lawyer's heart broke, and he gave himself to Christ.

That evening, back in the empty law office, the settlement was sealed in a way he never forgot. As he sat by the fire the presence of God swept over him wave upon wave, until he could scarcely bear it.

The Holy Spirit descended upon me in a manner that seemed to go through me, body and soul… it seemed to come in waves and waves of liquid love.

— Charles Finney, Memoirs

"I said, 'I shall die if these waves continue to pass over me,'" he wrote; "and yet I had no fear of death." The next morning a deacon came to remind him of a court case. "I have a retainer from the Lord Jesus Christ to plead his cause," Finney answered, "and I cannot plead yours." The courtroom had lost him for good.

The lawyer turned evangelist

He studied theology under a local minister, was licensed to preach by the presbytery in 1823–24, and married Lydia Root Andrews the following year. Then he went out into the "burned-over district" — the belt of upstate New York so scorched by successive revivals that observers thought no fire could catch there again. Under Finney it caught as never before. At Evans' Mills, Antwerp, Utica, Troy, and finally in the great Rochester revival of 1830–31, towns were turned upside down. He preached without notes, argued like the advocate he had been, fixed men with his eyes, and pressed for a verdict then and there.

The Rochester revival of the winter of 1830–31 was the crown of it. For six months Finney preached almost daily to the leading citizens of a booming canal town — lawyers, merchants, and their families — and the character of the whole city changed. Grog shops closed, quarrels were made up, and the awakening rippled out along the Erie Canal into town after town. Contemporaries counted conversions in the hundreds locally and believed the ripple touched tens of thousands across the region. It made Finney the most famous revivalist in America and fixed the pattern others would imitate for a century.

His conviction was that revival is not a miracle to be waited on passively but the fruit of ordinary means used rightly — and that ordinary people, convicted of sin, must decide.

A revival is nothing else than a new beginning of obedience to God.

— Charles Finney, Lectures on Revivals of Religion

To bring people to that beginning he pioneered what critics called the "new measures": protracted nightly meetings, plain extemporaneous preaching, the naming of individuals aloud in prayer, women praying in mixed assemblies, and the "anxious seat" — a bench at the front where the awakened sat publicly, unable any longer to hide. These are commonplace now; in the 1820s they scandalized the settled clergy.

The men who prayed him through

Finney never believed the power lay in the measures, or even in his own preaching. Again and again he traced it to hidden intercession. Two men in particular went before him into the fire on their knees.

"Father" Daniel Nash would arrive in a town weeks ahead of Finney, take a room, and give himself almost wholly to agonizing prayer while Finney preached. At Rochester, Abel Clary did the same — so burdened for souls, Finney wrote, "that he was not able to preach much, his whole time and strength being given to prayer." An eyewitness found Clary groaning on the floor, unable to rise.

Finney called Nash one of those men who "had such a powerful Spirit of prevailing prayer," and reckoned that the revivals rose and fell with this unseen labor. It was no accident, he thought, that when Nash died on his knees at the end of 1831, Finney's own itinerant work in the fields soon drew to a close. The visible preacher had always been carried by the invisible pray-ers.

The mill that stopped for God

One scene, told in his own Memoirs, captures the whole pattern — intercessors laboring in secret, and a conviction that fell without a sermon. Walking one morning through Mr. Wolcott's cotton factory near Whitesboro, Finney passed a young woman at a machine who was watching him and whispering, half in mockery, to a companion.

"The thread of one of the machines broke," Finney recalled, "and I observed that the girl's hands trembled so that she could not mend it." He came within a few feet and only looked at her, and she "sunk down, and burst into tears." Conviction ran down the line; operatives wept at their machines. The unconverted owner took one look and gave the order: "Stop the mill, and let the people attend to religion; for it is more important that our souls should be saved than that this factory run." The gates were shut, the hands gathered, and within days nearly the whole mill was converted.

Fire and opposition

Such power made enemies as well as converts. The emotional intensity of the new measures — and Finney's blunt, "denunciatory" preaching — alarmed the leaders of New England religion. The veteran revivalist Asahel Nettleton and the powerful Boston pastor Lyman Beecher set themselves against him, and in 1827 the two sides met face to face at the New Lebanon Convention to thrash it out. Beecher, by later report, warned him off:

I'll meet you at the state line, and call out all the artillerymen, and fight every inch of the way to Boston.

— Lyman Beecher, as remembered

The convention settled nothing, and the criticism only sharpened over the years. Old School theologians charged that Finney's stress on human ability and the sinner's will — worked out later in his Systematic Theology — had traded the sovereign grace of God for mere technique, making revival a thing men could manufacture. He lived under that accusation for the rest of his life. He was, by any reckoning, a controversial man; but tens of thousands dated their new obedience to God from the night they heard him.

Oberlin, and the long labor

From 1832 he pastored in New York City — first at Chatham Street Chapel, then at the Broadway Tabernacle built for him in 1836 — where he barred slaveholders from the Lord's Table, for his gospel had made him a fierce abolitionist. In 1835 he joined the new Oberlin Collegiate Institute in Ohio, an outpost of abolition and of coeducation, teaching theology and eventually serving as the college's president from 1851 to 1866. That same year, 1835, his Lectures on Revivals of Religion appeared and went round the world, shaping how the English-speaking church would think and pray about revival for generations.

The revivals did not end at the church door. Finney taught that a converted heart must show itself in a reformed life and a reformed society, and the awakenings he led poured energy into the great reform movements of the age — the crusade against slavery above all, but also temperance, education, and the opening of Oberlin to women and to Black students. Many of the era's most determined abolitionists dated their zeal to a Finney meeting. To him this was no distraction from the gospel; it was the gospel's fruit, obedience worked out where it cost something.

He preached and taught almost to the end, and died at Oberlin on August 16, 1875, at eighty-two. He left behind a divided verdict and an undivided passion: that no soul need wait, that God's work is done through praying people, and that revival begins the moment a heart turns, from the heart, to obey. "Religion," he insisted, "is something for man to do" — and having done it himself in a wood one autumn morning, he spent fifty years calling others to do the same.

fields.name: David Brainerd
fields.bio: David Brainerd (1718–1747) was a young missionary to the Native American peoples of colonial New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Expelled from Yale for his zeal, he gave his brief life to prayer and itinerant preaching among the Delaware and others, seeing a remarkable awakening shortly before dying of tuberculosis at twenty-nine. The diary he kept — published after his death by Jonathan Edwards — became one of the most influential missionary memoirs ever written, stirring generations that followed, from William Carey to Henry Martyn.
fields.bio_html:
David Brainerd lived twenty-nine years, spent barely four of them in ministry, saw no great crowds, founded no institution, and died coughing blood in another man's house. By every worldly measure his was a small, failed life. Yet the diary he kept — published after his death by Jonathan Edwards — has sent more men and women to the mission field than the biographies of a hundred famous preachers. He is proof that God measures a life differently than we do.

He was born on a Sabbath day, April 20, 1718, in Haddam, Connecticut, into a devout but sorrow-marked family; both parents were dead before he was fourteen. A serious, melancholy boy, he was much occupied with religion and much troubled by it, keeping fasts and reforming his conduct without finding peace. That came only in his twenty-second year. On July 12, 1739, walking alone at dusk, the weight lifted all at once.

As I was walking in a dark thick grove, unspeakable glory seemed to open to the view and apprehension of my soul… My soul rejoiced with joy unspeakable, to see such a God, such a glorious divine Being.

— David Brainerd, Diary, July 12, 1739

Expelled from Yale

That autumn he entered Yale to train for the ministry, and there his zeal outran his discretion. Caught up in the fervor of the Great Awakening then sweeping New England, the students grew critical of tutors they judged unconverted. Asked in private what he thought of one who had prayed without evident warmth, Brainerd said too much:

He has no more grace than this chair.

— David Brainerd, overheard at Yale, 1742

A freshman overheard and reported it. The rector demanded a public confession; Brainerd, believing the words private and the punishment unjust, refused — and for this, together with his attendance at a forbidden "Separate" meeting, he was expelled in the winter of 1742, in his third year. He never took a degree. The disgrace wounded him deeply and closed the ordinary doors of a New England pulpit to him. It also, providentially, turned him toward the one work for which he is remembered.

To the Indians

Licensed to preach in July 1742, he was taken up by a society for missions to the Native American peoples. In April 1743 he settled at Kaunaumeek, a lonely Housatonic village between Stockbridge and Albany, living in a wigwam and then a rough hut, sleeping on straw, learning the language, eating little, and riding many miles through the wilderness. He was often ill, often cold, and almost always alone. His diary from these years is a long record of physical hardship and spiritual desolation — and of a longing that swallowed every other consideration.

I cared not where or how I lived, or what hardships I went through, so that I could but gain souls to Christ.

— David Brainerd, Diary, July 21, 1744

Ordained by the Presbytery of New York in June 1744, he moved on to the Forks of the Delaware in Pennsylvania, and made hard, fruitless journeys to the Susquehanna. For a long time there was almost nothing to show for it. What sustained him was not results but prayer.

It should be said plainly that Brainerd was not a serene saint. His diary is famous — and to some readers troubling — for its relentless self-searching and gloom. He wrestled all his life with what we would now call depression, recording long seasons of "dejection," calling himself "the vilest creature living," and more than once longing simply to die. Edwards, when he published the diary, worried that its melancholy might mislead the young, and gently cautioned readers to imitate Brainerd's devotion without copying his despondency. Yet that very honesty is part of the book's strange power. Here is holiness not as untroubled triumph but as a sick, sorrowful, self-doubting man clinging to God through the dark — and being carried. It has consoled more discouraged believers than any tale of unbroken victory could.

The wrestling in the woods

Brainerd prayed the way other men work — to exhaustion. He set apart whole days for secret fasting and prayer; he "delighted greatly in sacred retirements," Edwards said, disappearing into the forest to pour out his soul for the people he had come to serve. One evening at the Forks, the night before he faced an idolatrous feast, he prayed until his body gave way.

"I was in such anguish, and pleaded with such earnestness and importunity, that when I rose from my knees I felt extremely weak and overcome," he wrote. "I could scarcely walk straight; my joints were loosed; the sweat ran down my face and body, and nature seemed as if it would dissolve." The next day he "withdrew into the woods" again and gave himself up afresh to God, "for life or death, for all hardships to which he should call me, among the heathen."

The wind at Crossweeksung

In June 1745 he came to Crossweeksung, a scattering of Delaware in New Jersey, and here the long, prayed-over drought broke into rain. He preached, not terror, but the free grace and compassion of Christ — and on August 8, 1745, to about sixty-five hearers, the answer came.

"The power of God seemed to descend upon the assembly 'like a mighty rushing wind,'" Brainerd wrote, "and with an astonishing energy bore down all before it… Almost all persons of all ages were bowed down with concern together, and scarcely one was able to withstand the shock of this surprising operation." Old men who had been "drunken wretches for many years," little children of six and seven, a conjurer, a murderer — all were crying to God for mercy. "I never saw any day like it, in all respects."

The change was not a passing emotion. Drunkenness was abandoned, debts were paid, quarrels were healed; within eleven months thirty-eight had made a public profession of faith, "all of whom appear to have had a work of special grace wrought in their hearts." Brainerd, careful and self-suspicious to a fault, was certain of one thing: he had not manufactured this. It had come as a gift, at the moment his own prospects looked worst, in answer to prayer.

A candle burned out

He had little time to enjoy it. The tuberculosis that had shadowed him for years now closed in; he coughed blood and could no longer ride his circuits. In the spring of 1747 he left the Indians and made his way to the home of Jonathan Edwards in Northampton, Massachusetts. There, nursed through his last nineteen weeks by Edwards's daughter Jerusha, he died at about six in the morning on Friday, October 9, 1747, not yet thirty years old. To the end his one desire was unchanged: "My work is done," he told them; "all my desire is to glorify God."

The little congregation at Crossweeksung was not left orphaned. Brainerd's younger brother John, also a missionary, took up the same work and shepherded the Delaware believers for years afterward, so that the awakening David had prayed into being outlived the man by a generation. What looked, at his deathbed, like a story cut off half-told, God quietly continued.

The diary that would not die

Two years later Edwards published An Account of the Life of the Late Reverend Mr. David Brainerd, built around the diary Brainerd had asked him to weigh. It became one of the most reprinted devotional books in the English language, and its quiet, wasting, faithful obedience lit fires that Brainerd never lived to see. John Wesley abridged and commended it. William Carey carried it to India and pressed it on others as a model. Henry Martyn read it at Cambridge and gave his life to missions in the East. Two centuries on, Jim Elliot filled his own journals in the same spirit before dying young in Ecuador. A short life, poured out among a forgotten people in the woods — and through it, God got to himself a name among the nations, exactly as Brainerd had prayed.

fields.name: John Bunyan
fields.bio: English writer and Puritan preacher, a Bedford tinker by trade who was imprisoned for more than a decade for preaching without a licence. During that confinement he wrote The Pilgrim's Progress, one of the most published allegories in the English language.
fields.bio_html:
He called himself the chief of sinners, and he meant it. John Bunyan was a mender of pots who spent twelve years in a county gaol rather than promise to stop preaching, and who dreamed there a dream that has been carried into more languages than almost any book but the Bible. He was not a scholar. He had, by his own reckoning, almost nothing when he began — no learning, no standing, no money, and for a long stretch of years, no peace. What he had was a conscience that would not let him alone and a Saviour who would not let him go.

The Tinker’s Son

He was born in 1628 at Harrowden, a hamlet in the parish of Elstow, just south of Bedford, and baptised in the Elstow font on 30 November of that year. His father was a tinker — a mender of pots and kettles — and John took up the trade after him. The family were poor, though not destitute; they owned the cottage they lived in. It was a small world, and Bunyan would spend nearly the whole of his life inside a few miles of it.

He learned to read and write, which was more than many of his neighbours could do, and then, as he tells it, he did his best to forget everything good he had ever been taught. In Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, the autobiography he wrote in prison and published in 1666, he is merciless about his own youth. He was a swearer and a Sabbath-breaker, the ringleader of the village young men in their sports. Modern readers, looking for the great scandal behind such self-accusation, generally fail to find one; his sins were the ordinary sins of an ordinary young man, magnified by a conscience that had been given eyes. That is worth noticing. Bunyan is not confessing to spectacular wickedness. He is confessing to being a sinner — which, it turns out, is harder.

In 1644 his mother and his sister died within weeks of each other, and his father remarried almost at once. That same year, at sixteen, Bunyan was mustered into the Parliamentary army and posted to the garrison at Newport Pagnell under Sir Samuel Luke. He saw little fighting. But he came home with one memory he never lost, and he set it down plainly:

When I was a soldier, I with others, were drawn out to go to such a place to besiege it; but when I was just ready to go, one of the company desired to go in my room: to which, when I had consented, he took my place; and coming to the siege, as he stood sentinel, he was shot in the head with a musket-bullet and died.

— John Bunyan, Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners

Another man stood in his place and took the shot that was meant for him. Bunyan records it among the mercies of his life — and then, with characteristic honesty, admits that at the time it did not move him at all. “Here, as I said, were judgments and mercy,” he writes, “but neither of them did awaken my soul to righteousness.”

Two Books and a Dish and a Spoon

He came home to Elstow, took up the tinker’s trade, and married. The record does not preserve his first wife’s name, which is one of the quiet griefs of Bunyan scholarship, for she may have done more for his soul than anyone before Gifford. They were, he says, as poor as poor might be — “not having so much household stuff as a dish or a spoon betwixt us both” — but she brought a dowry of two books left her by her godly father: The Plain Man’s Pathway to Heaven and The Practice of Piety. They read them together. The books did not convert him, he says, but they began something.

Their daughter Mary was born in 1650, and she was blind. She will matter enormously later.

Then, in the middle of a game of cat on the green — a stick-and-ball game the village young men played — something broke in on him. He had struck the ball one blow and was about to strike it a second time when, he says, “a voice did suddenly dart from heaven into my soul,” asking him whether he would leave his sins and go to heaven, or have his sins and go to hell. “At this I was put to an exceeding maze,” he wrote; “wherefore leaving my cat upon the ground, I looked up to heaven.” He stood there in the field, a young man with a stick in his hand, and felt himself looked at.

Three or Four Poor Women, Sitting at a Door in the Sun

What followed was not a conversion. It was the beginning of a long, wandering, agonising search that would take something like five years. Bunyan became outwardly religious, and rather pleased with himself about it. He was, he says, “a brisk talker” in matters of religion. And then he walked down a street in Bedford one day about 1651 and overheard a conversation that undid him.

They were poor women, sitting at a door in the sun, doing their work and talking. He drew near to listen, expecting to be able to join in. He could not. “I heard but understood not,” he writes, “for they were far above, out of my reach.” Their talk was of a new birth, of the work of God on their hearts, of how God had visited their souls with His love in the Lord Jesus, and of the promises that had held them up under the assaults of Satan. They spoke, too, of their own wretchedness of heart and unbelief, and they despised their own righteousness as filthy and insufficient to do them any good.

Bunyan went away shaken. He had thought himself a religious man. These women were speaking a language he did not know, out of an experience he did not have. He began to seek them out. He told them his condition, and they told their pastor, John Gifford, of him — and Gifford, a man with a hard past of his own, took the tinker in. He invited Bunyan to his house to hear him talk with others about the dealings of God with their souls. Bunyan sat under Gifford’s preaching, and said of him afterwards that his doctrine “was much for my stability.” Gifford taught his people to take no truth on trust from any man, but “to cry mightily to God, that He would convince us of the reality thereof” — because when temptation comes, borrowed convictions do not hold. Bunyan was to test that teaching to destruction. He joined the Bedford congregation in 1653 and was baptised by Gifford in the River Ouse.

The Years in the Dark

Any honest account of Bunyan must slow down here, because he did. The middle of Grace Abounding is one of the most harrowing records of spiritual distress in the English language, and it is the reason the book is still read. For months — years — Bunyan was tormented by the fear that he had committed the unpardonable sin.

The temptation came as a voice, and it came constantly: sell Christ, part with Him, let Him go. He fought it, he says, until he was almost out of breath, twenty times together. And then one morning, worn down, he felt the thought pass through his heart: Let Him go, if He will — and felt his heart consent to it. “Now was the battle won,” he writes bitterly, “and down fell I as a bird that is shot from the top of a tree, into great guilt, and fearful despair.”

What followed was years of horror. He was certain he was Esau, who sold his birthright for one morsel of meat and found no place of repentance afterwards though he sought it with tears. That verse followed him like a hound. It would “fly in my face like lightning.” He heard the sound of Esau’s fall in his ears. He was so raw that every sudden noise sounded to him like Fire! fire! He believed himself damned, and went about his work in Bedford as a man already sentenced.

It is important not to tidy this up. Bunyan was not being coy or rhetorical; he was, by any reasonable description, in profound and prolonged anguish. And he did not pray his way out of it in a week. He wrote it all down, decades later, because he thought some other poor soul in the dark might need to know that a man could be there and still be Christ’s.

The deliverance, when it came, came as suddenly and as unbidden as the despair:

But one day, as I was passing in the field, and that too with some dashes on my conscience, fearing lest yet all was not right, suddenly this sentence fell upon my soul, Thy righteousness is in heaven… I also saw moreover, that it was not my good frame of heart that made my righteousness better, nor yet my bad frame that made my righteousness worse; for my righteousness was Jesus Christ Himself. Now did my chains fall off my legs indeed.

— John Bunyan, Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners

His righteousness was not in his heart, where he had been frantically searching for it and never finding it. It was in heaven, at God’s right hand, and it was a Person. The chains fell off his legs — the man who wrote that sentence had not yet seen the inside of a prison. He would.

The Tinker in the Pulpit

The Bedford church discovered that their tinker could preach. He preached first to small gatherings and then to crowds, with an urgency that came straight out of the pit he had climbed from. “I preached what I felt,” he said — what he smartingly did feel.

Then the King came back. With the Restoration in 1660 the old penal laws returned, and preaching outside the Church of England became a crime. In November 1660 Bunyan rode out to preach at Lower Samsell, a farm near Harlington. He was warned that a warrant was out and that he should not go. He went. He would not, he reasoned, have his people say that their preacher had run at the first sign of trouble. They had just begun the meeting in prayer when the constable came in.

The indictment against him has a lovely, absurd pomposity to it: that John Bunyan, of the town of Bedford, labourer, “hath devilishly and perniciously abstained from coming to church to hear Divine service, and is a common upholder of several unlawful meetings and conventicles.” The sentence was three months. He served twelve years, because at the end of every offer of release stood the same condition — stop preaching — and he would not take it.

When one of the justices told him plainly that he must stretch by the neck for it, Bunyan gave the answer that has outlasted every one of his judges’ names:

I told him, as to this matter, I was at a point with him; for if I was out of prison to-day I would preach the gospel again to-morrow, by the help of God.

— John Bunyan, A Relation of the Imprisonment of Mr. John Bunyan

The Pulling of the Flesh from the Bones

Bedford gaol was not a dungeon. Bunyan was a prisoner of conscience, not a felon; he had visitors, a measure of liberty, and stretches of unofficial leave. He made long-tagged bootlaces by the thousand to send money home. Blind Mary came to the prison with a jug of soup for her father — the jug is still kept in Bedford.

And it very nearly broke him. Not the confinement. The family.

The parting with my wife and poor children, hath often been to me in this place, as the pulling the flesh from the bones… especially my poor blind child, who lay nearer my heart than all besides: Oh! the thoughts of the hardship I thought my poor blind one might go under, would break my heart to pieces.

— John Bunyan, Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners

“Poor child!” he writes, “thought I, what sorrow art thou like to have for thy portion in this world! Thou must be beaten, must beg, suffer hunger, cold, nakedness, and a thousand calamities, though I cannot now endure the wind should blow upon thee.” He knew exactly what he was doing to them: “I was as a man who was pulling down his house upon the head of his wife and children; yet, thought I, I must do it, I must do it.” He held on by two texts — Leave thy fatherless children, I will preserve them alive, and Verily it shall be well with thy remnant — and by one bare conclusion: “I must venture you all with God, though it goeth to the quick to leave you.”

His second wife Elizabeth — he had married her in 1659, a year after his first wife died — was barely out of girlhood and carrying his child when he was arrested. The shock put her into labour; she laboured eight days, and the baby died. In 1661 she stood before the judges at Bedford and petitioned for her husband, three times, and she was magnificent. She told Sir Matthew Hale: “My Lord, I have four small children that cannot help themselves, of which one is blind, and have nothing to live upon, but the charity of good people.” Hale asked how so young a woman came to have four children. She answered that she was only their step-mother, having not been married to him two years — and then told him about the eight days and the child that died. Hale looked very soberly at her and said, “Alas, poor woman!” Judge Twisden told her she made poverty her cloak. She got nothing. She went home.

The Ladder

Early in his imprisonment, not knowing the law, Bunyan became convinced that his sentence might end at the gallows. And the tempter met him there with the cruellest question of all: what if, when you come to die, you have no evidence upon your soul for a better state hereafter? He was ashamed, he said, at the thought of dying with a pale face and tottering knees in such a cause as this — of giving the enemy occasion to reproach the way of God for its cowardice. So he prayed. And nothing happened.

“Wherefore I prayed to God that He would comfort me, and give me strength to do and suffer what He should call me to; yet no comfort appeared, but all continued hid.” — Grace Abounding, §335. He was tossed like this, he says, for many weeks.

What came to him at last was not comfort but a duty. It was for the word and way of God that he was in this condition; therefore he was engaged not to flinch a hair’s breadth from it. God might choose whether to give him comfort now or at the hour of death — but he might not choose whether to hold his profession. “I was bound,” he wrote, “but He was free.” And so he made the most reckless resolution of his life: “I will leap off the ladder even blindfold into eternity, sink or swim, come heaven, come hell, Lord Jesus, if Thou wilt catch me, do; if not, I will venture for Thy name.”

“I was no sooner fixed in this resolution, but the word dropped upon me, Doth Job serve God for nought?” Bunyan saw it at once: to serve God with nothing left is the very mark of an upright heart. “Now was my heart full of comfort… I would not have been without this trial for much.” — Grace Abounding, §338–339.

The Dream in the Den

He wrote in prison, prodigiously — Christian Behaviour, The Holy City, Grace Abounding itself. And somewhere in those years, most likely in the later stretch of the long imprisonment, he began an allegory that he seems at first to have thought a distraction from more serious work.

It opens: “As I walked through the wilderness of this world, I lighted on a certain place where was a Den, and I laid me down in that place to sleep: and, as I slept, I dreamed a dream.” The Den was the gaol. Everything that follows — the burden, the Slough of Despond, the Valley of the Shadow of Death, Doubting Castle and Giant Despair, the river at the end with no bridge — came out of the life you have just read. Christian’s despair is Bunyan’s despair. The burden falls off Christian’s back at the cross because Bunyan’s chains fell off his legs in a field outside Bedford.

The Pilgrim’s Progress was published in 1678, after his release, and it went everywhere. Part Two, following Christiana and the children, came in 1685. A tinker who never went to university wrote the book that, for two centuries, sat beside the Bible on English-speaking shelves — because he wrote it in the plain speech of people who worked with their hands, and because every inch of it had been paid for.

Bishop Bunyan

He was released in 1672 under Charles II’s Declaration of Indulgence and licensed to preach. The Bedford congregation had already chosen him as their pastor while he was still in gaol. For sixteen years he rode — across Bedfordshire and the counties around it and down to London — preaching, settling disputes, visiting the scattered meetings, and writing. They called him Bishop Bunyan, half in affection and half in mischief, since a bishop was the one thing a Bedford Nonconformist could never be. He was briefly imprisoned again in the mid-1670s. In 1685, when persecution stirred once more, he quietly made over all his property to Elizabeth by deed of gift, so that they could not take it from her if they took him.

The River

In August 1688 Bunyan rode to Reading to reconcile a father and his son who had quarrelled. He succeeded. Then he rode on to London through a storm and arrived at his friend John Strudwick’s house on Snow Hill soaked to the skin. A fever took him. He died there on 31 August 1688, aged fifty-nine, and was buried in Strudwick’s vault in Bunhill Fields, among the Dissenters.

His last errand was making peace between a father and a son. It is hard to imagine a better one for the man who wrote that the way to the Celestial City runs through the valley, and that the pilgrim who goes down into it need not go alone.

fields.name: Thomas Watson
fields.bio: English Nonconformist Puritan preacher and rector of St Stephen Walbrook in London, ejected from his living in 1662. He is remembered for warm, vivid, and remarkably accessible devotional writing.
fields.bio_html:
Some men are remembered for what they did; Thomas Watson is remembered for what he said. The record of his life is thin — we do not know for certain where or when he was born, and even the year of his death was long guessed at wrongly. What survives instead is his voice: warm, brief, startlingly vivid, a preacher who could put more into one sentence than most divines managed in a page. Three and a half centuries on, he is among the most widely read of all the Puritans, and almost everything we love him for is on paper.

A life thinly recorded

Watson was born around 1620 — the date is an estimate, and his birthplace is uncertain, though Yorkshire is often suggested. Of his parents, his childhood, and his conversion, we know essentially nothing. This is not the biographer’s failure but the plain state of the record; Charles Spurgeon, who edited Watson two hundred years later and hunted for details, concluded flatly that the time of his birth and of his death was “nowhere mentioned.”

He emerges into view at Emmanuel College, Cambridge — the great nursery of Puritanism, which, as one contemporary observed, bred more Puritans and Nonconformists than perhaps seven of the other colleges combined. He took his BA in 1639 and his MA in 1642, and left behind the reputation of a laborious student. That reputation is worth pausing over. The compression and ease of his later writing — the sense that he is talking to you rather than lecturing — was not the fruit of a light mind. It was hard-won learning worn lightly, Hebrew and Greek and the church fathers digested until they came out as plain English. For a time he lived in the household of Lady Mary Vere, widow of Sir Horace Vere, a well-known haven of Puritan piety.

Sixteen years at Walbrook

In 1646 Watson came to St Stephen’s, Walbrook, in the heart of the City of London, first as lecturer and afterwards as rector. He stayed nearly sixteen years, and the church was constantly full. Around 1647 he married Abigail Beadle, daughter of John Beadle, a Puritan minister of Essex; they had at least seven children within thirteen years, four of whom died young. That last detail is recorded in a single clause, and then the record closes over it — but a man who wrote so tenderly about affliction working for good had buried four of his own children before he wrote a line of it.

His hearers valued his preaching. His contemporaries, strikingly, valued his praying even more. Edmund Calamy, in his account of the ejected ministers, called him a man of considerable learning and a judicious preacher, and then singled out one gift above the rest: he was “eminent in the gift of prayer.” Calamy offered a story as proof.

Before the Act of Uniformity, the learned Bishop Richardson came to hear Watson preach at St Stephen’s. He was pleased with the sermon — but he was moved by the prayer that followed it, so much so that he walked Watson home to thank him and asked earnestly for a written copy. “Alas!” Watson answered, “that is what I cannot give, for I do not use to pen my prayers; it was no studied thing, but uttered, pro re nata, as God enabled me, from the abundance of my heart and affections.” The bishop went away wondering that any man could pray like that unprepared. The story is Calamy’s, offered as evidence of a gift his generation thought remarkable.

The Tower, and a friend on the scaffold

Watson was a Presbyterian, and a royalist one. He protested against the execution of Charles I, and in 1651 he was drawn into the plot led by Christopher Love to bring in Charles II. He was imprisoned for it alongside Love and William Jenkyn. Love was beheaded. Watson petitioned for mercy and was released on 30 June 1652, and formally reinstated as vicar of St Stephen’s.

It is one of the sharper ironies of his life. The man who risked prison for the Stuart cause, and watched a friend die for it, would be turned out of his pulpit ten years later by the very king he had suffered to restore.

Black Bartholomew

The Act of Uniformity of 1662 required of ministers a conformity Watson could not give, and on 24 August — St Bartholomew’s Day — some two thousand were ejected from their livings. His loyalty counted for nothing. As Spurgeon put it, he had protested against the King’s execution and joined Love’s plot to bring in Charles II, “yet all this availed nothing, he was a Puritan”.

Three of his farewell sermons survive, preached to a congregation that knew it was losing him. In the second, on 2 Corinthians 7:1, he spoke of sixteen years among them with a candour that has not aged.

I have now exercised my ministry among you for almost sixteen years; and I rejoice and bless God that I cannot say, the more I love you, the less I am loved: I have received many signal demonstrations of love from you.

— Thomas Watson, Farewell Sermon at St Stephen’s, Walbrook (17 August 1662)

He would not promise to keep preaching to them, and would not promise to stop: “I desire to be guided by the silver thread of God’s word and providence.” Noting the Act’s language that ejected ministers should be as if naturally dead, he said that if he must die, he would leave them a legacy — and gave them twenty directions, urging them to treasure them “as so many jewels in the cabinet of your breasts.” Then, he told them, his strength was almost gone.

Preaching in the ruins

Ejected, Watson preached wherever he safely could — in barns, kitchens, outhouses, in dells and woods, to small illegal gatherings under threat of fine and imprisonment. Then in 1666 the Great Fire took the City, and St Stephen’s Walbrook with it. In the aftermath, with the parish churches burned, Watson and other Nonconformists fitted up large rooms for any who wished to come. There is something fitting in it: the man locked out of his church outlived the building, and went on preaching in its ruins.

Under the Declaration of Indulgence of 1672 he licensed the great hall of Crosby House in Bishopsgate Street, whose owner, Sir John Langham, favoured the Nonconformist cause. He preached there for several years, and from 1675 shared the pulpit with Stephen Charnock until Charnock’s death in 1680 — two of the finest minds of the age in one pastorate.

A cordial for hard times

In 1663, the year after he lost everything, Watson published A Divine Cordial — known now as All Things for Good — an exposition of Romans 8:28. It is worth remembering the timing. This is not comfort offered from a comfortable place; it is a newly silenced minister telling his people that the providence which had just wrecked his life was not out of control.

Several poisonous ingredients put together, being tempered by the skill of the apothecary, make a sovereign medicine, and work together for the good of the patient. So all God’s providences being divinely tempered and sanctified, do work together for the best to the saints.

— Thomas Watson, A Divine Cordial (1663)

That is Watson entire: a homely picture, exactly observed, carrying more weight than an argument. He never asks you to pretend the ingredients are not poison. He asks you to trust the apothecary.

God sweetens outward pain with inward peace. … After a bitter pill, God gives sugar. Paul had his prison songs. God’s rod has honey at the end of it.

— Thomas Watson, A Divine Cordial (1663)

On prayer — the gift his contemporaries marked in him — he was equally concrete. It is “a key that unlocks the treasury of God’s mercy”; it is “the Christian’s gun, which he discharges against his enemies”; it is “the sovereign medicine of the soul.” And, most simply: “Prayer keeps the heart open to God, and shut to sin.”

Barnston

His health at last gave way, and he retired to Barnston in Essex, his wife’s home country. He died there suddenly in 1686, and was buried on 28 July in the grave of John Beadle, his father-in-law.

He is said to have died alone in his closet, at private prayer. The detail is old and consistently repeated, but honesty requires the qualification its own sources give it: the earliest widely circulated account, in Spurgeon’s memoir, says he “died suddenly, in his closet at prayer, as is supposed” — and it misdates the death to about 1689 or 1690, whereas the burial register puts it at July 1686. So it is tradition rather than eyewitness: no one saw him go. He was found. What can be said with confidence is that a man his contemporaries thought eminent in prayer was last at prayer — and that if the tradition is right, the door closed on him mid-sentence, speaking to the God he had spent forty years commending to everyone else.

The long afterlife

Watson’s greatest work appeared only after his death: A Body of Practical Divinity, one hundred and seventy-six sermons on the Westminster Shorter Catechism, published in 1692 with the attestation of twenty-five leading ministers. It became a people’s theology, found for generations in the cottages of Scottish peasants — a folio that taught the unlearned to think.

His reach ran further than he could have known. Philip Doddridge records that in July 1719, a dissolute young soldier named James Gardiner, killing an hour before a midnight assignation, idly opened a book his mother had slipped into his baggage — Watson’s The Christian Soldier; or, Heaven Taken by Storm. What Gardiner reported next — a blaze of light, a vision of Christ crucified, a voice asking “O sinner, did I suffer this for thee, and are these thy returns?” — belongs to Gardiner’s testimony rather than to Watson’s biography. But the ejected minister, thirty years in his grave, was still preaching.

Spurgeon, who did more than anyone to restore him, judged him “concise, racy, illustrative, and suggestive,” combining “sound doctrine, heart-searching experience and practical wisdom.” His college principal, George Rogers, put it more bluntly: “I know of no work with so much sermon matter within the same compass.” Where Owen and Howe and Charnock must be quarried, Watson hands you the stone already cut.

We cannot tell you where he was born, or how he came to Christ, or what he looked like across a table. The man is mostly gone. But open All Things for Good and he is entirely there — unhurried, affectionate, reaching for honey and rods and bitter pills, determined that you should not kill yourself with care. Of a life so poorly recorded, it is a strange mercy that the best of it survived.

fields.name: Richard Baxter
fields.bio: English Puritan church leader and pastor at Kidderminster, ejected from the Church of England in 1662. A prolific author of practical divinity whose pastoral and devotional works became enduring Christian classics.
fields.bio_html:
Richard Baxter preached as a man who expected to die — not as a turn of phrase, but as a plain reading of his own body. For some fifty years he carried an assortment of illnesses that his physicians could neither name nor mend, and he began nearly every work of his life on the assumption that he would not live to finish it. He was wrong about that for half a century. In the meantime he wrote something in the region of a hundred and sixty books, turned a careless weaving town into one of the most famous parishes in England, refused a bishopric, lost his pulpit, and was hauled before the cruellest judge of the age. He is one of the strangest and most human figures the English church has produced: a man of enormous tenderness who could not stop arguing, a peacemaker who quarrelled, a dying man who outlived nearly everyone who pitied him.

A Shropshire Boyhood, and a Book at the Door

He was born on 12 November 1615 at Rowton in Shropshire, in his maternal grandfather’s house, and baptised at High Ercall. His father was also called Richard Baxter; his mother was Beatrice, born Adney. In February 1626 the family moved to Eaton Constantine. The religious instruction available to him as a boy was, by his own reckoning, poor — a succession of local clergy of varying seriousness — and the awakening of his conscience came not through a preacher but through second-hand books that arrived almost by accident.

The first was lent to his father by a poor day-labourer of the town: an old, torn copy of what Baxter calls Bunny’s Resolution — a devotional book written by Parsons the Jesuit and corrected for Protestant use by Edmund Bunny. Reading it, Baxter felt his heart moved as no sermon had yet moved it. Then a pedlar came to the door with ballads and a few good books, and his father bought Richard Sibbes’s The Bruised Reed. That book, he wrote, “opened more the Love of God to me, and gave me a livelier apprehension of the Mystery of Redemption.” Later a household servant turned out to own a fragment of William Perkins’s works, and that confirmed him. Neither he nor his father, he admitted, then knew a single person with any real understanding of religion; he had never so much as heard anyone pray without a book.

And thus (without any means but Books) was God pleased to resolve me for himself.

— Richard Baxter, Reliquiae Baxterianae

It is worth pausing on that sentence, because it explains a great deal of what followed. Baxter was converted by print, in a house with no Christian conversation in it. For the rest of his life he behaved as though a book pressed into the right hands could do what he himself could not travel far enough or live long enough to do.

The Want of Academical Honours

Baxter never attended university. This was not a Puritan principle or a pose of humility; it was a disappointment, and he said so. He had gone to the free school at Wroxeter under a schoolmaster named John Owen, and had done well enough at Latin to be ready for Oxford. Then, as he put it, “When I was ready for the University, my Master drew me into another way which kept me thence, where were my vehement desires.” He was sent instead to Ludlow Castle to read with Richard Wickstead, chaplain to the Council there. The Oxford he wanted never happened, and he felt the lack of it for sixty years. He knew exactly what it would cost him: “I knew that the want of Academical Honours and Degrees was like to make me Contemptible with the most, and consequently hinder the Success of my Endeavours.”

So he taught himself, ferociously and unsystematically, and the self-teaching shows in everything he wrote — the enormous range, the impatience with schools of thought, the habit of settling every question personally from first principles as though no one had asked it before. In 1638 he became master of the free grammar school at Dudley and was ordained by John Thornborough, Bishop of Worcester. He moved on to Bridgnorth in Shropshire for nearly two years. He was, by then, a young man in a hurry, and already unwell.

Kidderminster

In the spring of 1641, at twenty-six, he was invited to Kidderminster in Worcestershire, a town of handloom weavers, and was legally appointed on 5 April. The parish held around eight hundred families. Its previous ministry had been negligible, and its reputation was for drink and ignorance.

What Baxter did there over the next two decades became the model that half the pastors of England would afterwards try to copy. He preached, of course. But he was equally convinced that preaching alone would not do it, and so he and his assistant set aside two days a week and took fourteen families every week, working through the parish family by family, sitting down with each household in turn, no strangers admitted — aiming to cover the whole parish in a year and then begin again. Out of this practice came The Reformed Pastor (1656), the book that made personal, house-by-house catechising a Puritan ideal rather than an eccentricity. He kept, by his own count, six hundred communicant members out of those eight hundred families, and he would not gather a select congregation of the willing out of the parish: “I think Parish Work the best.”

The results embarrassed him to describe. He described them anyway, because, as he said, he owed God the sacrifice of thanksgiving and would not withhold it for fear of being thought proud. The congregation outgrew the building and they had to put in five galleries. On Sundays, walking through Kidderminster, you could hear a hundred families singing psalms and going over the sermon in their houses.

when I came thither first, there was about one Family in a Street that worshipped God and called on his Name, and when I came away there were some Streets where there was not past one Family in the side of a Street that did not so

— Richard Baxter, Reliquiae Baxterianae

He never got over it. “O what am I, a worthless Worm,” he wrote, “not only wanting Academical Honours, but much of that Furniture which is needful to so high a Work, that God should thus abundantly encourage me, when the Reverend Instructors of my Youth, did labour Fifty years together in one place, and could scarcely say they had Converted one or two of their Parishes!”

It was at Kidderminster, too, that a young gentlewoman named Margaret Charlton arrived — proud, fashionable, fond of romances, openly disdainful of the poor weavers of the town — and was converted under his preaching on conversion. Soon afterwards she fell into what Baxter called “a Cough and seeming Consumption, in which we almost despaired of her life.” He and his praying neighbours could not bear that someone so newly changed should be taken away at once, and they resolved to fast and pray for her. She recovered.

Baxter records the outcome plainly, and without embellishment. Margaret’s pulse “suddenly amended,” and the danger passed. “When God had recovered her,” he wrote, “her Mother invited those that fasted and prayed for her, to keep a Day of Thanksgiving for her Deliverance.” Margaret herself put her response in writing: “I here now renew my Covenant with Almighty God, and resolve by his grace to endeavour to get and keep a fresh sense of his mercy on my soul.” (A Breviate of the Life of Margaret Baxter, 1681)

The War, and the Chaplain

The Civil War broke out in August 1642 and Baxter, who wanted no part of it, was swept into it anyway. He tried neutrality, found the town unsafe, retired to Gloucester, then to Coventry with some thirty other fugitive ministers, where he served as chaplain to the garrison. After the Battle of Naseby he became chaplain to Colonel Edward Whalley’s regiment, on the advice of the Coventry ministers, and stayed until early 1647. He attended sieges but never fought. What he found in the New Model Army alarmed him permanently: a swarm of sectaries and enthusiasts arguing every doctrine of the faith into fragments, and he spent his chaplaincy trying, largely unsuccessfully, to argue them back.

In 1647 his body finally stopped him. A catastrophic nosebleed — one of many — ended his army service and left him languishing for months. Characteristically, he read providence into it, and reckoned afterwards that God had taken him out of the army before the army killed him.

Written in the Time of His Languishing

Baxter’s health is not a footnote to his life; it is the engine of it. He suffered from violent nosebleeds “in such excessive quantities, as often threatned my Life,” which he eventually concluded came from “Latent Stones in my Reins, occasioned by unsuitable Diet in my Youth” — kidney stones. To that were added a rheumatic head, a stomach that he said turned everything into wind, blood so sharp it excoriated his fingertips, and, after years of bleeding by physicians, a condition he named Praematura Senectus: premature old age, the infirmities of a man of eighty added to all the rest. He reckoned two great mercies in it. The first was that for all his bodily misery, he was never overwhelmed with real melancholy.

Convalescing at the house of Lady Rouse at Rous Lench in Worcestershire, far from home, with no book to consult but his Bible, and in continual expectation of death for months together, he wrote The Saints’ Everlasting Rest. He wrote it for himself, as a dying man’s meditation on the country he expected to enter within the year. Its title-page said as much: written by the author for his own use in the time of his languishing, when God took him off from his public employment. He then preached it at Kidderminster and published it in 1650, and it became one of the most loved devotional books in the English language. He lived another forty-one years.

Still thinking I had little time to live, My fervent heart to win mens Souls did strive.

I Preach’d, as never sure to Preach again, And as a dying man to dying men!

— Richard Baxter, Poetical Fragments (1681)

The Bishopric Refused

At the Restoration in 1660 Baxter came to London, was made a chaplain to the King, and for a short season stood near the centre of English religious life. He worked at the Savoy Conference of 1661 for a settlement broad enough to hold the moderate Puritans inside the Church of England, and drafted a Reformed Liturgy for the purpose. It was rejected.

Then came the offer. Colonel Birch approached him privately on behalf of the Lord Chancellor with the bishopric of Hereford — privately, Baxter noticed, so that a bishopric might not be publicly refused. Baxter would not give a flat denial while there was any hope of a broad settlement, but he was never in any doubt: “I told him that I was resolved never to be Bishop of Hereford, and that I did not think that I should ever see cause to take any Bishoprick.” He would live peaceably under whatever government the King set up, he said; he could not have a hand in executing it.

On 16 May 1662 he preached his farewell in the great church at Blackfriars. The Act of Uniformity required every minister to conform by St Bartholomew’s Day, 24 August 1662. Baxter did not conform. Nearly two thousand ministers went out with him in what became known as the Great Ejection — Black Bartholomew, the Dissenters called it — and English Nonconformity was born. Baxter was forty-six, and would never hold a parish again. He never returned to Kidderminster.

Three weeks later, on 10 September 1662, he married Margaret Charlton at Bennet-Fink Church. He was newly ejected, without a living, in poor health, and much older than she was; the marriage lasted nineteen years and was, by every surviving account including his own, exceptionally happy. Margaret managed their precarious life through the persecutions, and when she died on 14 June 1681 Baxter sat down within six weeks and wrote A Breviate of the Life of Margaret Baxter — a grieving husband’s memoir so candid about her gifts, her nerves, and her superiority to him in practical judgement that it remains one of the most moving documents of Puritan marriage.

The same year he published Poetical Fragments, verse written mostly for himself and for near friends in sickness. Among them was a hymn he called “The Covenant and Confidence of Faith,” to which he attached a single quiet footnote: This Covenant my Dear Wife in her former Sickness subscribed with a cheerful will.

My whole, though broken heart, O Lord! From henceforth shall be thine: And here I do my Vow record: This hand, these words are mine. All that I have, without reserve, I offer here to thee: Thy Will and Honour all shall serve, That thou bestow’dst on me.

Now it belongs not to my care, Whether I die or live: To love and serve thee is my share: And this thy grace must give. If life be long, I will be glad, That I may long obey: If short; yet why should I be sad, That shall have the same pay.

Persecution, and the Trial

The years after 1662 were shabby and grinding. He retired to Acton to study. He was imprisoned for holding a conventicle and got out on habeas corpus. His licence to preach was withdrawn; a meeting house he opened in Oxendon Street was shut after a single use. In 1680 officers came to his house and carried off his books and goods. In 1684 he was hauled three times to the sessions house and bound over for £400.

In February 1685 he was arrested on a charge of libelling the Church of England in his Paraphrase on the New Testament. He came to trial at the Guildhall on 30 May 1685 before Sir George Jeffreys, the Lord Chief Justice, whose brutality is not a matter of legend but of record. Baxter was sixty-nine and physically wrecked. Jeffreys had no intention of trying the case; he abused the old man from the bench, and the defence Baxter had prepared was never allowed to be heard. He was convicted, fined 500 marks, and imprisoned until it should be paid. He stayed in prison about eighteen months, until the government remitted the fine and let him go in late 1686. He published no account of the trial in his lifetime.

I now see more Good and more Evil in all Men than heretofore I did: I see that Good men are not so good, as I once thought they were, but have more Imperfections… And I find that few are so bad, as either their malicious Enemies, or censorious separating Professors do imagine.

— Richard Baxter, Reliquiae Baxterianae

That is Baxter reviewing his own mind in old age, and it is the nearest thing he ever wrote to a self-portrait. He was an irenic man who spent his life in controversy and knew it. He longed for Christian unity and managed to fall out with almost every party that might have supplied it — bishops, Independents, the army sectaries, and a fair number of his own allies. He wrote too much, conceded too little in argument, and repented of the sharpness afterwards. He is not improved by being tidied up.

Almost Well

After the indulgence of 1687 his last years were quiet. He served, unpaid, as assistant to Matthew Sylvester, valuing the younger man’s meekness and sound principles, and supplying from the pulpit what Sylvester lacked in delivery. He kept writing to the end.

When a visitor near the close asked how he did, Baxter answered: “Almost well.” The day before he died, Dr William Bates came and offered some words of comfort, and Baxter replied: “I have pain: there is no arguing against sense; but I have peace: I have peace!” He died at about four o’clock on the morning of Tuesday, 8 December 1691, aged seventy-six. Churchmen and Dissenters came to the funeral together, which in that year in that city meant something. He was buried beside Margaret and her mother in Christ Church, Newgate, and Bates preached the sermon.

Five years later Sylvester published the mass of autobiographical papers Baxter had left him as Reliquiae Baxterianae — sprawling, indiscreet, unrevised, and one of the great memoirs in the language. In it a man with no degree, no health, no pulpit for the last twenty-nine years of his life, and no talent whatever for leaving an argument alone, gives God the credit for a street in Kidderminster where the psalms could be heard through the windows.

fields.name: Jonathan Edwards
fields.bio: American Congregationalist preacher and theologian, a central figure of the First Great Awakening. He pastored in Northampton, Massachusetts, and briefly served as president of the College of New Jersey (later Princeton).
fields.bio_html:
He is remembered, unfairly, for a single sermon about a spider dangling over a fire. But the man who preached it spent most of his life on his knees in the woods, watching real spiders with delight, and writing some of the most careful prose ever produced in America about the beauty of God. Jonathan Edwards was a pastor who was fired by his own congregation, a missionary on a violent frontier, and a college president for five weeks. He was also, by common consent, the finest theological mind the American church has produced. The two facts belong together.

A Minister's Son in the Connecticut Valley

Jonathan Edwards was born on 5 October 1703 in East Windsor, Connecticut, the fifth of eleven children and the only son of Timothy Edwards, the town's minister. His mother, Esther, was the daughter of Solomon Stoddard, the formidable pastor of Northampton, Massachusetts — a man so dominant in the Connecticut Valley that people called him its pope. Jonathan grew up in a house of ten sisters and a great deal of Latin, and the shadow of his grandfather's pulpit fell across his whole life.

He was a precocious boy by any measure. He entered Yale College in 1716, just shy of his thirteenth birthday, and graduated in 1720 as valedictorian, staying on for two more years of graduate study in divinity.

Here a beloved story needs gentle correcting. It is often said that Edwards wrote a brilliant scientific essay on flying spiders at the age of eleven or twelve. The essay is real and it is wonderful — but the child-prodigy dating comes from his great-grandson and biographer Sereno Dwight, and modern scholarship has revised it. Edwards jotted his first observations in a notebook, Of Insects, around 1720–21 as a teenager, and sent the polished “Spider Letter” to Paul Dudley of the Royal Society on 31 October 1723, when he was twenty. The truth is less astonishing and more characteristic: a young man lying in the New England grass, tracking the gossamer of ballooning spiders across an autumn sky, and finding in them not merely mechanics but generosity — evidence, he wrote, of the exuberant goodness of a Creator who provided not only for the necessities but for the pleasure and recreation of all sorts of creatures, even the insects.

That instinct never left him. Edwards looked at the world and saw it leaking glory.

A New Sense of the Heart

His piety, however, was not yet his own. As a boy he prayed, by his own account, five times a day in secret, and he and his schoolmates built a booth in a swamp, in a very retired spot, as a place of prayer. Yet he later judged these seasons to be religious excitement rather than grace. And there was a doctrine he could not swallow. From his childhood up, he wrote, his mind had been full of objections against the doctrine of God's sovereignty — the idea that God might choose whom he would seemed to Edwards a horrible doctrine.

Then, around 1721, reading a doxology he must have read a hundred times before, something broke open.

As I read the words, there came into my soul, and was as it were diffused through it, a sense of the glory of the Divine Being; a new sense, quite different from any thing I ever experienced before.

— Jonathan Edwards, Personal Narrative

The text was 1 Timothy 1:17: Now unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory for ever and ever, Amen. What changed was not his information but his taste. The doctrine he had hated became, in his phrase, an exceeding pleasant, bright, and sweet doctrine. This is the hinge of everything Edwards would later write: the difference between knowing that God is holy and actually tasting it — what he called the sense of the heart. Holiness, he said, now appeared to him to be of a sweet, pleasant, charming, serene, calm nature, bringing an inexpressible purity, brightness, peacefulness and ravishment to the soul.

He became a man who walked. He spent most of his time thinking of divine things, year after year, often walking alone in the woods and solitary places for meditation, soliloquy, and prayer, and converse with God; and it was always his manner at such times, he said, to sing forth his contemplations. Prayer stopped being a duty and became a reflex — it seemed natural to him, he wrote, as the breath by which the inward burnings of his heart had vent.

Seventy Resolutions

Beginning in 1722, aged eighteen and serving a small Presbyterian congregation in New York, Edwards started writing resolutions — rules for a life he intended to spend entirely. He added to them over roughly a year; number thirty-five is dated 18 December 1722, the seventieth 17 August 1723. He resolved to read the whole list over once a week for the rest of his life.

They are ferocious. Resolved, never to lose one moment of time; but improve it the most profitable way I possibly can. Resolved, never to do anything, which I should be afraid to do, if it were the last hour of my life.

Resolved, to live with all my might, while I do live. … Resolved, that I will live so, as I shall wish I had done when I come to die.

— Jonathan Edwards, Resolutions, nos. 6 and 17

What saves the list from mere self-improvement is the sentence he wrote above it, before he wrote a single “Resolved.” He knew exactly what he was attempting, and how little he could manage it.

“Being sensible that I am unable to do anything without God's help, I do humbly entreat him by his grace to enable me to keep these Resolutions, so far as they are agreeable to his will, for Christ's sake.” — the prayer Edwards placed at the head of his seventy Resolutions, 1722.

The Young Lady in New Haven

In 1723, on the blank leaf of a Greek grammar, the same young man wrote something quite unlike a resolution. He had met Sarah Pierpont, daughter of the minister of the New Haven church. He was twenty; she was thirteen. He was, plainly, undone.

He wrote that there was a young lady in New Haven who was beloved of that Great Being who made and rules the world; that she would sometimes go about from place to place singing sweetly, and seemed to be always full of joy and pleasure, and no one knew for what. She loved to be alone, he wrote, walking in the fields and groves, and seemed to have some one invisible always conversing with her. He noticed her strange sweetness of mind and singular purity of affection — and that you could not persuade her to do anything wrong or sinful if you would give her all the world.

It is the loveliest thing he ever wrote, and it is not a love letter but a piece of theology: he had found a person who lived in the reality he had only just tasted. They married on 28 July 1727 and had eleven children. The marriage lasted thirty-one years, and he would call it, at the very end, an uncommon union.

Northampton and the Surprising Work of God

Edwards was ordained at Northampton on 15 February 1727 as his grandfather Stoddard's colleague. When Stoddard died in February 1729, the twenty-five-year-old inherited the most important pulpit in New England outside Boston.

In November 1734 he preached a series on justification by faith alone. What followed astonished him. Through the winter and spring the town was seized. Edwards reckoned that more than three hundred souls were savingly brought home to Christ in Northampton in the space of half a year, out of a town of some eleven hundred — and, he noted with his usual precision, about the same number of males as females. The town, he wrote, seemed to be full of the presence of God; never so full of love, nor of joy, and yet so full of distress.

He described it in A Faithful Narrative of the Surprising Work of God (1737), with careful case studies — Abigail Hutchinson, a young woman who died joyfully, and Phebe Bartlet, converted at four. It went through twenty printings by 1738 and made Edwards internationally famous. He had, in effect, invented the modern revival narrative.

Enfield, 1741

The greater Awakening came with George Whitefield's tour in 1740. On 8 July 1741, Edwards preached at Enfield, Connecticut — a town notorious for resisting the revival while its neighbours were swept — on Deuteronomy 32:35, Their foot shall slide in due time. The sermon was “Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God.”

The caricature has him roaring. The eyewitness record says otherwise about the room, if not the man: Stephen Williams, who was present, recorded that before the sermon was done there was such moaning and crying out through the whole house — What shall I do to be saved? — that the minister was obliged to stop preaching. Edwards read from a manuscript in a level voice. The terror was in the text, not the theatrics; and the sermon's actual climax is not the spider but the open door, the offer of mercy.

He spent the following years thinking about what he had seen, including its counterfeits. Religious Affections (1746) is his mature verdict: true religion, in great part, consists in holy affections — not in raw emotion, and not in cold assent, but in a heart genuinely changed toward God. In 1747 he published An Humble Attempt, calling Christians everywhere into united, extraordinary prayer for revival and for the nations. Remember that book.

Dismissed

Then came the reversal that no admirer can smooth over.

Stoddard had admitted to the Lord's Table anyone of upright life, whether or not they professed conversion; the practice had stood in Northampton for decades. Edwards came to believe it was wrong — that communion belonged to those who could make a credible profession of faith. When he said so publicly in 1749, the town turned.

The quarrel was not only theological. It ran through years of local grievance: disputes over his salary, his handling of the “Bad Book” affair in which he named respectable young people from the pulpit, and the long enmity of the powerful Williams clan. On 22 June 1750 an ecclesiastical council voted for his dismissal by 10 to 9, and the congregation ratified it overwhelmingly — more than two hundred to twenty-three. After twenty-three years, the most celebrated preacher in America was voted out by the people who knew him best.

On 1 July 1750 he preached his Farewell Sermon, from 2 Corinthians 1:14, on the day when pastor and people would meet again before the judgement seat. It is restrained to the point of severity. There is no self-pity in it. He was forty-six, unemployed, with a wife and ten children at home.

The Frontier Years

In August 1751 he was installed at Stockbridge, a mission settlement on the Massachusetts frontier, as pastor to a small English congregation and missionary to the Housatonic Mahican and, later, Mohawk peoples. It was a demotion by every worldly measure: a remote village, a mission school, a shrinking salary, and the French and Indian War closing in.

He was not a passive figure there. He fought the mission's tangled management, and he took the Native people's side against the local grandee Colonel Ephraim Williams — whose clan had helped drive him from Northampton, and whose relatives were now the chief seekers after Indian land. Edwards reported to the Boston commissioners that the Indians had a very ill opinion of Colonel Williams and the deepest prejudice against him, he having often molested them with respect to their lands and other affairs. He wrote letter after letter to Boston on their behalf. He was eventually vindicated — the commissioners declared themselves well satisfied as to his general conduct, and in February 1754 the mission's English patron Isaac Hollis made him overseer of the boarding school. It came too late; most of the Mohawks had already left over the years of mismanagement.

His advocacy and his blind spots sat side by side. He never learned Mahican or Mohawk, preaching through interpreters, and he shared his era's assumption that the gospel arrived bundled with English civilisation. Yet he wrote roughly a hundred and ninety original sermons for the Stockbridge congregation — far more than he troubled to compose for the English one — and he told his hearers plainly that we are no better than you in no respect, only as God has made us to differ and has been pleased to give us more light, and that wealth and worldly power were no evidence whatever of God's favour.

Honesty requires more here. Edwards also owned enslaved people. In June 1731 he travelled to Newport and purchased a girl named Venus, about fourteen years old; over the years the household included others — Joab, Rose, Titus, Joseph, Sue. In a 1741 draft defending a fellow minister he rejected the Atlantic slave trade as cruel while defending slaveholding itself. This is not a footnote to be managed; it is a real and grievous failure in a man who could dissect the human heart better than almost anyone who ever lived, and who did not turn that scalpel here. George Marsden's 2003 biography was the first major life to treat it squarely, and it should be treated squarely. It is worth noting, without using it as absolution, that his son Jonathan Edwards Jr. became an outspoken abolitionist, preaching in 1791 against the injustice and impolicy of the slave trade — asking why slaveholders should be exempt from the golden rule.

And in that hard village, with a quill and no library to speak of, Edwards wrote his greatest work. Freedom of the Will (1754). Original Sin, finished and published in 1758. The two dissertations — Concerning the End for Which God Created the World and The Nature of True Virtue — written at Stockbridge and published posthumously in 1765. The exile produced the treatises.

A Dark Cloud

In 1757 the College of New Jersey — later Princeton — called him to its presidency after the death of his son-in-law Aaron Burr. Edwards did not want it. In a remarkable letter to the trustees of 19 October 1757 he laid out his objections with almost comic candour, describing himself as having a constitution peculiarly unhappy, attended with a low tide of spirits, often occasioning a kind of childish weakness and contemptibleness of speech, presence and demeanor. He also told them he had a great work he meant to finish: a History of the Work of Redemption, a body of divinity in an entire new method, thrown into the form of a history. He submitted the decision to a council of ministers. They said go. He wept, and went.

He was installed on 16 February 1758. Smallpox was in Princeton, and on 23 February he was inoculated by Dr. William Shippen. The inoculation took badly; pustules formed in his throat and mouth, and he could not swallow. He weakened for a month. Shippen recorded that he showed a calm, cheerful resignation and patient submission throughout, without so much as one discontented expression.

He had been president for five weeks. His daughter Lucy was nursing him. Knowing he was dying, he gave her a message for her mother.

Dear Lucy, it seems to me to be the will of God that I must shortly leave you; therefore give my kindest love to my dear wife, and tell her, that the uncommon union, which has so long subsisted between us, has been of such a nature, as I trust is spiritual, and therefore will continue forever.

— Jonathan Edwards, last words to his daughter Lucy, March 1758

Those around the bed began to grieve aloud over what the college had lost. Edwards, whom they thought unconscious, spoke once more: Trust in God, and ye need not fear. He died on 22 March 1758, aged fifty-four.

Sarah, herself ill, received the news by letter. On 3 April she wrote to their daughter Esther: A holy and good God has covered us with a dark cloud. She followed him within months.

What Came After

He died with his great history unwritten, dismissed by his own church, buried on a campus he had barely seen. By the metrics he would have been tempted to use at twenty, the life reads as a series of closing doors.

But recall An Humble Attempt, that 1747 plea for Christians to unite in extraordinary prayer for revival and for the nations — a book that seemed, in his lifetime, to accomplish very little.

In 1784, more than a quarter-century after Edwards's death, an English Baptist named John Sutcliff came across An Humble Attempt and put its plea to his association: set aside an hour on the first Monday evening of every month for extraordinary prayer for the revival of religion and the spread of Christ's kingdom. They did. Sutcliff republished Edwards's book in 1789. In 1792, out of that praying circle in Northamptonshire, came the Baptist Missionary Society — and William Carey sailed for India. The prayer meeting Edwards asked for was convened, and answered, by men he never met.

He was not a plaster saint. He was voted out by his neighbours, he held people in bondage, he could be rigid, and he knew his own heart was worse than anyone guessed — he said he had a vastly greater sense of his own wickedness after his conversion than ever before. What he had was a settled conviction that God is infinitely, actually beautiful, and that the chief business of a human life is to see it and say so. He spent himself on that, with all his might, while he did live.

fields.name: George Whitefield
fields.bio: English Anglican cleric and one of the founders of Methodism and the evangelical revival. A famed open-air preacher, he toured Britain and colonial America and became a leading figure of the Great Awakening.
fields.bio_html:
He was the loudest voice of his century, and he began it carrying tankards.
