Before George Whitefield stood on a mound outside Bristol and spoke to two hundred coal miners — before the fields of two continents filled with people who had never darkened a church door — he was a boy in a blue apron, washing mops in his mother’s inn. He never quite forgot it. Of all the things that might be said about the man who helped set the Great Awakening alight, the one he insisted on himself was that God had found him low and lifted him.

The Boy in the Blue Apron

Whitefield was born in December 1714 at the Bell Inn in Southgate Street, Gloucester, where his mother kept the house. His schooling ended early. His mother’s circumstances were declining, and the boy who had shown a gift for speaking and acting decided that more Latin would only spoil him for a tradesman. So he went to work in the family business, and he described the descent without flinching:

I put on my blue apron and my snuffers, washed mops, cleaned rooms, and, in one word, became professed and common drawer for nigh a year and a half.

— George Whitefield, A Short Account of God’s Dealings with the Reverend Mr. George Whitefield

Even here there were signs. He had “sometimes the care of the whole house” upon his hands, and still, in the odd hours, he composed two or three sermons and dedicated one of them to his elder brother. A tapster writing sermons in an inn is either a comic figure or a prophetic one, and it took years to discover which.

Oxford, and the Long Road to Grace

In November 1732 he matriculated at Pembroke College, Oxford, as a servitor — the lowest rank of undergraduate, a student who paid his way by waiting on wealthier men. He was a servant again, in a gown. But at Oxford he found the small, mocked company known as the Holy Club, and through Charles Wesley he found the book that undid him: Henry Scougal’s The Life of God in the Soul of Man, which told him that true religion was not doing but union — Christ formed within.

The discovery did not arrive as relief. It arrived as a demand, and Whitefield, being Whitefield, threw his whole body at it. He fasted Wednesdays and Fridays through Lent, thirty-six hours together. He prayed prostrate under the trees in Christ Church Meadow. He gave away his money, refused fruit, wore filthy gloves and patched shoes for the sake of humility, and drove himself so hard that by the spring of 1735 his health broke and he had to leave the university. He was trying, with real courage and total futility, to earn what could only be given.

When it came, it came quietly, and he never got over it.

But oh! with what joy — joy unspeakable, even joy that was full of and big with glory, was my soul filled, when the weight of sin went off, and an abiding sense of the pardoning love of God, and a full assurance of faith broke in upon my disconsolate soul! Surely it was the day of my espousals, a day to be had in everlasting remembrance.

— George Whitefield, A Short Account of God’s Dealings with the Reverend Mr. George Whitefield

Every sermon he preached for the next thirty-four years was, in some sense, an attempt to hand that morning to somebody else.

The Ice Is Broken

Bishop Martin Benson ordained him deacon at Gloucester on 20 June 1736. He was twenty-one. He preached his first sermon the following Sunday in St Mary de Crypt, the church where he had been baptized, before a congregation full of people who remembered him in his childish days. It went rather well. Word came back to him afterwards, and he passed it on with obvious delight: a complaint had been made to the bishop that he had driven fifteen people mad. The worthy prelate, he was told, wished that the madness might not be forgotten before the next Sunday.

Fame arrived almost at once, and with it the closing of doors. The churches that had thronged to hear the boy preacher began to bolt themselves against his doctrine of the new birth. And so, in the bleak February of 1739, denied pulpits and unwilling to be silent, he did the thing that changed everything. He rode out to Kingswood, where the colliers lived — men reputed to be little better than heathens, whom no one had troubled to evangelize — climbed a mount, and preached in the open air to about two hundred of them.

Blessed be God that I have now broken the ice! I believe I was never more acceptable to my Master than when I was standing to teach those hearers in the open fields. Some may censure me; but if I thus pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.

— George Whitefield, Journals, 17 February 1739

Within weeks the two hundred had become thousands, and at length, by a moderate computation, something near twenty thousand. These were people with no religious reputation to protect, no righteousness to defend, and Whitefield noticed that this made them quick to believe. His account of what he saw has outlived nearly everything else he wrote:

Having no righteousness of their own to renounce, they were glad to hear of a Jesus, who was a friend to publicans, and came not to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance. The first discovery of their being affected, was, to see the white gutters made by their tears, which plentifully fell down their black cheeks, as they came out of their coal-pits.

— George Whitefield, quoted in John Gillies, Memoirs of the Life of the Reverend George Whitefield (1772)

It is worth pausing there. The image endures not because it is dramatic but because it is exact: grace is the thing that shows up as a clean line on a dirty face. He had taken the field, and he never left it.

The Atlantic and the Awakening

Whitefield crossed the ocean at an age when crossing it was an ordeal — seven visits to America, thirteen Atlantic passages in all, months at a time in a wooden ship. In 1739–40 he rode from Georgia to New England and back, preaching daily, and the scattered local stirrings of religion fused behind him into what we now call the Great Awakening. He preached in fields, from courthouse steps, in Philadelphia streets where Benjamin Franklin — unconverted, affectionate, and skeptical — measured the carrying power of his voice and printed his journals. He was, in effect, the first figure known personally to the whole seaboard, and he was known for one message: you must be born again.

Bethesda, and Its Shadow

The burden of his life was an orphanage. He began building Bethesda near Savannah on 25 March 1740, and for thirty years he begged for it, collected for it, defended its accounts, and poured his own money into it. Some of his most affecting preaching was fundraising, and he was scrupulous about it: sworn audits confirmed he had never converted a penny of it to his own use, and had charged the house with none of his travelling expenses.

And it is here that honesty requires the hardest paragraph. Bethesda was expensive, and Whitefield became convinced it could not survive on free labour. In 1747 he used £300 given him at Charleston to buy a South Carolina plantation and enslaved people to work it for the orphanage’s support, writing that it was “impossible for the inhabitants to subsist without the use of slaves.” Georgia’s founding charter had banned slavery; Whitefield lobbied the Trustees to overturn that ban, arguing to them that “had negroes been allowed, I should now have had a sufficiency to support a great many orphans,” and that Georgia “never can be a flourishing province, unless negroes are employed.” The prohibition fell in 1751. He campaigned for that outcome, he welcomed it, and he owned enslaved men and women until his death.

He cannot be excused on the grounds that no one knew better; he knew better himself. He wrote that the enslaved were “brought in a wrong way from their native country,” and that it was “a trade not to be approved of” — then reasoned that since it would continue regardless, he might as well profit by it and evangelize the people he bought. He had earlier rebuked Southern planters, in print, for their cruelty to those they held. That is precisely what makes it damning rather than merely tragic: the man who could see, across an entire ocean, that a coal miner had a soul, looked directly at slavery, named it wrong, and built his charity on it anyway. The gospel he preached would eventually arm the abolitionists. It did not reach his own accounts. Any honest love of Whitefield has to hold this without softening it.

Two Friends, One Gospel

His friendship with John Wesley was the great affection and the great wound of his public life. They had been brothers in the Holy Club; it was Whitefield who handed Wesley the open-air fields at Kingswood. But Wesley preached and printed Free Grace against predestination, and Whitefield — a convinced Calvinist — answered with a letter of remonstrance in December 1740. The rupture was public, painful, and exploited by lesser men on both sides. Whitefield came to regret the noise of it deeply, and refused to let the breach harden into enmity. They preached in each other’s pulpits again. They differed to the end and loved each other to the end.

The proof came posthumously. His friend Robert Keen had often asked him, half in jest, who should preach his funeral sermon if he died abroad — must it be his old friend Mr. John Wesley? Whitefield’s answer, given again and again, was three words: “He is the man.” And so when the news reached London, Wesley was engaged by the executors, and on Sunday 18 November 1770 he stood in Whitefield’s own chapel in Tottenham Court Road before an immense multitude gathered from every corner of the town, and preached his rival’s funeral. Wesley recorded that it was an awful season; all were still as night. Whichever of them was right about election, that scene is one of the more beautiful arguments for the faith they shared.

Weary in the Work, Not of It

The scale of his labour is hard to credit. His friend Henry Venn testified that for many years Whitefield preached from forty to sixty hours every week. The figure most often attached to his name — that he preached upwards of eighteen thousand sermons — deserves care rather than repetition. It is not a modern guess: Augustus Toplady, who knew him, reported that it came from a book in which Whitefield himself minuted the times and places of his ministerial labours, and the same number was later cut into his cenotaph. Even so, it is a claim resting on a record we can no longer inspect, and the honest form of it is that a contemporary, citing Whitefield’s own notebook, put the total above eighteen thousand. Call it an estimate on good authority rather than a counted fact. The truth it gestures at is not in dispute.

It cost him his body. Asthmatic and worn out at fifty-five, he was urged to slow down and would not. Told he should preach less often, he replied simply that he had rather wear out than rust out.

On Saturday 29 September 1770 he rode fifteen miles from Portsmouth to Exeter and preached in the fields to a great multitude. Before he went out, a friend named Clarkson, seeing him more uneasy than usual, told him he was fitter for bed than for the pulpit. “True, sir,” Whitefield said — and then turned aside, clasped his hands, looked up, and prayed:

Lord Jesus, I am weary in thy work, but not of thy work. If I have not yet finished my course, let me go and speak for thee once more in the fields, seal thy truth, and come home and die.

He preached for two hours. Then he dined, rode on to Newburyport, ate a small supper, said he was tired, and went upstairs. He read his Bible with Dr. Watts’s psalms lying open beside him, knelt at the bedside, and closed the evening with prayer. Waking in the night unable to breathe, he prayed again — that God would bless the preaching he had done, and the preaching he meant to do that day, that more souls might be brought to Christ; and for a blessing on his Bethesda. He died at about six on the morning of 30 September 1770, in the parsonage of the Old South Presbyterian Church.

The prayer at Exeter was answered to the letter, and within the day. He was given the fields once more; he sealed the truth; he came home and died. His travelling companion, Richard Smith, was at his side through the night and wrote the account down — which is the only reason we have both halves of it, the asking and the granting.

At his own desire he was buried where he lies still, in a vault beneath the pulpit at Newburyport — under a preaching place, which is exactly right. He had asked for one more sermon and then rest, and received both, and the man who had spent thirty-four years telling strangers in open fields that they must be born again went to find out whether he had told them the truth.

Read him for the fire, and for the joy that started it. Read him, too, with your eyes open. He was a servitor who became a voice for millions and never stopped being astonished by grace — and he was a man who held people as property while preaching that Christ had died for them. Both are true. He would be the first to tell you that whatever was good in him was borrowed, and the last to claim the loan had made him worthy of it.

fields.name: John Wesley
fields.bio: English Anglican cleric and evangelist who founded Methodism. A tireless itinerant preacher and organiser, he was a central figure of the 18th-century evangelical revival.
fields.bio_html:
John Wesley rode further, preached oftener, and slept less than almost any man of his century, and he did it for more than fifty years on roads that would break a modern traveller in a week. He founded no denomination on purpose. He died an Anglican priest, insisting to the end that he had never left the Church of England. Yet the movement he organised — Methodism — outlived him, crossed oceans, and reshaped the religious life of two nations. What makes his story worth telling is not the scale of it. It is that the man at the centre of all that motion spent his first thirty-five years desperately, methodically, and unsuccessfully trying to earn what he was finally given for nothing.

A brand plucked out of the burning

He was born at Epworth rectory in Lincolnshire on 17 June 1703, the fifteenth child of Samuel Wesley, a difficult and often debt-ridden parson, and his remarkable wife Susanna. Of the nineteen children Susanna bore, fewer than half lived to grow up. The parish resented Samuel; on more than one occasion its rougher members expressed the resentment with fire.

On the night of 9 February 1709, the rectory burned. The family scrambled out into the garden and counted heads, and one was missing. John, not yet six, had been left asleep in an upstairs room. He woke to find the roof alight, climbed onto a chest, and appeared at the window. There was no ladder and no time to fetch one. Neighbours made a ladder of themselves — one man standing on another’s shoulders — and pulled the boy through the window. Moments later the roof fell in.

Susanna never got over it, and never meant to. She took the rescue as a summons, and reached for Zechariah 3:2 to name it: her son was a brand plucked out of the burning. Two years later, on 17 May 1711, she wrote a private meditation that reads less like sentiment than like a contract.

“I do intend to be more particularly careful of the soul of this child, that Thou hast so mercifully provided for, than ever I have been; that I may do my endeavours to instil into his mind the disciplines of Thy true religion and virtue.” — Susanna Wesley’s meditation, 17 May 1711, written two years after the fire that nearly took her son.

The phrase stuck to Wesley for life. He adopted it himself in his mid-thirties, and in 1753, gravely ill and expecting to die, he drafted his own epitaph: Here lieth the body of John Wesley, a brand plucked out of the burning. He then lived another thirty-seven years.

The school of Susanna

The deepest formation of Wesley’s life happened in his mother’s kitchen. Susanna Wesley — whose own writings are held in this library — ran the rectory as a school, a monastery, and a small republic of the soul. School hours were inviolable, nine to twelve and two to five. Each child learned the alphabet in a single day, beginning the day after their fifth birthday. Each got one evening a week alone with their mother, and John’s was Thursday; he was still writing to her about those Thursdays as an Oxford don.

In 1732 the grown son asked his mother to write down her method. She did, on 24 July, and the letter is one of the founding documents of Methodism, though it never mentions the word. Its centre is a conviction that is bracing and, to modern ears, hard: “As self-will is the root of all sin and misery, so whatever cherishes this in children insures their after wretchedness and irreligion; whatever checks and mortifies it, promotes their future happiness and piety.”

Judge the doctrine as you will — here is what matters biographically. When John Wesley later built a movement out of small groups, fixed hours, searching questions, written rules, and relentless self-examination, he was not inventing a system. He was reproducing his mother’s house on a national scale. It is fair to say that Susanna organised Methodism before her son was old enough to name it.

Oxford and the Holy Club

From his mother’s kitchen Wesley went to Charterhouse School in London, and from Charterhouse up to Christ Church, Oxford, in 1720. He took his degree in 1724 and stayed. He was ordained deacon on 19 September 1725, elected a Fellow of Lincoln College on 17 March 1726 — a genuine distinction, and a living — and ordained priest on 22 September 1728. Returning to Oxford, he found that his younger brother Charles had gathered a handful of undergraduates for prayer, study, fasting, and visits to the town’s prisons and poor. John took it over, as he took most things over.

The university found them ridiculous. The nicknames came fast: Bible Moths, the Holy Club, and the one that lasted — Methodists, for their methodical, clockwork piety. By 1732 there was a pamphlet about them. George Whitefield, a servitor working his way through Pembroke, joined and was changed by it.

They fasted, they communed weekly, they parcelled out their hours, they examined their motives to the point of scruple. And by his own later verdict, John Wesley — ordained priest, Oxford Fellow, and the most disciplined man in the room — was not yet a Christian. The machinery was perfect. It was simply not connected to anything.

Georgia: the humbling

In October 1735 he sailed for the new colony of Georgia, to serve the settlers and, he hoped, to convert the Indians. The voyage taught him more than the mission did.

On 25 January 1736 the Simmonds ran into an Atlantic storm. A company of Moravians — German pietists, emigrating with their women and children — were in the middle of a psalm when, as Wesley recorded, the sea “broke over, split the mainsail in pieces, covered the ship, and poured in between the decks.” The English passengers panicked. Wesley panicked. And the Germans, he wrote in six words that clearly cost him something to set down, “calmly sang on.”

Afterwards he went and asked one of them the question that was eating him. “Were you not afraid?” The man answered, “I thank God, no.” Wesley pressed: “But were not your women and children afraid?” The reply came mildly. “No; our women and children are not afraid to die.”

Wesley was a priest of the Church of England, sailing to save souls, and he had just discovered that he was more frightened of drowning than the peasants in the hold. It is the hinge of his life. He never forgot it, and to his great credit he wrote it down rather than editing it out.

Georgia itself went badly and then worse. He was rigid where he needed tact, and his pastoral care of a young woman named Sophy Hopkey blurred into a courtship he could neither commit to nor relinquish. When she married another man, Wesley repelled her from Communion on a technicality. Her husband’s family had him indicted. In December 1737 he slipped out of the colony and sailed for home, a failure by any public measure. Sailing back, he set down the verdict himself: he had gone to America to convert others, and had never been converted himself.

Aldersgate

In London the Moravians pursued him. Peter Böhler, a young man ten years his junior, told Wesley what he had no wish to hear — that he lacked saving faith. Wesley, a priest, asked whether he should therefore stop preaching. Böhler’s answer is one of the great pieces of pastoral counsel: “Preach faith till you have it; and then, because you have it, you will preach faith.”

He preached it for eleven weeks without having it. Then, on the evening of 24 May 1738, he went to a society meeting in Aldersgate Street — unwillingly, he notes, which is the most Wesleyan detail in the whole account. Someone was reading aloud Luther’s preface to Romans.

“About a quarter before nine, while he was describing the change which God works in the heart through faith in Christ, I felt my heart strangely warmed. I felt I did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation; and an assurance was given me that He had taken away my sins, even mine, and saved me from the law of sin and death.”

— John Wesley, Journal, 24 May 1738

Note what the moment gave him: not new doctrine, and not a new standard of holiness. He had those already, in punishing quantity. What he received was assurance — the thing the Moravian had in the storm. The disciplined man was finally told he could stop auditioning.

The fields

Whitefield, meanwhile, had begun doing something scandalous: preaching outdoors, to colliers, in the open air. He begged Wesley to come to Bristol and take it up. Wesley recoiled. He was, he admitted, “so tenacious of every point relating to decency and order that I should have thought the saving of souls almost a sin if it had not been done in a church.”

He submitted. On 2 April 1739, borrowing David’s words to Michal, he wrote: “At four in the afternoon, I submitted to be more vile and proclaimed in the highways the glad tidings of salvation, speaking from a little eminence in a ground adjoining to the city, to about three thousand people.” The fastidious Oxford Fellow had become a hedge-preacher, and the Church of England’s pulpits began closing against him. Challenged for trespassing on other men’s parishes, he replied with the sentence that became Methodism’s motto.

“I look upon all the world as my parish; thus far I mean, that, in whatever part of it I am, I judge it meet, right, and my bounden duty to declare unto all that are willing to hear, the glad tidings of salvation.”

— John Wesley, Journal, 11 June 1739

The long road

From that spring until he was too frail to mount a horse, Wesley was almost never still. He rose at four, preached at five to workers on their way to the pits and mills, and covered his miles with a book propped open in the saddle, having trained his horse to keep the road while he read. He was stoned, mobbed, bulled, and refused lodging; he was also, by the end, the most beloved man in England.

The famous figures — roughly 250,000 miles on horseback and some 40,000 sermons — deserve an honest caveat. Wesley never tallied them himself. They are traditional estimates, extrapolated by later biographers from the itineraries in his Journal, and the numbers wobble between sources: 225,000 miles or 250,000; 40,000 sermons or 42,000. Treat them as a fair order of magnitude rather than an audit. The Journal itself, kept for over fifty years, is the real evidence, and it is staggering enough without arithmetic.

The method

Wesley’s durable genius was not oratory — Whitefield outpreached him — but organisation. He gathered converts into societies, then broke the societies into classes of about a dozen, each with a leader who met them weekly and asked how their souls prospered. Nobody could hide. He commissioned lay preachers, ordinary tradesmen, when no clergy would help him, and gathered them into an annual Conference from 1744. In 1784 he secured the movement’s legal future with the Deed of Declaration, and — the step that finally made separation from the Church of England inevitable — ordained ministers for America himself, sending Thomas Coke, Richard Whatcoat, and Thomas Vasey to a new nation whose bishops would not serve it.

There was a doctrine to match the machinery. Wesley preached grace at every stage of the Christian life — grace that goes before conversion and awakens the sinner, grace that justifies through faith, grace that keeps working long after forgiveness — and he refused to let salvation stop at pardon. His most contested teaching, Christian perfection, or entire sanctification, has been misheard ever since: he never claimed that believers stop sinning, but that love for God and neighbour can grow until it governs a life, and that every Christian should pursue that maturity through the ordinary means of grace — prayer, Scripture, the Lord’s Supper, fasting, works of mercy. It was the Holy Club’s old programme, resurrected on the far side of Aldersgate: the same discipline, now running on assurance instead of anxiety.

The works of mercy were not a footnote. The societies were engines of practical compassion as much as of piety — Wesley visited prisoners all his life, established schools, and organised medical care for the poor who could never have afforded a physician, convinced that a Christianity which did not transform both the believer and the street the believer lived on was not the real article.

He was equally practical about money. His sermon The Use of Money gives three rules, and they are routinely misquoted — the first word is gain, not earn, and the order matters, because giving comes last for a reason.

“Gain all you can, without hurting either yourself or your neighbour, in soul or body — save all you can, by cutting off every expense which serves only to indulge foolish desire — and then, give all you can, or, in other words, give all you have to God.”

— John Wesley, The Use of Money, Sermon 50

He obeyed his own rule. As his book royalties grew, he held his living expenses flat and gave away the remainder, dying with almost nothing but a well-worn coat, a few coins, and the Methodist Church.

Whitefield: the friend he fought

The friendship that launched the revival nearly broke it. Whitefield was a convinced Calvinist; Wesley was not, and in 1739 he preached and then published Free Grace, an unsparing assault on predestination. It wounded Whitefield, who felt the harmony of the awakening — when all had been “like little children” — had been shattered by his friend’s pen. They divided, and the revival ran in two channels thereafter.

But they did not stay divided, and this is where both men grew. They reached what one of Wesley’s preachers called an agreement to differ, and the affection outlasted the argument. The proof came at the end. Asked repeatedly who should preach his funeral sermon should he die abroad, Whitefield kept naming the man who had attacked his theology in print: “He is the man.” Whitefield died in America in 1770, and on 18 November John Wesley stood up and preached his funeral sermon, generously.

Molly

The record must be honest here, and the honesty is not flattering. In February 1751 Wesley married Mary Vazeille — Molly — a well-to-do widow with four children. It went wrong quickly and stayed wrong for thirty years. He would not stop travelling; she would not accept a husband who was never home and whose correspondence with other women she read and resented. She left, returned, and left again.

On 23 January 1771 she set out for Newcastle intending never to come back, and Wesley recorded it in his Journal in three flat Latin clauses — Non eam reliqui: non dimisi: non revocabo — which his editors render: I did not desert her; I did not send her away; I will not recall her. The English version so often quoted is a translator’s, not Wesley’s. Either way it is a cold sentence, and it is his. She died on 8 October 1781; he was away preaching and learned of it only after she was buried. The man who could organise the spiritual lives of tens of thousands could not manage the one nearest to him. He knew it, and never really explained it.

The last battle

Wesley’s finest hour came last. He had loathed slavery since Georgia, but in February 1772 an anti-slavery tract by the Quaker Anthony Benezet lit the fuse. His Journal entry for the 12th is one of the great sentences in the literature of abolition: he had been reading, he wrote, “a very different book, published by an honest Quaker, on that execrable sum of all villanies, commonly called the slave trade.” In 1774 he published Thoughts upon Slavery, refusing every economic evasion of his age: “I absolutely deny all slave-holding to be consistent with any degree of even natural justice.”

He was still at it at eighty-seven. On the morning of 24 February 1791, six days before his death, having read a tract by a “poor African” — generally identified as Olaudah Equiano’s Interesting Narrative — he took up his pen for a young Member of Parliament who was losing, year after year, a bill to abolish the slave trade.

“Unless the divine power has raised you up to be as Athanasius contra mundum, I see not how you can go through your glorious enterprise in opposing that execrable villainy, which is the scandal of religion, of England, and of human nature. Unless God has raised you up for this very thing, you will be worn out by the opposition of men and devils. But if God be for you, who can be against you? … Go on, in the name of God and in the power of His might, till even American slavery (the vilest that ever saw the sun) shall vanish away before it.”

— John Wesley, letter to William Wilberforce, 24 Feb 1791

It is the last letter of his that survives. He closed it, as he closed his life, by praying for somebody else.

“That He who has guided you from youth up may continue to strengthen you in this and all things is the prayer of, dear sir, Your affectionate servant.” — Wesley’s closing words to Wilberforce, written six days before his death. Wilberforce was not worn out. The slave trade was abolished throughout the British Empire in 1807, and slavery itself in 1833, the year Wilberforce died.

The best of all

He died at his house beside City Road Chapel on 2 March 1791, aged eighty-seven, after an illness of a few days, surrounded by friends. Near the end, with almost no breath left, he startled them by singing Isaac Watts: I’ll praise my Maker while I’ve breath. And at least twice, to the people gathered round the bed, he said the thing he had spent fifty-three years riding across England to tell strangers — that the whole of it, the fire and the fields and the failure and the mobs and the miles, came down to one fact:

“The best of all is, God is with us.”

He left behind a coat, a few silver spoons, and a movement. He would have thought only one of those worth mentioning — and he would have said, correctly, that it began with a woman praying over a boy she had nearly lost to a fire.

fields.name: Augustine of Hippo
fields.bio: Augustine of Hippo (354–430) was born in Roman North Africa to a pagan father and a praying Christian mother, Monica, whose tears followed him through years of ambition, pleasure, and the Manichaean religion. In a Milan garden in 386 he heard a child chanting "take up and read," opened Paul's letters, and was undone. Baptised by Ambrose, he returned to Africa and served some thirty-five years as bishop of Hippo, writing the Confessions and The City of God and contending for grace against the Donatists and Pelagians. He died in 430 as the Vandals besieged his city.
fields.bio_html:
Aurelius Augustinus was born on 13 November 354 in Thagaste, an unremarkable inland town of Roman North Africa, in what is now Algeria. His father, Patricius, was a modest landowner, a pagan of quick temper who received baptism only at the very end of his life. His mother, Monica, was a Christian of stubborn, weeping faith, and it is her prayers, more than any teacher or book, that shape the story of her son. Between them they produced a boy of dazzling ability and dangerous appetite, and they scraped together money they did not have to send him away to school — first to nearby Madauros, and then, at seventeen, to Carthage.

Augustine would spend the next thirty years telling the story of what happened to him, and he told it as a prayer. The Confessions, written when he was in his forties, is addressed not to the reader but to God, and its opening page contains the sentence that has become the truest summary of his life and of every restless life since.

Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.

— Augustine of Hippo

A cauldron of unholy loves

Long before Carthage there was a pear tree. Augustine devotes several pages of the Confessions to a boyhood night when he and a gang of friends stripped a neighbour's pear tree and flung the fruit to the pigs. The pears were poor, he had better at home, and he did not even want them. That was exactly the point. I loved mine own fault, he wrote, not that for which I was faulty, but my fault itself. A trivial theft became a window onto the whole mystery of evil: a heart delighting in the forbidden simply because it is forbidden.

Carthage enlarged the appetite. His first line for the city has never been bettered.

To Carthage I came, where there sang all around me in my ears a cauldron of unholy loves.

— Augustine of Hippo

He was clever, ambitious, and hungry for applause, and he took a woman into his house — he never names her in the Confessions — with whom he lived faithfully for well over a decade. She bore him a son, and he called the boy Adeodatus, "given by God," a name of startling grace from a young man then running as fast as he could from the Giver. In his nineteenth year, two years after his father's death, an assigned text broke over him: Cicero's Hortensius, an exhortation to philosophy. It ruined him for lesser things. "Every vain hope at once became worthless to me," he wrote, "and I longed with an incredibly burning desire for an immortality of wisdom." He turned to the Scriptures, found their Latin crude beside Cicero, and turned away again.

Instead he fell in with the Manichees, an austere dualist sect that flattered his intellect by promising knowledge without the humiliation of faith, and that conveniently located the source of evil somewhere outside his own will. He remained among their "hearers" for almost nine years, from his nineteenth year to his twenty-eighth — years he later described without flinching as wallowing in a deep pit.

The son of these tears

All that time his mother prayed. Augustine says she wept for him more than mothers weep for the bodily death of their children, because she could see the death he was actually dying. She was given a dream: standing on a wooden rule, grieving, she was met by a shining young man who asked why she wept, and who told her to look — and there, standing on the same rule beside her, was her son. She held that dream for nine years while nothing visibly changed.

Monica's tears, Augustine wrote, "watered the ground under her eyes in every place where she prayed." She would not stop. She badgered a bishop — himself a former Manichee — to argue with her clever, ruined son, until at last, wearied by her, he sent her away with a word she took, in Augustine's phrase, "as if it had sounded from heaven": Go thy ways and God bless thee, for it is not possible that the son of these tears should perish.

Disillusioned at last with the Manichees — their celebrated teacher Faustus proved charming and empty when Augustine finally put his questions to him — he decided in 383 to advance his career in Rome. Monica followed him to the harbour and refused to be left behind. He lied to her, said he was seeing a friend off, and sailed by night while she was at prayer. From Rome he secured, in 384, the prestigious chair of rhetoric in Milan, then the seat of the imperial court. He had climbed almost as high as ambition could carry a provincial boy. He had never been more miserable.

Milan

Two things began quietly to work on him there. The first was Ambrose, Milan's formidable bishop, who received the young professor kindly. Augustine came for the style and stayed for the substance: Ambrose read the Old Testament in a way that showed him the Scriptures he had dismissed were deeper, not shallower, than Cicero. The second was a handful of Platonist books, which broke the Manichaean spell by teaching him to conceive of God and the soul as spiritual realities rather than as some rarefied stuff.

His mind moved. His will did not. Monica, now with him in Milan, arranged a respectable marriage, and the woman he had lived with for fifteen years was sent back to Africa — "torn from my side," he wrote, "my heart which clave unto her was torn and wounded and bleeding." She vowed never to know another man and left their son behind. Augustine, unable to wait the two years until his betrothed came of age, promptly took another. He records it without excuse; it is one of the passages that makes the Confessions so hard and so trustworthy. He wanted God, and he wanted everything else, and he knew exactly what he was doing when he prayed the prayer he later remembered with shame.

Give me chastity and continency, only not yet.

— Augustine of Hippo

The garden

The crisis broke in the late summer of 386. Augustine, hearing of others who had simply given everything up, was thrown into a storm of self-loathing. He fled into the garden of the house he shared with his friend Alypius, threw himself down under a fig tree, and wept — asking himself, again and again, how long he would go on saying tomorrow, and tomorrow.

Then, from a neighbouring house, he heard a child's voice — boy or girl, he could not tell — chanting a little singsong over and over: Tolle, lege; tolle, lege. Take up and read; take up and read. He could not remember any children's game with such words. He stopped crying, got up, and went back to where Alypius sat with the volume of Paul's letters. He opened it and read the first passage his eyes fell on, from Romans 13: "not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying; but put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, in concupiscence." He read no further, and needed none. "Instantly," he wrote, "at the end of this sentence, by a light as it were of serenity infused into my heart, all the darkness of doubt vanished away." Alypius read the next line — him that is weak in the faith, receive — and applied it to himself. The two men went indoors and told Monica.

Nearly thirty years of a mother's weeping ended in that room. A year later, resting at Ostia on the road home to Africa, Monica told her son: "One thing there was for which I desired to linger for a while in this life, that I might see thee a Catholic Christian before I died. My God hath done this for me more abundantly."

Baptism, and the graves along the way

Augustine resigned his chair and withdrew that autumn to a friend's country villa at Cassiciacum with his mother, his son, and a few companions, writing his first dialogues and testing the new faith against everything he had learned. At the Easter Vigil of 387 he was baptised by Ambrose, together with Alypius and with Adeodatus, who was "not quite fifteen" and whose brilliance frightened his father. Augustine put the boy's own words into a dialogue, The Teacher, and wrote of him simply: "I had no part in that boy, but the sin."

On the journey home, at the port of Ostia, mother and son leaned together at a window over a garden and talked their way upward — past the sun and stars, past their own minds — until for one instant they touched the Wisdom in which all things are made, and then fell back into the noise of speech. Days later Monica took a fever. Asked where she should be buried, she said: "Lay this body any where; let not the care for that any way disquiet you: this only I request, that you would remember me at the Lord's altar, wherever you be." She died in her fifty-sixth year and his thirty-third. He closed her eyes, forced back his tears in public, and afterwards wept alone — and then wept at having wept. Within two or three years Adeodatus, too, was dead, still in his teens.

Bishop of Hippo

Back in Thagaste, Augustine sold his inheritance and gathered a small household to live in prayer, study, and shared poverty. He wanted nothing public. But in 391, visiting the port city of Hippo Regius, he was standing in the congregation when the people laid hands on him and pressed him on the old bishop, Valerius, for ordination. Augustine wept — not, his friend and biographer Possidius insists, from wounded pride, but because he saw what the care of a church would cost him. Around 395 he was consecrated as Valerius's coadjutor, and on the old man's death shortly afterwards he became bishop of Hippo, an office he held for some thirty-five years.

It was an ordinary provincial charge and he gave it everything: preaching constantly, settling lawsuits between neighbours, writing letters across the empire, keeping a frugal table and an open one, living with his clergy under a common rule. Hundreds of his sermons and letters survive. From this unremarkable harbour town he became the most influential theologian the Western Church has produced. Around 397 he began the Confessions. After Alaric's Goths sacked Rome in 410, he laboured for more than a decade over The City of God, tracing all of history as the story of two cities built by two loves. Near the end of his life he went back over everything he had written and published the Retractations, correcting himself in public — a scholar's act of penitence.

Two long controversies consumed him. Against the Donatists, an African party who held that the Church must consist of the pure and that sacraments from unworthy hands were void, he argued that the Church in this world is a mixed field of wheat and weeds, and that the power of the sacraments rests on Christ, not on the minister. Against Pelagius, who taught that a person could take the first step toward God unaided, he insisted — out of the memory of his own paralysed will in that garden — that everything begins with grace. A single line from the Confessions carried it: "Give what Thou enjoinest, and enjoin what Thou wilt." Augustine later recalled that when a fellow bishop quoted that sentence in Pelagius's hearing, Pelagius could not bear it and nearly came to a quarrel over it. Augustine knew which side of that hinge he lived on, because he had never once rescued himself.

Too late loved I Thee, O Thou Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new! too late I loved Thee!

— Augustine of Hippo

The siege

His last years darkened. In 429 the Vandals crossed into North Africa, burning towns, scattering congregations, and driving bishops and their people before them. In 430 they laid siege to Hippo itself. Augustine, in his seventy-sixth year, kept working and kept praying while the enemy sat outside the walls.

Possidius, who was with him, records the prayer of his last months: that God would be pleased either to free the besieged city, or, if something else seemed good in His sight, to make His servants brave to endure His will — "or at least that He may take me from this world unto Himself."

In the third month of the siege he took a fever. He asked that the shortest of David's penitential psalms be copied out and hung on the wall where he could see them from his bed, and he read them there and wept, Possidius says, freely and constantly — the great doctor of grace dying as a penitent. About ten days before the end he asked to be left alone except for his physicians and his food, so that nothing would interrupt his prayer. He died on 28 August 430, with the Vandals still at the gates. He left no will, because, as Possidius put it, as a poor man of God he had nothing to leave. What he left instead was his clergy, his monasteries, and his library, which he charged them to keep carefully. They did — and through it Hippo, which the Vandals burned, outlived them by fifteen centuries.

Augustine is honoured across the Christian world, by Catholics, Orthodox, and Protestants alike, as one of the greatest teachers of the faith. But that is not why people still read him. They read him because he hid nothing: not the theft of the pears, not the woman he sent away, not the prayer that asked for purity and secretly hoped to be refused, not the decades in which he knew better and did nothing. And because through all of it moves the patience of a God who would not let him go, and the prayers of a mother who would not either. He wrote his life down so that we would recognise our own restlessness in his — and then look, as he did, past the man to the only place it ever comes to rest.

fields.name: Lemuel Haynes
fields.bio: Abandoned as an infant and indentured until he was twenty-one, Lemuel Haynes (1753–1833) taught himself Scripture, Latin, and Greek by firelight. He served as a Minuteman and marched to Ticonderoga, and in 1785 became the first Black man ordained by a mainstream Protestant denomination in America. He pastored mostly white congregations for nearly fifty years — thirty of them at West Rutland, Vermont — and wrote the early antislavery essay “Liberty Further Extended.” Dismissed in old age, he preached to the end, asking only that his gravestone call him a sinner trusting wholly in Christ.
fields.bio_html:
He was born on the eighteenth of July, 1753, in West Hartford, Connecticut, and he was given away before he could remember it. His father was a Black man; his mother was a white woman of a respectable New England family. Neither of them kept him. He did not even carry their name — he bore, most likely, the name of the man in whose house he happened to be born. At five months old he was carried up into the Massachusetts hills, to Granville, and bound out as an indentured servant to a farmer named David Rose until he should turn twenty-one.

It is the sort of beginning that usually ends a story before it starts. His earliest biographer, who had known him from boyhood, wrote of him plainly: he was an orphan “not by the bereaving hand of God, but by the cold neglect of those who ought to have been his most affectionate guardians.” Tradition in Granville held that as a boy he once came upon his mother at a relative’s house in a neighbouring town, and that she slipped away rather than speak to him.

And yet the same providence that let him be abandoned set him down in a house where the Sabbath was kept, where family prayer was offered morning and evening, and where Friday nights were given to teaching the household the Scriptures. Deacon Rose was often sent for to pray beside the sick and the dying. His wife, Lemuel said afterward, “treated me as though I was her own child,” and he remembered a saying among the neighbours: that she loved Lemuel more than her own children. The boy who had been given away had been given, as it turned out, to people who would not let him go.

The chimney corner

The indenture required that he be schooled “in common with other children,” which in a frontier village meant a few winter months a year with a barely-trained master, often missed because there was work to do. So he taught himself. New England chimneys in that generation were enormous — a fireplace eight feet across and a yard deep, with a stone block inside where the children could sit. That block was Lemuel Haynes’s school. He gathered pine knots by day so that he could read by their light at night, because candles were a luxury he rarely had. He read the Bible until he could recite most of the texts bearing on the doctrines of grace and name the book, chapter, and verse of each. And no boy in the neighbourhood did more manual labour than he did.

Meeting an old schoolmate one day, he asked how the young man’s studies were coming, and then offered his own method — a sentence that explains the whole strange arc of his life.

I make it my rule to know something more every night than I knew in the morning.

— Lemuel Haynes

Under the apple tree

Religion frightened him before it comforted him. As a small boy left alone in a thunderstorm he thought the last day had come, and the fear of dying unprepared never entirely left him. Later a display of the northern lights — widely taken then for a sign of the judgment — sent him into weeks of terror. “I cannot express the terrors of mind that I felt,” he wrote long afterward to a friend who had asked him about it. Then, one evening, alone in an orchard: “One evening, being under an apple-tree mourning my wretched situation, I hope I found the Saviour.”

He never lost the modesty of that “I hope,” and he never lost the tree. All his life, whenever he came back to Granville, he went and stood under it, and when he could he picked some of the fruit and carried it home. “It is sweet to my taste,” he said.

“I spent much time in what I called secret prayer,” he wrote of those years. As a boy he would slip away into the woods during the break between the Sabbath services to pray alone; as an old man he was still, in his biographer’s phrase, “much in his closet,” where he “watched, and prayed, and fasted much.” He kept no diary of his soul. The habit was the record.

A minuteman, and a manuscript

His indenture ran out and the Revolution came in. In 1774 he enlisted as a minuteman, drilling one day a week and holding himself ready. After Lexington he marched with the Granville company and joined the army at Roxbury. The next year he volunteered for the expedition north to Fort Ticonderoga; passing through Bennington on a Sabbath, the troops halted, and the young soldier sat and heard a sermon on Romans 5:1 that he remembered for the rest of his life. He came home and nearly died of typhus while getting in a wheat crop, and his neighbours came and finished the field for him.

That same year, 1776, with the ink hardly dry on the Declaration of Independence, he wrote something no one would print for two hundred and seven years. He called it Liberty Further Extended: Or Free Thoughts on the Illegality of Slave-Keeping. He set the Declaration’s own words at the head of it and turned them, without flinching, on the men who had written them. Tyranny, he began, “had its origin from the infernal regions,” and so “it is the duty, and honor of every son of freedom to repel her first motions.” Every privilege men enjoy comes from God, he argued, and any human law contradicting the decrees of heaven “is void.” God, he wrote, quoting Acts 17, “hath pleased to make of one Blood all nations of men.”

Liberty is equally as precious to a Black man, as it is to a white one, and Bondage equally as intolerable to the one as it is to the other.

— Lemuel Haynes

He was twenty-three when he wrote it. The manuscript was never finished and never published in his lifetime; it lay unread in an archive until a historian found it in 1983. Unlike many white antislavery men of the next generation, he never favoured shipping free Black Americans off to Africa. He wanted abolition, and he wanted them to stay.

“It’s Lemuel’s sermon”

The Rose household read a printed sermon aloud on Saturday evenings — Watts, Doddridge, Davies, Whitefield — and Lemuel was the reader. One evening he slid a manuscript of his own into the book and read that instead. The old deacon, whose eyes were dim, was delighted, and asked at the end whose work it was. Was it Davies? Watts? Whitefield? Haynes hesitated, and finally admitted: “It’s Lemuel’s sermon.”

That evening changed everything. Friends urged him toward college, and a door opened at Dartmouth, but “I shrunk at the thought.” Instead he studied Latin with the Reverend Daniel Farrand of Canaan, Connecticut, working in the fields to pay his board, then kept a school at Wintonbury while the Reverend William Bradford taught him Greek so that he could read the New Testament in the original. On the twenty-ninth of November, 1780, a group of ministers examined him “in the languages and sciences” and in “practical and experimental religion,” and licensed him to preach. He was twenty-seven.

They called him back to Granville — the parish where he had been known only as a servant boy — and he preached there five years. In 1783 he married Elizabeth Babbitt, a young schoolteacher whom he had counselled through a long spiritual darkness and who, when she came out of it, proposed to him. He commended the matter to God, asked the advice of several ministers, and accepted. They had ten children.

On the ninth of November, 1785, his old teacher Daniel Farrand preached at his ordination from 1 Chronicles 17:16 — “Who am I, O Lord God, or what is my house, that thou hast brought me hitherto?” No text was ever better chosen. Lemuel Haynes became the first Black man ordained by a mainstream Protestant denomination in America. He went next to Torrington, Connecticut, where one man was so offended that a Black man should be in the pulpit that he sat through the service with his hat deliberately on his head. Years later that man told the story on himself: “The preacher had not proceeded far in his sermon before I thought him the whitest man I ever saw. My hat was instantly taken off and thrown under the seat.” He went home converted.

Thirty years at West Rutland

On the twenty-eighth of March, 1788, he accepted a call to the West Parish of Rutland, Vermont — a raw frontier state with barely four or five Congregational ministers west of the Green Mountains and a confident unbelief circulating among its leading men. He stayed thirty years. He found forty-two members, most of them elderly, and would leave behind a church into which more than three hundred had been gathered.

He preached without regard for what was popular. His only questions about a doctrine, said the man who knew him longest, were: “Is it true? Is it profitable? Is it seasonable?” He wept in the pulpit over people in danger. He said it was “a great deal for ministers to keep ego out of the pulpit,” and when his family praised his preaching after he had gone to his room, he would stop his ears so as not to hear it.

For fifteen years almost nothing happened. Roughly thirty people joined the church in all that time. The prayer meeting was kept up week after week and hardly anyone came. “The spirits of God’s people have been sunk,” he wrote; “our harps were hung upon the willows.” By November of 1802 he had privately decided to resign.

Then, he wrote, “it pleased God to arrest the attention of a very thoughtless youth,” who came to him on a Sabbath evening in distress. They called a meeting that week and the house was packed. “The work spread from week to week, till it was difficult to find any dwelling-house that would hold the people.” In one crowded house the floor gave way and dropped the congregation into the cellar; no one was much hurt, and nobody stopped coming. One hundred and three were added to the church. “Thus it has pleased the Lord to do wonders among us, to the praise of his glorious grace.”

In 1804 the trustees of Middlebury College conferred on him an honorary Master of Arts — the first such degree given to a Black man in America. The next June the Universalist preacher Hosea Ballou came to preach in Haynes’s own pulpit and afterward invited him to add remarks. Haynes rose and delivered, on the spot, a sermon he had built while listening — from Genesis 3:4, “And the serpent said unto the woman, Ye shall not surely die.” Universal salvation, he argued, was a very ancient doctrine indeed, and the devil was its first and most successful preacher: “an old preacher,” “a very cunning, artful preacher,” who “mixes truth with error, in order to make it go well.” Printed the following year, it ran through edition after edition on both sides of the Atlantic.

Dismissed

The end at Rutland was not clean. He was an unbending Federalist in a parish and a state torn by party feeling, and he preached politics with a satire that stung. On the twenty-ninth of April, 1818, an ecclesiastical council dissolved the pastoral relation. The record calls it mutual; the council commended him warmly as “a tried and faithful minister of Jesus Christ”; and to his friends he wrote calmly, “No impeachment of my moral or ministerial character was pretended. I fully acquiesce in the event.”

He also said something else. He had lived among the people of Rutland thirty years, he remarked, and they were “so sagacious that at the end of that time they found out” that he was a Black man — the word he actually used was the ugly one — “and so turned him away.” Historians still argue over how much of the dismissal was politics and how much was race. He seems to have known.

He was sixty-four, and it did not stop him. “Since my dismission I have not been idle a single Sabbath,” he wrote that September. “I am astonished, and even ashamed, at the pressing calls I have to preach. I know I am unworthy.” He served the church at Manchester, Vermont, for some three years, and in 1822 settled at South Granville, New York, where he preached for the last eleven years of his life.

Nothing in myself

Early in 1833 he wrote his last sermon, on the words “and serve him day and night in his temple.” That March gangrene appeared in one of his feet, and for three weeks he was in constant pain. When it eased he went straight back to work, and in April preached a funeral sermon on the eternal house not made with hands, looking so pale that people thought he was preaching his own. His final public sermon was from Luke 4:16 — “and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day.” Then he went home to die. The Rutland ministers appointed a committee to see that the old man lacked nothing, and the churches sent help until after his death.

I have been examining myself and looking back upon my past life, but I can find nothing in myself and nothing in all my past services to recommend me at the bar of Jehovah. Christ is my all. His blood is my only hope of acceptance.

— Lemuel Haynes

His last months were not cloudless — he had, his biographer admitted, “seasons of desertion and doubt.” In the same conversation he said, “I have been praying for the faith of assurance, and feel that I have almost attained it. My pains are great; but, blessed be God, they are not eternal. I long to be in heaven.” When a friend who had left his own sick parish to come asked whether he should stay, Haynes answered, “Oh, yes, I want your company to all eternity. Do pray for me.”

He died on the twenty-eighth of September, 1833, aged eighty. A plain marble stone was set over him. Only afterward did his family find, in his own handwriting, the epitaph he had written for himself years before, in the strength of his days.

Here lies the dust of a poor hell-deserving sinner, who ventured into eternity trusting wholly on the merits of Christ for salvation.

— Lemuel Haynes

The inscription went on to invite his children, and anyone who read it, to trust their eternal interest on the same foundation. It is a fitting last word for a man who had been handed nothing, who had learned his Greek by pine-knot light, who had argued for the liberty of his own people while a young nation congratulated itself on freedom, and who wanted it recorded on his gravestone that he had nothing of his own to offer God.

fields.name: William Law
fields.bio: William Law (1686–1761) was an English priest whose refusal to swear allegiance to George I cost him his Cambridge fellowship and any career in the established church. Barred from preferment, he wrote instead — and A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life (1729) became one of the most influential devotional books in English, shaping John Wesley, George Whitefield, and Samuel Johnson. His later turn to the mysticism of Jacob Boehme divided his admirers and ended his friendship with Wesley. He spent his last twenty years at King's Cliffe in fixed hours of prayer, plain living, and open-handed charity, giving away nearly all he had.
fields.bio_html:
In the churchyard of King's Cliffe, a stone village on the edge of the old forest of Rockingham, lies a man who never held a parish of his own, never rose an inch in the church he loved, and never once permitted anyone to paint his portrait. He founded no movement and gathered no following. Yet William Law wrote a book that John Wesley could not shake off, that George Whitefield said worked powerfully upon his soul, that made Samuel Johnson think in earnest about God for the first time in his life, and that Edward Gibbon — the great sceptic, no friend to religious enthusiasm — admitted would kindle any spark of piety in a reader into a flame.

He was born in 1686, the fourth of eight sons in a household of eleven children, to Thomas Law, a grocer of King's Cliffe, and his wife Margaret. A grocer's son with a good head was sent to Cambridge to make something of himself, and on 7 June 1705 William Law was admitted a sizar of Emmanuel College — a poor scholar, earning his keep. He read the classics, mathematics, and philosophy, and by 1711 he had done everything a young man was supposed to do: he took his degree, was elected a fellow of his college, and was ordained. He was twenty-five. The road ahead was straight, respectable, and entirely closed to him within three years.

The oath he would not swear

Queen Anne died in 1714 and the crown passed to George of Hanover. Every man holding office in church or university was required to swear allegiance to the new king and to abjure the exiled Stuart line. Law would not do it. He had already sworn to the House of Stuart, and he held that an oath, once given before God, is not a thing a man revises when the political weather changes. It was a scruple of conscience, and it cost him everything a young clergyman had. Deprived of his fellowship, he became a Non-Juror — one of that small, stubborn company of English clergy who paid for their consciences with their careers and lived on the margins of the establishment for the rest of their lives.

He was never restored. He served briefly as a curate at Fotheringay and in London, but preferment was impossible; when Dean Thomas Sherlock offered him advancement, the oath still stood in the way and Law declined. Instead of a bishopric he got obscurity, private teaching, and time to write. The Church of England's loss of a clergyman was the English-speaking world's gain of a devotional master.

His pen, at first, was a weapon. In 1717 he entered the Bangorian controversy with Three Letters to the Bishop of Bangor, still regarded as the most forcible writing the whole dispute produced. In 1723 he took apart Bernard Mandeville's cynical Fable of the Bees. But in 1726 something deeper surfaced: A Practical Treatise upon Christian Perfection. The controversialist was becoming a physician of souls.

The book that would not let go

By 1727 Law had joined the household of Edward Gibbon at Putney as tutor to the son of the house — the father of the historian who would one day write The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire. He remained ten years and became, in the family's own reckoning, the honoured friend and spiritual director of them all. And there, at the end of 1728, he published the book that carries his name: A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life.

Its argument is disarmingly simple and almost impossible to escape. Everyone grants, Law observed, that prayer must be offered according to the will of God. Very well — then why should the other twenty-three hours be exempt?

Devotion is neither private nor public prayer; but prayers, whether private or public, are particular parts or instances of devotion. Devotion signifies a life given, or devoted, to God.

— William Law

From that seed the whole book grows. He drew portraits — Flavia, who spends on herself and gives the poor her leftovers; Miranda, who divides her fortune with the needy and keeps only her own share of it — so sharply observed that Gibbon thought them not unworthy of La Bruyère. But Law's satire was never cruelty. It was diagnosis. And in the second chapter he laid his finger on the nerve:

And if you will here stop, and ask yourselves, why you are not as pious as the primitive Christians were, your own heart will tell you, that it is neither through ignorance nor inability, but purely because you never thoroughly intended it.

— William Law

That sentence has undone a great many readers. It leaves no room for the comfortable excuse. You are not more holy because you have never seriously meant to be.

Wesley, Whitefield, and the Revival

The effect was extraordinary and almost immediate. Samuel Johnson picked it up at Oxford expecting a dull book he could laugh at, and later told Boswell he had found Law quite an overmatch for him — it was, he said, the first occasion of his thinking in earnest about religion. George Whitefield got hold of a small edition at Oxford and recorded that God worked powerfully upon his soul through it; he began to pray and sing psalms three times a day. Charles Wesley called reading it a turning point. John Wesley first came to see Law at Putney in 1732, and for years he carried the Serious Call and Christian Perfection with him and pressed them on his preachers. Henry Venn, Thomas Scott, James Hervey, John Newton — the men who lit the Evangelical Revival were reading William Law before they were reading each other. Half a century later, in 1784, the young William Wilberforce would be shaken by the same book.

An anonymous reader, it is said, was so moved by the Serious Call that he pressed a thousand pounds into Law's hands. Law appears to have turned it straight into a school at King's Cliffe for fourteen poor girls, founded in 1727, who were to be clothed and taught reading, knitting, and every useful kind of needlework. He had written a book about giving away money; he gave away the money the book earned him.

Fixed hours and a rule of life

A third of the Serious Call is about prayer — not prayer as mood, but prayer as appointment. Law urged a rule of life built on fixed hours: early in the morning, then nine o'clock for humility, noon for universal love and intercession, three o'clock for resignation to the will of God, and evening for self-examination and confession. He was blunt about the cost of the first of them: it is as much your duty to rise to pray, he wrote, as to pray once you have risen.

Prayer is the nearest approach to God, and the highest enjoyment of Him, that we are capable of in this life.

— William Law

He kept his own rule to the end. At King's Cliffe he rose every morning at five and gave the hours before breakfast to prayer, meditation, and study; at nine the whole household — family and servants together — gathered for prayers. A servant read a chapter of Scripture aloud and Law explained it. He was at church on Wednesdays, Fridays, and Sundays, and went to bed at nine.

Boehme, and the parting with Wesley

Around 1735 a physician friend, Dr George Cheyne, put into Law's hands a book that led him to the writings of Jacob Boehme, the German shoemaker-mystic. Law was captivated. He taught himself German in order to read Boehme in the original, and his last works — An Appeal to All that Doubt (1742), The Spirit of Prayer (1749–50), The Way to Divine Knowledge (1752), The Spirit of Love (1752–54) — are steeped in him. The moral rigour of the Serious Call gave way to something inward and luminous, all about the birth of Christ within the soul.

Not everyone followed him there, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. This is where Law divided his admirers, and the division has never quite healed. In May 1738, fresh from his Aldersgate experience, John Wesley wrote to his old mentor with a reproach that still stings: how would Law answer it to their common Lord that he had never given Wesley this advice — never directed him first of all to a living faith in the blood of Christ? Law replied, with some dignity, that he had commended Thomas à Kempis and had constantly insisted on the same truth, and asked whether the quarrel was not partly a contest about words. But the friendship was over. In 1756 Wesley published an open letter saying he had scarce met with a greater friend to darkness, except the illuminated Jacob Behmen himself. Law never answered it publicly. He was, we are told, deeply hurt.

Something in that tension is worth sitting with. The man who had taught the Revival to be serious about holiness could not, in the end, walk with the Revival. And yet Wesley went on quoting him with admiration in his sermons for the rest of his life, and went on printing his books. Coleridge and Blake would later prize the Boehme volumes that Law's household paid to publish. Great teachers are rarely tidy.

King's Cliffe: a household of prayer and alms

When old Edward Gibbon died in 1737 the Putney years ended. Law lodged briefly in London and then, towards the close of 1740, went home for good to King's Cliffe. He was not alone for long. Archibald Hutcheson, a member of Parliament, had died that year wishing that his widow Elizabeth should live a retired and religious life under Law's direction; Hester Gibbon, sister of Law's old pupil, made the same choice. By 1744 the three of them were settled in Law's house at King's Cliffe, an ancient manor the village still called King John's Palace.

They set out, quite deliberately, to obey the Serious Call to the letter — to spend in charity everything not strictly necessary. Between them the two women had close to three thousand pounds a year, a very large income for the time. Almost all of it went out again. Law's school for fourteen girls was joined by a school for eighteen boys, raised to twenty in 1746; they built almshouses; Law kept a great theological library. Four cows were kept and their milk given away to poor neighbours. Every day Law tasted the soup made for the poor, and those who knew him said the one thing that could make him short-tempered was soup that had not been well enough made.

His own life was plain to the point of austerity — dinner at noon, tea at which he ate only raisins, a brisk walk in the fields, one pipe and a glass of water before bed. He loved music, insisting that anyone could be taught to sing well enough for devotion, and he was fond of animals and of children.

The charity was not universally admired. The rector complained that the household's giving was indiscriminate, and on 21 February 1753 the more considerable inhabitants of King's Cliffe formally petitioned the justices of the peace that Law and his family were the cause of the miserable poverty of the parish, drawing beggars from miles around. Law signed a reply. They would continue as they had begun; if the parish preferred, they would leave it altogether. They stayed. The beggars, as one historian dryly put it, proved too strong for the considerable inhabitants.

I give to all, because I pray to God to forgive all; and I cannot refuse an alms to those whom I pray God to bless.

— William Law

Almost in the act of singing

He caught a chill at the annual audit of his school, and after a fortnight's illness died on 9 April 1761, aged seventy-five. He had written a letter the day before without so much as mentioning that he was ill. He died, those with him said, almost in the act of singing the Angels' Hymn. He was buried at King's Cliffe, in the village where he was born, a few steps from the schools he had founded. Mrs Hutcheson lived on until 1781 and died at ninety-one; Hester Gibbon until 1790, dying at eighty-six — her nephew the historian noting, not unkindly, that she still lived in a hermitage at Cliffe, having long survived her spiritual guide and faithful companion Mr William Law.

He left no portrait, no monument, no denomination. He left a book. Two and a half centuries later the Church of England and the Episcopal Church still keep his memory on 10 April, and readers who have never heard of the Bangorian controversy or the Non-Jurors still find themselves stopped mid-page by a plain man asking a plain question: not whether they can be holy, but whether they have ever thoroughly intended it.

fields.name: Thomas à Kempis
fields.bio: Thomas à Kempis (c. 1380–1471) was a German-born Dutch monk who spent roughly seventy years in a single monastery outside Zwolle, copying manuscripts, keeping his community's chronicle, and teaching its novices. Formed at Deventer among the Brethren of the Common Life, he wrote for those young men four small booklets of counsel that became The Imitation of Christ — after the Bible, the most widely read Christian book ever written. Long circulated anonymously and long disputed, it is now credited to him. His was a hidden, unhurried life, and that hiddenness is the soil the book grew in.
fields.bio_html:
There is a strange arithmetic at the heart of this man's life. He wrote what is very likely the most widely read Christian book ever composed after the Bible itself — a little volume that has been translated into more languages than almost any other work of devotion, carried in the pockets of soldiers and scholars and dying men for six centuries. And he did it while going almost nowhere, meeting almost no one, and taking such care to leave no trace of himself that for three hundred years learned men argued about whether he had written it at all.

Thomas à Kempis spent roughly seventy years inside a single monastery on a low hill outside a provincial Dutch town. He held no great office. He preached to no crowds. He was never canonised. The record of his days is a record of copying, praying, teaching young men, and writing small books for their use. That is the whole of it — and that is precisely the point. The Imitation of Christ did not come out of a life of incident. It came out of a life of stability, and the two facts belong together.

Better of a surety is a lowly peasant who serveth God, than a proud philosopher who watcheth the stars and neglecteth the knowledge of himself.

— Thomas à Kempis

The hammer's son

He was born Thomas Hemerken — the name means something like "little hammer," and was later Latinised to Malleolus — in the town of Kempen in the Rhineland, in the diocese of Cologne. The year was 1379 or 1380; the sources cannot settle it, and neither should we. He is known to us by the place rather than the family: Thomas of Kempen, Thomas à Kempis.

His parents were John and Gertrude Hemerken, working people. Exactly what his father did is another small uncertainty: some accounts make him a smith, others simply a poor labouring man. His mother, by several accounts, kept a small school in the town. Nothing about the household suggested that one of its sons would be read for six hundred years.

There was an elder brother, John, some fourteen years ahead of him, and John went first — first to school, and later into the religious life. Thomas followed him both times. It is worth pausing on that, because it is a pattern in this life: Thomas rarely struck out. He followed, he stayed, he remained. In a century of restless reformers he was constitutionally a man who did not move.

Deventer, and the Modern Devotion

In 1392, at about twelve or thirteen, Thomas travelled to Deventer in the Netherlands to attend its famous school. He stayed some seven years, and those years made him.

Deventer was the heartland of what came to be called the devotio moderna, the Modern Devotion — a renewal movement begun by Geert Groote, who had died before Thomas was old enough to know him. Groote's followers, the Brethren of the Common Life, were not monks in the old sense. They lived together, worked with their hands, copied manuscripts for their bread, and pursued an interior, practical, unshowy Christianity: less speculation, more obedience. They were suspicious of learning that made a man proud and of devotion that made a man conspicuous.

At Deventer, Thomas came under the care of Florens Radewijns, Groote's successor and the movement's steadying hand. Radewijns took the boy in, paid his way, and shaped him. Decades later Thomas would write the lives of both men — one reason we know as much as we do about the Modern Devotion is that this quiet man in Zwolle wrote its history down. Everything characteristic of The Imitation — the distrust of clever talk, the insistence that Christ is followed rather than discussed, the tenderness toward beginners — is already in the air he breathed there as a schoolboy.

The hill of St Agnes

In 1399 Thomas went to Mount St Agnes, a new house of Canons Regular on a rise outside Zwolle, where his brother John was among the community and would serve as its prior. He arrived at about nineteen or twenty. He would die there, in the same house, at about ninety-one.

He was not, however, rushed into vows. The community was poor and unfinished — there were, in the early days, scarcely any buildings, no garden, no benefactors, no funds — and Thomas seems to have waited years on the threshold. He was clothed as a novice around 1406, when the cloister was at last completed, made his profession in 1407, and was ordained priest in 1413. From arrival to priesthood was fourteen years. Whatever else may be said of his vocation, it was not impulsive.

The poverty of those first years he recorded himself, in his Chronicle of the Canons Regular of Mount St Agnes — a plain, affectionate house-history that is our best window into the world he lived in. He describes evenings when supper ended with almost nothing left to divide the next day, and times when there were no cooking pots, or no suitable food at all. In one passage the cook, Gerard, anxious about the morning, came to Father John and asked sadly, "What shall I set before them to-morrow?" Thomas records the answer: John "consoled his sadness with kindly words, and exhorted him to have faith in the Lord, who doth not fail them that hope in Him."

That same day, Thomas writes in the Chronicle, "when that day had drawn on to evening, Everard of Eza, Curate of Almelo, came unexpectedly in his chariot as if sent by God to comfort the poor." He had brought fine meal and flesh, and gave it to the brothers for their common use. They "gave thanks to God and to Everard that of his bounty he had provided for them and succoured them in their so great need."

The desk, and the whole Bible by hand

What did he actually do, for seventy years?

He copied. This was the Brethren's trade and their discipline, and Thomas was extraordinarily good at it. He copied a missal for the use of his community. He copied out the entire Bible by hand — a labour that survives in several great volumes, and which some accounts say he undertook more than once. Consider what that means as a spiritual exercise rather than a clerical one: years of moving through the whole of Scripture at the speed of a pen, one word at a time, with no possibility of skimming. It is hard to imagine a slower or more thorough way to let a book get inside a man.

Around that work he wrote his own: sermons and short treatises for novices, prayers, hymns, letters, the lives of Groote and Radewijns and of Lidwina of Schiedam, the Chronicle of his house. And, between roughly 1418 and 1427, four small booklets of counsel for young religious that would be gathered together and carried out of that cloister into the whole world.

A Latin motto has long been attached to him — In omnibus requiem quaesivi, et nusquam inveni nisi in angulo cum libro: everywhere I have sought rest, and nowhere found it save in a corner with a book.
