It is worth being honest about this one, because it is quoted constantly as though it came from The Imitation, and it does not. It survives as a motto associated with his portrait and with early printed editions rather than as a line from his own published text. Whether or not the words are literally his, the description is exact.

Sub-prior, and master of novices

He was twice elected sub-prior of Mount St Agnes — the sources differ on the exact years, some giving 1425 and others 1429 — and once served as procurator, the house's business officer. That last appointment appears not to have gone well; later accounts describe him as simple in worldly matters and inclined to absent-mindedness, a man who withdrew from lively conversation and was relieved to be given back to his books.

But as sub-prior he was master of the novices, and this is the office that produced the book. Everything in The Imitation of Christ was written for particular young men whose faces he knew — anxious, ambitious, distractible beginners, learning to keep silence and to obey. That is why it does not read like theology. It reads like a wise old man talking quietly to someone who is struggling, which is exactly what it was.

I had rather feel contrition than be skilful in the definition thereof.

— Thomas à Kempis

The third and fourth books of The Imitation turn almost entirely into prayer — a dialogue between the soul and Christ, in which the writer stops instructing and starts asking. Anyone who wants to know how Thomas à Kempis prayed need only read them; his own hours, the daily round of the monastic office he kept for seven decades, are woven straight through the text.

"Speak, Lord, for Thy servant heareth. I am Thy servant, grant me understanding, that I may know Thy testimonies. Incline my heart to the words of Thy mouth: let Thy speech distil as the dew." So opens the second chapter of Book III — the prayer of a man who had spent his life copying other men's words and wanted, above all, to hear one Voice speak them.

Exile

The one great disruption came late. In 1429 a bitter dispute over who should hold the see of Utrecht brought an interdict down on the region, and the community was driven from the hill. "Alas! Holy God!" Thomas wrote in the Chronicle, "on the day before the Feast of St. Lambert we ceased from our singing by reason of the Interdict that was published against us!" The silencing of the sung office is the loss he names first.

The exile lasted until 1432. Thomas spent much of it at Bethany, near Arnhem, nursing his brother John, who was old and ill. John died there in November 1432. Thomas had followed him to school, followed him into religion, and now sat with him at the end; then he went home to the hill and stayed there for another thirty-nine years.

The quarrel over the book

The Imitation of Christ went out into the world anonymously, which was entirely in character — the Brethren's whole instinct was to efface the author. In 1441 Thomas completed and signed a codex in his own hand containing all four books together with nine other treatises; that manuscript survives in Brussels and is the single strongest piece of evidence for his authorship.

It did not settle the matter. For centuries rival claims were pressed with real heat: for Jean Gerson, the chancellor of Paris, whose name is close enough to invite confusion, and for a supposed Italian abbot called Giovanni Gersen. National pride, monastic pride, and genuine scholarly puzzlement all played their part. The honest summary is this: the case was seriously disputed for a very long time, and modern scholarship has come down decisively on the side of Thomas à Kempis — on the strength of the autograph manuscript, of contemporary witnesses who named him, and of the Dutch turns of phrase that show through the Latin. There is a fine irony in it: a man who took such pains to disappear behind his subject very nearly succeeded in losing his own book.

The end, and what came after

He died on 25 July 1471, in his ninety-first or ninety-second year, having outlived nearly everyone he had entered with. The Chronicle he had kept for so long was taken up by an anonymous successor, who recorded the death of the brother Thomas Hämerken, born at Kempen in the diocese of Cologne, and noted that he departed after Compline — after the last office of the day, the prayer said as the light goes. Some older reference works give a different date; the house's own chronicle is the better witness.

He was buried at Mount St Agnes. The monastery is long gone; his remains were eventually brought into Zwolle, and in 1897 a monument was raised over them in St Michael's Church bearing the words Honori, non memoriae Thomae Kempensis, cujus nomen perennius quam monumentum — to the honour, not the memory, of Thomas of Kempen, whose name is more lasting than any monument.

A story is often told that when his coffin was opened long after his death, scratches were found inside the lid and splinters under his fingernails, and that the Church therefore refused him canonisation on the grounds that a saint would not have fought so hard to live. It is a memorable tale and it should be labelled plainly: there is little evidence for any part of it. He was in fact never canonised, but the coffin story is legend, not history.

Vanity of vanities, all is vanity, save to love God, and Him only to serve.

— Thomas à Kempis

What remains is the arithmetic we began with. Seventy years in one house; a pen, a choir stall, a cell, a succession of nervous young novices; no travel, no controversy sought, no reputation built. And out of it, a book that has done more to shape ordinary Christian devotion than most councils and most kings — read by Ignatius of Loyola and John Wesley and Thomas More, by Samuel Johnson and by generations of people who never wrote anything down at all.

It is a rebuke to a great deal of what we assume about influence. Thomas à Kempis did not go out and find a hundred million readers. He stayed put, minded his own soul, copied the Scriptures until they were in his bones, and wrote plainly for the twenty young men in front of him. The hiddenness was not the price of the book. It was the soil it grew in.

fields.name: Clement of Rome
fields.bio: Clement of Rome (c. 35 – c. 99) led the church at Rome in the generation after the apostles and wrote the earliest Christian document to survive outside the New Testament. His one surviving letter was sent to Corinth around AD 96, where a faction had deposed the church's elders, and it argues from Scripture for humility, order and love before closing in prayer for the sick, the imprisoned and the emperor. Three generations later it was still being read aloud in Corinthian worship.
fields.bio_html:
Of all the writers in this library, Clement of Rome is the one we know least and owe most. He stands at the very hinge of the church's story, in the generation that had to learn how to be Christian without the apostles alive to ask. He wrote one letter. It survived. And because it survived we can hear, in ordinary Greek, what a pastor in Rome thought worth saying to a divided congregation while some of the men who had walked with Peter and Paul were still living.

Almost everything else about him is contested, and honesty requires saying so plainly. Irenaeus, writing around AD 180, lists him as the third to hold the office of oversight in Rome after the apostles, following Linus and Anacletus, and says that Clement had seen the blessed apostles and conferred with them. Origen and later writers identified him with the Clement whom Paul names as a fellow worker in Philippians 4:3, whose name is in the book of life. That identification is old and it is attractive, and it cannot be proved. Other traditions made him a freedman of the imperial household, or confused him with the consul Titus Flavius Clemens whom Domitian executed. The letter itself names no author at all. It is sent from the Church of God which sojourns at Rome to the Church of God sojourning at Corinth, in the plural voice of a congregation rather than the singular voice of a bishop. It was the church at Corinth, and then Dionysius of Corinth a lifetime later, who called it Clement's.

What is not contested is the occasion. Some time around AD 95 or 96, word reached Rome that the church in Corinth had done something extraordinary: it had deposed its presbyters. These were men of blameless conduct, Clement says, who had ministered faithfully and given no cause. A younger faction had simply pushed them out. Forty years after Paul had written to the same city about factions and parties, the same city was tearing itself apart again over the same thing.

The letter

Clement does not begin by scolding. He begins by remembering them at their best, and the remembering is so warm that it hurts:

Moreover, ye were all distinguished by humility, and were in no respect puffed up with pride, but yielded obedience rather than extorted it, and were more willing to give than to receive. Thus a profound and abundant peace was given to you all, and ye had an insatiable desire for doing good.

— Clement of Rome, to the Corinthians, chapter 2

Then he names the disease. He calls it jealousy, or envy, and he traces it through the whole of Scripture like a physician tracing an infection: Cain against Abel, Esau against Jacob, Joseph's brothers, Saul against David, and then, terribly and recently, envy in the church itself. In the fifth chapter he turns to his own generation, and gives us the earliest account outside the New Testament of the deaths of Peter and Paul, describing Paul as having reached the limits of the west before his witness before the rulers. He goes on to a great multitude of the elect who, having through envy endured many indignities and tortures, furnished us with a most excellent example. He is writing in a city that has recently watched Christians die, and he is telling a church that its quarrel over which men should serve at the table belongs to the same family of sins as the malice that killed them.

His remedy is not clever. It is order, humility, and love. He points to the ranks of an army, to the harmony of the body, to the seasons that keep their appointed order without complaint, to the sea that does not pass its bounds. He points, at length and with evident delight, to the resurrection, which he argues from day following night, from the sown seed that dissolves before it rises, and from the story of the phoenix, which he plainly believed to be a bird that lived in Arabia. That last argument has embarrassed his readers for nineteen centuries, and it is worth leaving in view: the earliest Christian letter we possess outside the New Testament reasons from natural history that was simply wrong, in the service of a hope that was not. The man is not infallible. He is faithful.

Then, near the end, he writes on love, and the prose lifts:

Who can describe the bond of the love of God? The height to which love exalts is unspeakable. Love unites us to God. Love covers a multitude of sins. There is nothing base, nothing arrogant in love. Love admits of no schisms: love gives rise to no seditions: love does all things in harmony.

— Clement of Rome, to the Corinthians, chapter 49

And he asks the men at the centre of the quarrel to do the hardest thing in the letter: to leave. Whoever among you is noble-minded, he writes, let him say, if it is on my account that sedition and disagreement have arisen, I will go away, only let the flock of Christ live in peace. It is a request nobody could enforce from six hundred miles away. He asks it anyway.

The prayer

The letter closes in prayer, and the prayer is the reason many readers who came for the history stay for the man. He prays for the sick, the fallen, the fainthearted, the hungry, the imprisoned; and then, astonishingly for a Christian writing while Rome was killing Christians, he prays at length for the emperor and the governing authorities, that God would direct their counsel toward what is good.

May God, who seeth all things, and who is the Ruler of all spirits and the Lord of all flesh, grant to every soul that calleth upon His glorious and holy Name, faith, fear, peace, patience, long-suffering, self-control, purity, and sobriety, to the well-pleasing of His Name, through our High Priest and Protector, Jesus Christ.

There is a strange and moving story attached to that prayer. The only manuscript known to Europe for centuries was the great fifth-century Codex Alexandrinus, and a whole leaf of it had been lost. For hundreds of years readers came to the end of chapter 57 and fell into a hole; the long intercession was known only to have existed. Then in 1873 a Greek metropolitan, Philotheos Bryennios, found a complete copy in a library in Constantinople, and the church got its oldest surviving prayer back. Older translations, including the one this library will use, still carry the gap where the leaf was lost.

What came of it

The letter worked. Around AD 170, Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, wrote to Rome that Clement's letter was still being read aloud in the Corinthian assembly on the Lord's Day, three generations after the quarrel it settled had been forgotten.

That is the measure of the man. He had no authority in Corinth that Corinth was obliged to recognise, no office anyone could have defined for him, and no weapon but Scripture, patience, and the memory of what that church had once been. He used them, and a congregation that had thrown out its elders sat down again and listened. Some churches went on reading the letter beside the Gospels for two hundred years; a few ancient manuscripts of the New Testament bind it in.

Of his death, nothing reliable is known. The stories that he was exiled to the Crimea, set to work in the marble quarries, and drowned with an anchor about his neck belong to a much later legend, and the anchor that appears beside him in art comes from that legend rather than from any early record. It is a small irony that a man who wrote so plainly about the danger of exalting oneself should have been given, centuries on, a martyrdom he probably did not have. The letter needs no embellishment. It is the sound of the church, in its second generation, discovering that the gospel would have to be lived out in the unglamorous work of keeping the peace, and choosing to do it.

Why he is worth reading

There is a particular comfort in Clement for anyone who has watched a church quarrel. He does not treat the Corinthian collapse as a scandal that disqualifies the gospel. He treats it as an illness with a known cause and a known cure, and he writes as a man who fully expects the cure to work. He assumes that ordinary Christians can be reasoned with from Scripture, that pride can be repented of, that a congregation which has behaved disgracefully can be spoken to with respect. Nothing in the letter is cynical.

His voice is also, quietly, the voice of a man who prays. The letter is stitched through with Old Testament quotation the way a life is stitched through with habit; he does not reach for the Scriptures to win an argument so much as think in them by reflex. And when he has finished arguing, he does not close with a flourish. He closes on his knees, praying for the sick and the imprisoned and the emperor who may well have been killing his friends. Whatever else is uncertain about Clement of Rome, the letter tells us what he did with his mornings.

Clement of Rome died around the end of the first century; reference works conventionally date him from about AD 35 to about AD 99, though neither end of that span rests on solid evidence and the dates beside his name here should be read as the tradition's best estimate rather than as record. He left one letter, one prayer, and a church at Corinth that stopped fighting.

fields.name: Ignatius of Antioch
fields.bio: Ignatius of Antioch (c. 35 – c. 108) was bishop of Antioch in Syria and wrote seven short letters while being marched under guard across Asia Minor to be killed in the arena at Rome. Written in snatched hours by a man with weeks to live, they are almost entirely about other people: the unity of the churches he was leaving, the reality of Christ's suffering, and the congregation in Syria he asked everyone to pray for. They are among the most urgent documents in Christian literature.
fields.bio_html:
Ignatius of Antioch wrote seven short letters in the last few weeks of his life, in snatched hours, under guard, on a forced march across Asia Minor to the arena. They are among the most urgent documents in Christian literature. Nothing in them is theoretical. A man who knows exactly how he is going to die is writing to churches he will never see again, and he spends the letters not on himself but on them.

He was born around AD 35, probably in Syria, and he was bishop of Antioch when he was arrested, most likely in the reign of Trajan, around AD 107 to 110. Antioch mattered: it was the third city of the empire, the church where the disciples were first called Christians, the base from which Paul and Barnabas had been sent out. Later writers said Ignatius was the second or third to hold the oversight there after Peter, and a tradition that cannot be verified made him a hearer of the apostle John. He called himself Theophorus, God-bearer, and he seems to have used it as a name rather than a boast.

Why he was condemned, we do not know. There was no empire-wide persecution at the time; Trajan's own correspondence with Pliny shows a policy of not hunting Christians down but punishing those brought before the courts who would not recant. Something local brought Ignatius before a magistrate, and the sentence was the beasts at Rome. That in itself is odd enough to be worth noticing: it would have been simpler to kill him in Antioch. Instead he was sent fifteen hundred miles to die as public entertainment in the capital.

The journey

The road went overland through Asia Minor, and it is the road that gave us the letters. At Smyrna his guards halted long enough for delegations from the surrounding churches to reach him: Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles all sent their bishops and deacons to greet a condemned man. He wrote back to each of them, and then wrote ahead to the church at Rome. Further on, at Troas, he wrote three more, to the Philadelphians, to the Smyrnaeans, and to Polycarp, the young bishop of Smyrna who had come to see him and who would himself be burned alive half a century later.

The conditions were not gentle, and he describes them with a flash of dry humour that has kept its edge for nineteen centuries:

From Syria even unto Rome I fight with beasts, both by land and sea, both by night and day, being bound to ten leopards, I mean a band of soldiers, who, even when they receive benefits, show themselves all the worse.

— Ignatius, to the Romans, chapter 5

The letter to Rome is the strangest of the seven, and the one people remember. He had heard that the Christians in the capital, who had influence, intended to use it to get his sentence commuted. He writes to beg them not to. The plea is not bravado; it is closer to a man pleading for water:

I am the wheat of God, and let me be ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ. I do not, as Peter and Paul, issue commandments unto you. They were apostles; I am but a condemned man.

— Ignatius, to the Romans, chapter 4

Modern readers find this difficult, and they should. There is a hunger for martyrdom in Ignatius that later Christian teaching deliberately reined in; the church came to insist that no one should seek death, and it was right to. But it is worth reading him closely before judging him. He is not in love with pain, and he never recommends his path to anyone else. What he wants is Christ, with an appetite he can barely put into words, and the arena is simply the door that has been opened in front of him. He is afraid of one thing only: that he will be spared and go on living as a half-hearted man.

What he actually wrote about

Given the circumstances, the astonishing thing about the letters is how little they are about Ignatius. Six of the seven are pastoral letters about ordinary church problems, written by a man with weeks to live.

He writes about unity, again and again, because the congregations were fragmenting. His remedy is to gather everything around the bishop, the presbyters and the deacons, and around the one table: do nothing without the bishop, hold one Eucharist, sing together like a choir with one voice. These are the earliest letters in which the threefold ministry appears as a settled fact, and they have been fought over by every church since. Read devotionally rather than constitutionally, the concern underneath is simpler and harder to argue with. He has seen what a divided church looks like from the inside, and he is spending his last strength trying to prevent it.

He writes against a teaching that was already circulating: that Christ only appeared to have a body, and only seemed to suffer. Ignatius has no patience with it whatsoever. If the Lord only seemed to suffer, he says, then I am only seeming to be in chains, and why have I given myself over to death? A man in irons has a shortcut to the heart of that argument that no scholar can match.

And he writes about prayer, constantly, in the form of requests. He asks nearly every church to pray for him, and he asks with no dignity at all, as a man asks for help.

Remember in your prayers the Church in Syria, which now has God for its shepherd, instead of me. Jesus Christ alone will oversee it, and your love will also regard it.

That sentence is the pastoral heart of the whole collection. He has been taken away from his congregation and he cannot get back to them, and what he does about it is hand them to God and beg other churches to hold them up.

Somewhere on the road he received word that the persecution at Antioch had lifted. In the letter to the Smyrnaeans he wrote back: Your prayers have reached to the Church of Antioch, and it is at peace. He then asked them to elect a delegate to travel to Syria and rejoice with the congregation he would never see again.

The man in the letters

Ignatius is easy to admire and hard to like at first meeting. He interrupts himself. He piles up images faster than he can develop them, calling the Ephesians stones of the temple of the Father, prepared for the building, hoisted into place by the cross as by a builder's hoist, with the Holy Spirit for a rope, faith for the ascent and love for the road. It is four metaphors deep before the sentence ends, and it holds together anyway. He apologises for his own vehemence and then does it again a paragraph later. There is nothing polished here, and the roughness is part of the evidence: nobody composing a devotional forgery would write this badly and this fast.

He is also, for all his talk of beasts, tender. He tells Polycarp to bear the ailments of everyone, to be patient with the difficult ones, to not be overwhelmed by those who seem worth little, to stand firm like an anvil under the hammer. He remembers the slaves in the congregations and warns that they must not be despised, and equally that they must not grow proud. He asks after named individuals and sends greetings to a widow and her household. A man three weeks from the arena is worrying about whether a young bishop is being too hard on himself. He tells Polycarp not to let the widows be neglected, to speak to the congregation one by one as an athlete's trainer does, and to seek out those nobody else has time for. Whatever the arena did to his imagination, it did not make him grand. The last recorded instincts of Ignatius of Antioch are the instincts of a parish minister making sure the difficult people are not forgotten.

Rome

Of his death we have no eyewitness account. The later Acts of his martyrdom are legendary in their details, and the honest summary is that he was taken to Rome and executed, almost certainly in the arena, some time between AD 107 and 110. Polycarp, writing to Philippi shortly afterward, refers to Ignatius and to the letters, and asks for any further news of him, which suggests the end came soon and the word travelled slowly.

A word about the texts themselves, because it matters for anyone reading him. Ignatius' letters were popular enough to be enlarged: an ancient editor padded the seven genuine letters and forged six more, and for centuries the church read the inflated version. Nineteenth-century scholarship, above all J. B. Lightfoot's, sorted it out, and the shorter recension of the seven letters is what scholars now regard as authentic. Older editions print both side by side, which is why a reader can meet the same sentence twice in slightly different clothes.

What survives is a small book, readable in an evening. It is the sound of a man walking toward his death with his mind entirely on other people's churches, other people's quarrels, other people's faith. He asked to be remembered as the least of them. He is remembered because, at the end, he was thinking about them and not about himself.

fields.name: Cyprian of Carthage
fields.bio: Cyprian of Carthage (c. 200–258) was a celebrated North African rhetorician who was converted in middle age, gave away his fortune, and was made bishop within two years. In twelve crowded years he led his church through the Decian persecution and the great plague that still bears his name, organising relief for the pagans who had wanted him dead, and wrote the first Latin commentary on the Lord's Prayer. He was beheaded at Carthage on 14 September 258.
fields.bio_html:
Cyprian of Carthage was a middle-aged celebrity lawyer when he became a Christian, and he had almost exactly twelve years left to live. Into them he packed a conversion, a fortune given away, a bishopric he did not want, two persecutions, a plague, three furious controversies, some of the warmest devotional prose in Latin, and his own execution. He is the first great pastor of the Western church whose letters we can still read, and the first African bishop to die under the sword.

He was born Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, probably around AD 200 to 210, into wealth in Carthage, the second city of the Latin West. He was trained as a rhetorician and taught rhetoric publicly, which in that world meant he was a public figure: fashionable, sought after, dining well, moving among men who ran the province. He was somewhere past forty when an elderly presbyter named Caecilianus began talking to him about Christ, and it undid him. Cyprian took the old man's name as his own and never stopped acknowledging the debt; when Caecilianus died he took his widow and family into his household.

Born again in middle age

What conversion felt like from the inside, Cyprian wrote down almost immediately afterwards, in a letter to his friend Donatus. It remains the best thing he ever wrote, and one of the few first-person accounts of Christian conversion to survive from the ancient world:

While I was still lying in darkness and gloomy night, wavering hither and thither, tossed about on the foam of this boastful age, and uncertain of my wandering steps, knowing nothing of my real life, and remote from truth and light, I used to regard it as a difficult matter that a man should be capable of being born again.

— Cyprian, to Donatus

He is honest about why he thought it impossible. He lists his own chains one by one: the banquets, the gold and purple, the crowds of clients, the horror of being an ordinary private citizen with nobody in attendance. He had assumed his vices were simply parts of himself, indigenous to him, and had given up expecting anything better. Then came baptism, and the thing he had thought could not happen happened:

After that, by the agency of the Spirit breathed from heaven, a second birth had restored me to a new man, then, in a wondrous manner, doubtful things at once began to assure themselves to me, hidden things to be revealed, dark things to be enlightened, what before had seemed difficult began to suggest a means of accomplishment, what had been thought impossible, to be capable of being achieved.

— Cyprian, to Donatus

He acted on it at once. He sold estates and gave the proceeds to the poor, and adopted a strict simplicity of life that seems to have astonished a city that had watched him dine for twenty years. Within two years, and against his own protest, the Christians of Carthage acclaimed him their bishop. Five senior presbyters never forgave him for it, and their resentment shadowed the rest of his ministry.

The persecution, and the charge of cowardice

He had been bishop barely a year when the emperor Decius, in January 250, ordered every citizen of the empire to sacrifice to the gods and obtain a certificate proving it. It was the first systematic, empire-wide attempt to destroy the church, and it worked far better than anyone expected. In Carthage, Christians queued at the altars. Some sacrificed outright; many more bought certificates without sacrificing. The bishop of Rome was executed. Cyprian went into hiding.

He was attacked for it then and has been attacked for it since, and he did not pretend otherwise. His defence, argued through a stream of letters from his hiding place, was that the mob had been shouting his name in the amphitheatre and that his death at that moment would have finished the church in Carthage rather than strengthened it. So he governed by correspondence for over a year: comforting the imprisoned, restraining the confessors who had begun handing out pardons to the lapsed on their own authority, holding a shattered congregation together at a distance. Whether he was right is still argued. What is not in doubt is that eight years later, when the choice came again, he did not run.

The persecution ended and left him a harder problem: what to do with the thousands who had failed. The rigorists said the lapsed could never be received back. Cyprian refused both easy answers. Those who had sacrificed must do genuine penance and could then be restored; those who had merely bought certificates were treated more leniently; and no one, he insisted, could be restored by the say-so of an individual confessor outside the church's discipline. The controversy pushed him into writing his treatise on the unity of the church, with its famous and much-quarrelled-over sentence:

He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his mother.

— Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church

The plague

Then, in 252, an epidemic hit Carthage that would rage across the empire for years and take an emperor with it. Historians still call it the Plague of Cyprian, because his deacon Pontius left the fullest description of what it did to a city. People fled their own houses. The dying were put out in the street. Bodies lay about, Pontius wrote, and nobody regarded anything besides his cruel gains.

Cyprian called the congregation together. He argued from the Sermon on the Mount that loving those who love you is what the tax collectors do, that God sends rain on aliens as well as on his own people, and that a son of God ought to imitate his Father. Then he organised the city's relief: money from those who had it, labour from those who had not, the sick nursed and the dead buried without asking whether the household was Christian or pagan. The population that had been screaming for his blood two years earlier was nursed through the plague by the people it had wanted to kill.

Out of those months came his treatise on the mortality, written for Christians frightened that they were dying of the same disease as everyone else. His answer is bracing rather than consoling: the plague is not a punishment aimed at believers but a proving, and a Christian who cannot face dying has not yet grasped what he claims to believe.

Teaching a church to pray

Somewhere in these years Cyprian wrote the little book on the Lord's Prayer that is still the readiest way into his mind. It is the first Latin commentary on the prayer, and its premise is disarming: we would not know how to address God at all if God had not told us.

He, among the rest of His salutary admonitions and divine precepts, Himself also gave a form of praying, Himself advised and instructed us what we should pray for. He who made us to live, taught us also to pray.

He works through the prayer clause by clause, and keeps noticing that it is plural. We do not say my Father, he observes, but our; our prayer is public and common, and when we pray we pray not for one but for the whole people, because we are all one. For a bishop trying to reassemble a church that had betrayed itself under pressure, that was not a grammatical observation. It was the whole programme.

Curubis and the sword

In 257 the emperor Valerian moved against the church's leadership directly. Cyprian was summoned, refused to sacrifice, and was exiled to Curubis, a small coastal town, where he continued writing to his people. A year later the policy hardened: bishops were to be executed. He was brought back to Carthage and kept under a form of house arrest, and he used the time to write to the churches.

Pontius records that on the night of his arrival at Curubis Cyprian was shown in a vision the sentence of his own death, and asked for a delay until the morrow, which was granted. He understood the day to mean a year. He was beheaded a year later, on the very day the vision had been given.

On 14 September 258 he was tried by the proconsul Galerius Maximus, condemned, and taken out to a level place surrounded by trees, into which people climbed to see. Pontius describes it with the eye of a man who was there. The crowd was so large that people climbed the trees to see, which reminded him of Zacchaeus. Cyprian bound his own eyes with his own hands rather than wait to be blindfolded, and tried to hurry the executioner, whose right hand was shaking so badly that he could barely hold the blade.

He was the first bishop of Carthage to die a martyr. His people gathered the body by torchlight. What he left behind is unusually complete for a third-century figure: over eighty letters, a dozen short treatises, and a body of pastoral practice that the Latin church would draw on for a thousand years. But the sentence that keeps drawing readers back is still the one he wrote in the first flush of grace, before any of it happened, when he was simply a middle-aged man astonished that God had changed him: what had been thought impossible, to be capable of being achieved.

fields.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
fields.bio: Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373) was bishop of Alexandria for forty-five years and spent seventeen of them in exile, driven from his city five times by four emperors for refusing to concede that the Son of God was a creature. He wrote On the Incarnation and the Life of Antony, which carried the monastic ideal into the West, and his festal letter of 367 is the earliest surviving list of exactly the twenty-seven books of the New Testament.
fields.bio_html:
Athanasius was bishop of Alexandria for forty-five years and spent seventeen of them in exile. He was driven from his city five times, by four different emperors, and each time he came back. He was short, dark, and slight, and his enemies, who included most of the imperial court for most of his life, accused him of murder, sorcery, treason, sacrilege and interfering with the grain supply of Constantinople. Every one of the charges collapsed. What he would not do was sign a document he believed to be false, and that single refusal, held for half a century, is very largely why the Christian church still confesses that Jesus Christ is God.

He was born in Alexandria around AD 296, into a Greek-speaking Egyptian world where the church had just come through the worst persecution in its history. He grew up knowing Coptic as well as Greek, which mattered later: when the empire turned against him, the Egyptian countryside hid him. He was still a young deacon, secretary to Bishop Alexander, when he travelled to the council at Nicaea in 325. He had no vote there. He was perhaps twenty-seven.

The question at Nicaea

The argument that consumed his life had been started by an Alexandrian presbyter named Arius, and it was not a quibble. Arius taught that the Son, though the highest of all creatures and the agent of creation itself, was nevertheless a creature: there was, he said, a time when he was not. It was an attractive position. It kept God safely simple and unchangeable, it fitted the philosophy of the age, and it could quote Scripture.

Athanasius saw with unusual clarity what it cost. If the Son is a creature, then what came into the world in Jesus Christ was not God but the best thing God had made, and the whole Christian hope collapses into a rumour. In the little book he wrote as a young man on the incarnation, he put the alternative in one line that the Greek church has never stopped quoting:

For He was made man that we might be made God; and He manifested Himself by a body that we might receive the idea of the unseen Father; and He endured the insolence of men that we might inherit immortality.

— Athanasius, On the Incarnation, 54

He is not saying that human beings become divine beings. He is saying that God has come the whole way down, taken a real body, died a real death, and by doing so has made it possible for creatures to share the life of God. Everything else in Athanasius follows from that sentence, including all the trouble.

Five exiles

He became bishop of Alexandria in 328, aged about thirty, and within seven years he was in Trier, on the Moselle, banished by Constantine after a synod stacked against him. That was the first. The second sent him to Rome. The third, and the strangest, began on a Thursday night in February 356.

He was presiding at a crowded night service of preparation for Communion in the church of Theonas when soldiers surrounded the building and broke in the doors. Athanasius took his seat in the apse and ordered the deacon to begin the 136th psalm, the people answering at every verse, for his mercy endureth for ever, while the troops pushed up toward the chancel. He refused to move until the congregation was safe. At the last moment monks and clergy seized him and carried him out half-fainting in the confusion.

He disappeared for six years and fourteen days. Where he went was the desert. The Egyptian monks, whose life he had learned to love and whose founder he had known, hid the most wanted man in the empire among the cells and caves of the Nile valley and the western oases, and no one betrayed him. Two more exiles followed, under Julian and under Valens; a persistent tradition says that in the last of them he hid for four months in his father's tomb.

Out of the years in hiding came the most widely read book he ever wrote. The Life of Antony is the biography of the old hermit whom Athanasius had known personally, and it did more than any other single text to carry the monastic ideal into the West. It reached as far as a garden in Milan, where a young African professor named Augustine heard the story of two officials who read it and abandoned their careers on the spot, and could not get it out of his head.

The letter that fixed the New Testament

Every year the bishop of Alexandria wrote a festal letter announcing the date of Easter, and every year Athanasius used it to teach. The thirty-ninth of them, sent out in 367, contains a list. It names the four Gospels, Acts, the seven catholic epistles, the fourteen letters of Paul, and the Revelation of John: the twenty-seven books of the New Testament, in an order any modern reader would recognise, and it is the earliest surviving list to name exactly those and no others.

These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.

— Athanasius, Festal Letter 39

He was not inventing a canon by decree. He was writing down what the churches had come to read, and the fact that his list is the one the church kept says something about how carefully he had listened.

What he passed on

Athanasius wrote the Life of Antony as a man who had watched the old monk at close quarters, and the book is more careful than its reputation suggests. Its miracles are told with a persistent refusal to credit Antony himself. A girl is brought across the desert to be healed and Antony will not even let her in, sending word instead that the accomplishment of this is not mine, wretched man that I am, but her healing is the work of the Saviour.

Athanasius records that Antony told the family the Lord had already inclined to the girl as she prayed, and that she would be healed where she was. They went out and found the parents rejoicing and the child whole.

That instinct, deflecting everything away from the holy man and back onto Christ, is Athanasius as much as it is Antony, and it is the reason his own life reads the way it does. He is not a mystic and he almost never talks about his inner experience. What he gives instead is a fixed point: God has actually come, in a body, to where we are. Everything he suffered was in defence of that one plain claim, and everything he wrote was an attempt to keep it from being explained away.

Alone, and not alone

The phrase attached to him in the Latin church, Athanasius against the world, is a later coinage rather than anything he said, and it is only half true. He was often outnumbered at councils to the point of absurdity, and there were stretches in the 350s when nearly every bishop who mattered had signed something he could not sign. But he was never actually alone. He had Alexandria, which rioted for him. He had the monks, who hid him. He had a network of correspondents that reached from the Egyptian desert to Rome to the Rhine, and he wrote to all of them, endlessly, in a Greek that is plain and quick and occasionally very funny at his opponents' expense.

He was also capable of generosity that his reputation for stubbornness does not predict. In his later years he worked patiently with bishops who had once signed against him, arguing that many of them had meant the right thing in the wrong words, and he made room for them. A man who had spent decades refusing to compromise on the substance turned out to be flexible about almost everything else.

He came home for the last time in 366 and had seven quiet years. He died in Alexandria on 2 May 373, in his own bed, in his own city, having outlived the emperors who exiled him. Eight years later the council at Constantinople settled the question in the words the church still says on Sundays, that the Son is of one being with the Father. Athanasius did not live to hear it. He had held the line long enough for someone else to.

What is worth taking from him is not mainly the doctrine, which most Christians now inherit without effort, but the temperament that defended it. He was told, repeatedly and by people with the power to destroy him, that he was the only obstacle to peace and that a single signature would end everyone's trouble. Five times he chose the road out of the city instead. He seems never to have thought of himself as heroic; he thought of himself as a bishop who was not free to say what was not true.

fields.name: John Chrysostom
fields.bio: John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) was the greatest preacher of the ancient church, named golden-mouthed by later generations for the sermons that filled churches in Antioch and Constantinople. A lawyer who abandoned the courts, he preached verse by verse through whole books of the Bible and unsparingly against wealth and luxury, which cost him his see. He died in 407 on a forced march into exile, with the doxology that had been his motto on his lips: Glory be to God for all things.
fields.bio_html:
They did not call him Chrysostom while he lived. The name is Greek for golden-mouthed, and the church gave it to him afterwards, because for sixteen years in Antioch and six in Constantinople people packed the churches to hear a small, thin, ascetic man explain the Bible verse by verse, and could not get enough of it. He is the greatest preacher the ancient church produced. He is also the preacher it exiled, marched to death across Asia Minor, and then, thirty-one years too late, carried home in state.

He was born in Antioch around AD 347. His father Secundus, an officer in the Syrian army, died while he was an infant. His mother Anthusa was left a widow at twenty, refused every offer of remarriage, and raised her son and daughter alone. She did it so conspicuously well that the greatest pagan orator of the age, Libanius, on hearing about her, exclaimed: Bless me, what wonderful women there are among the Christians.

The lawyer who ran away

Anthusa gave her son the best education money could buy, which meant Libanius himself. John was his finest pupil. He went into the courts, where a gifted advocate could climb to prefect or consul, and by his own account he took to the life completely: he was, he says, a never-failing attendant at the courts of law, and passionately fond of the theatre.

It did not hold. What broke it was the ordinary corruption of the trade, taking a fee to make the worse case look the better, which struck him as accepting Satan's wages. He was baptised in his early twenties and wanted to leave at once for the monks in the mountains. His mother stopped him. She took him into the room where he had been born, sat him down by the bed, and asked him for one thing: not to make her a widow a second time.

He stayed. What he did instead was turn the house into a monastery, eating little and seldom and only the plainest food, sleeping on the bare floor, rising through the night to pray, and keeping almost unbroken silence in order to break himself of the habit of speaking ill of people. His old friends from the courts called him unsociable and morose. Only after Anthusa died did he go to the mountains, and there, in four years under an old Syrian monk and two more alone in a cave, he ruined his health for good. His stomach and kidneys never recovered. He came back down to Antioch an invalid, and remained one for the rest of his life.

Long afterwards Libanius, near death and asked whom he wished to succeed him, is said to have answered: John, if only the Christians had not stolen him from us.

Ordained deacon in 381 and presbyter in 386, he began to preach, and the city discovered what it had. He worked through whole books of the Bible in sequence, taking the plain sense, refusing allegory where the text did not invite it, and then turning without warning from exegesis to the people in front of him: their money, their servants, their theatre-going, their treatment of the poor. He is exceptionally hard on wealth and exceptionally warm to the actual poor, and after sixteen hundred years the discomfort has not worn off.

The year the city expected to die

In the spring of 387 a new tax provoked a riot in Antioch, and the mob did the one unforgivable thing: they pulled down the bronze statues of the emperor Theodosius and dragged them through the streets, including the statues of his late wife and his sons. When the city sobered up it understood that it might be destroyed. Cities had been.

Into that terror Chrysostom preached twenty-one sermons over Lent, the Homilies on the Statues, while the bishop Flavian made the journey to plead in person with the emperor. They are the sermons of a pastor holding a panicking congregation together day by day, alternating between comfort and unsparing moral demand.

Antioch fasted and prayed through the whole of that Lent while Flavian was gone. He came back with the emperor's pardon, and Chrysostom preached the twenty-first homily on Easter Day to a city that had been spared. Large numbers of pagans were converted in the aftermath, so that, as the record has it, the calamity was turned into a blessing to the church.

From those Antioch years also comes his treatise on the priesthood, cast as a conversation with his friend Basil, and still the most searching book on pastoral ministry the early church produced. Its argument is that the work is so weighty, and the soul of the man who does it so exposed, that fleeing from it may be the sanest response, and it is written by someone who had fled from it himself.

Taken to the capital

In 397 the see of Constantinople fell vacant, and John was chosen without being consulted. He was got out of Antioch under military escort, to prevent the congregation rioting, and consecrated in February 398 by Theophilus of Alexandria, who wanted the appointment for his own candidate and never forgave him.

He was a disastrous choice from the court's point of view, which is to say the right one. He cut the episcopal household budget to nothing and sold the palace furnishings and the church silver to build hospitals. He disciplined clergy who lived comfortably. He preached at the capital exactly as he had preached at Antioch, on luxury, greed and the poor, in a city where the empress Eudoxia's household embodied all three. He was warned. He kept going, and at some point he preached a sermon on Jezebel that nobody at court mistook for a purely historical study.

In 403 Theophilus arrived with a bodyguard and a chest of presents, convened thirty-six mostly Egyptian bishops at a suburb across the Bosphorus, and had Chrysostom deposed in absentia on twenty-nine charges, including immorality, treason, eating alone, and calling the empress Jezebel. He refused to appear before a packed court, and when the sentence came he would not let the city fight for him: a word would have raised an insurrection, and he gave himself up to the officers instead.

Constantinople erupted anyway. The people besieged the palace; that night an earthquake shook the city and terrified Eudoxia into begging her husband to bring him back. Messengers went out with apologies, a fleet of small boats rowed out to meet him, the Bosphorus filled with torches and singing, and the people carried him bodily into the church and made him preach. It lasted a few months.

When I was driven from the city, I felt no anxiety, but said to myself: If the empress wishes to banish me, let her do so; the earth is the Lord's. If she wants to have me sawn asunder, I have Isaiah for an example. If she demands my head, let her do so; John the Baptist shines before me. Naked I came from my mother's womb, naked shall I leave this world.

— John Chrysostom, letter to Bishop Cyriacus

The road to Comana

The second exile, in 404, was final. He was sent to Cucusus in the Armenian mountains, and from there he kept writing: a stream of letters to his friends, and above all seventeen to Olympias, the wealthy young widow who had become a deaconess and given her fortune away, and who was now heartbroken and ill. For her he wrote the treatise arguing that no one is really injured except by himself.

His whole theology of suffering compressed into one sentence, which he had used as a doxology all his life and which his friends knew as his motto: Glory be to God for all things.

Eudoxia, still not satisfied, forbade correspondence and ordered him moved to Pityus on the Caucasus, the most inhospitable posting in the empire. The guards took a sick sixty-year-old man on foot for three months. He never arrived. On 14 September 407, five or six miles short of Comana in Pontus, he was carried into the chapel of the martyr Basiliscus, put on white baptismal robes, received communion, and commended his soul to God. His last words were his old doxology: Glory be to God for all things. Amen.

They buried him beside Basiliscus. Thirty-one years later, in 438, his body was brought back to Constantinople and laid beneath the altar of the church of the Holy Apostles among the emperors and patriarchs. The young emperor Theodosius II and his sister Pulcheria, the children of Eudoxia and Arcadius, met the coffin at Chalcedon, knelt down before it, and asked heaven's forgiveness in their parents' names for what had been done to him.

What survives is enormous: more of Chrysostom's preaching has come down to us than of any other Greek father, because people wrote it down as he spoke. Read him for the exegesis if you like, but read him first for the tone. He assumes the person in front of him can change, and he will not let go of that assumption, whether he is arguing a friend back from a broken vow, or telling a terrified city that God has not abandoned it, or writing from a mountain village to a woman whose life has come apart, insisting that no one can really be harmed except by himself.

fields.name: John Cassian
fields.bio: John Cassian (c. 360–435) spent some fifteen years among the desert fathers of Egypt asking them how to pray, and the rest of his life writing down their answers in Latin for monks in southern France. His Institutes and Conferences carried the whole desert tradition into the Western church; Benedict told his monks to read the Conferences aloud every evening. Ordained deacon by John Chrysostom, he later carried the appeal of Chrysostom's supporters to Rome.
fields.bio_html:
John Cassian spent roughly fifteen years walking from cell to cell in the Egyptian desert, asking old men how to pray. Then he spent the rest of his life writing down what they told him, in Latin, for monks in southern France who would never see Egypt. Almost everything the Western church came to know about the desert fathers, it knows because Cassian took notes. Benedict, writing his Rule a century later, told his monks to read Cassian's Conferences aloud every evening, and for a thousand years they did.

He was born around AD 360, most likely in Scythia Minor, the province at the mouth of the Danube in what is now Romania — the Greek tradition calls him John the Roman, and his Latin is the Latin of a man educated well and early. He came from a family with money. As a young man, with a friend named Germanus whose name will appear on nearly every page he ever wrote, he left for the Holy Land and entered a monastery near Bethlehem.

It was not enough. The two of them had heard that the real thing was further south, and they got permission to go to Egypt for a short visit. They stayed for something like fifteen years.

The desert

What they found in the settlements of Scetis and the Cells was the first generation after Antony: hundreds of men living alone or in twos and threes across miles of desert, weaving baskets, reciting the psalms, and possessing between them a body of practical knowledge about the human interior that nothing in Cassian's education had prepared him for. He and Germanus went from elder to elder and asked questions. The record of those conversations is the Conferences — twenty-four dialogues, each with a named abba, on chastity, on discouragement, on friendship, on the will, on Scripture, and above all on prayer.

The two conferences with Abba Isaac, the ninth and tenth, are the reason people still read the book. Isaac's teaching is that prayer is not an activity you perform at intervals but a state you can live in, and that the obstacle is not sin so much as the mind's inability to stay still. His remedy is startlingly practical: take one verse of Scripture and use it, constantly, as the mind's ballast.

For keeping up continual recollection of God this pious formula is to be ever set before you: O God, make speed to save me: O Lord, make haste to help me. This verse has not unreasonably been picked out from the whole of Scripture for this purpose, for it embraces all the feelings which can be implanted in human nature, and can be fitly and satisfactorily adapted to every condition, and all assaults.

Isaac then walks through an ordinary day, showing the verse in use: at waking, at the first temptation, at the fixed hour of prayer, before supper, in the small hours when sleep will not come. It is one of the earliest descriptions of what later ages would call the practice of the presence of God, and the line runs from this page through the Rule of Benedict — which opens every office with exactly this verse — to the Jesus Prayer, to the Cloud of Unknowing, to a great deal of modern contemplative practice.

Cassian also describes prayer that has gone past words. He writes about a state in which the soul, kindled beyond speech, pours itself out with unspeakable groans, and he is careful to say that this cannot be manufactured and should not be sought for its own sake. He also insists, against a natural misreading, that the man weeping over his sins in terror and the man silent in delight at the goodness of God are equally far along; what matters is not which you feel but that you have stopped performing.

Cassian is careful never to promise that the formula produces feeling. His claim is smaller and steadier: that a mind given one verse to hold will, over years, stop being blown about — and that the man who prays it in terror at his own sin and the man who prays it in silent delight have arrived at the same place by different roads, since, as the Lord Himself says, he begins to love the more who knows that he has been forgiven the more.

Constantinople, and a letter to Rome

Around the year 400 the peace of the Egyptian desert broke apart in the Origenist controversy, and Cassian and Germanus left. They went to Constantinople, and there the story joins another already in this library: they were taken in by the archbishop, John Chrysostom, who ordained Cassian a deacon and put the two friends in charge of the cathedral treasury.

They were therefore in the city for everything that followed — the Synod of the Oak, the false charges, the deposition, the exile. Cassian took Chrysostom's side without hedging. When the clergy loyal to the archbishop needed someone to carry their appeal to Pope Innocent I in Rome, describing what had been done, they chose Germanus and Cassian to take it. He was, in other words, not only a contemplative but a man who had watched the church behave abominably at close range and had walked across a continent to say so.

Of his years in Rome little is known. Somewhere around 415 he arrived at Marseilles and settled, founding two monasteries — one for men, one for women — and beginning to write.

The books

The Institutes came first: the practical manual, covering how a monastery is actually run, what the monks wear, how the offices are kept, and then, in its second half, the eight principal faults — gluttony, lust, avarice, anger, dejection, listlessness, vainglory, pride. That list, revised by Gregory the Great, became the seven deadly sins of the medieval West. Cassian's treatment of them is not moralising; it is closer to clinical observation, and the chapters on acedia, the listlessness that empties out the middle of the afternoon and makes a man certain he is in the wrong place, are still quoted by people who have never read another word of patristic literature.

Then the Conferences, in three instalments, which are the deeper book. What holds them together is a single conviction, stated in the first conference: the immediate goal of the monastic life is purity of heart, and everything else — fasting, vigils, poverty, solitude — is an instrument, worthless the moment it is mistaken for the point.

Not everyone approved. The thirteenth conference deals with grace and free will, and its refusal to say that the first movement toward God is always and only God's brought Cassian into conflict with the followers of Augustine; Prosper of Aquitaine attacked him in print. The label later attached to his position, semi-Pelagianism, is a sixteenth-century coinage and a poor summary of what he actually says, which is the observation of a man who had watched hundreds of people struggle and could not bring himself to describe their striving as nothing. It is worth knowing about, and it is worth not letting it obscure the rest.

Why he is worth reading

The temptation with the desert fathers is to read them as extremists whose lives have nothing to do with ordinary Christian existence, and Cassian quietly forecloses that. He is writing for men in Gaul with rain and mud and neighbours, not for hermits in Scetis, and the translation is deliberate: he keeps what transfers and says plainly when something does not. Egyptian fasting, he notes, does not suit Gallic bodies or Gallic winters.

What transfers is the diagnosis. He is extraordinarily good on the mind that will not stay where it is put — on the way a wandering thought during prayer is not a moral failure to be flogged but a symptom to be understood, and on the fact that what you think about all day is what you will find yourself thinking about the moment you kneel. That observation is fifteen hundred years old and has not aged a day.

What he was for

Cassian is the hinge between the Christian East and the Christian West. Without him, the desert tradition would have stayed in Greek and Coptic, and Benedict — and therefore European monasticism, and therefore a great deal of Europe — would have been built on something else. He knew he was a translator rather than an originator, and he says so constantly: this was delivered to us by a few of those who were left of the oldest fathers, and it is only divulged by us to a very few.

He is also, for a writer so old, unusually easy to be with. He does not command; he reports a conversation, including the parts where he and Germanus did not understand and had to ask again. When Abba Isaac finishes his teaching on unceasing prayer, the two of them go away and come back the next day to say, in effect, that it was wonderful and they cannot do it — and the tenth conference exists because they admitted that.

He died at Marseilles around 435, an old man who had begun as a boy in a monastery on the Danube frontier and had spent his working life carrying one thing a very long way. There is no reliable likeness of him; the devotional images that survive are icons made long after, so this page carries his initials instead of a face. What he would have wanted carried is not his face anyway. It is the verse: O God, make speed to save me.

fields.name: Anselm of Canterbury
fields.bio: Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109) was a monk of Bec who became an unwilling archbishop and was exiled twice for refusing to treat the church's offices as the king's property. He is remembered for the argument at the heart of the Proslogion, but that book is a prayer from first line to last, written by a man who said he did not seek to understand in order to believe, but believed in order to understand. His private prayers changed how the medieval West prayed.
fields.bio_html:
Anselm of Canterbury is remembered for an argument, which is unfortunate, because the argument is embedded in a prayer and was never meant to be prised out of it. The Proslogion is not a work of philosophy with some devotional decoration; it is a man on his knees, addressing God directly for its entire length, who happens partway through to see something and cannot stop himself from working it out on the page. Read as a treatise it is clever. Read as it was written, it is one of the most moving things in medieval literature.

He was born in Aosta, in the Alpine north of Italy, in 1033. His mother Ermenberga was devout and, by every account, the parent he loved; his father Gundulf was harsh, and after his mother died the household became intolerable. At about twenty-three Anselm left home, crossed the Alps, and spent three years wandering through Burgundy and France with no settled plan, a detail his admirers tend to hurry past and which is probably the most human thing about him.

What ended the wandering was a teacher. Lanfranc, the most famous scholar in northern Europe, was prior of a small, poor monastery at Bec in Normandy, and Anselm went to hear him. In 1060, aged twenty-seven, he took vows there. He became prior three years later and abbot in 1078, and for over thirty years Bec was the whole of his life: teaching, arguing gently with his own students, and writing the books that made his name while nobody outside the cloister was watching.

Faith seeking understanding

The first of them, the Monologion, was written because his monks asked for a meditation on God that used reasoning alone, without appeal to Scripture's authority. It worked, but it took many linked arguments, and that dissatisfied him. He wanted to know whether one argument existed that needed nothing but itself.

His own account of what happened next is the best thing ever written about intellectual obsession:

Although I often and earnestly directed my thought to this end, and at some times that which I sought seemed to be just within my reach, while again it wholly evaded my mental vision, at last in despair I was about to cease, as if from the search for a thing which could not be found.

— Anselm, preface to the Proslogion

He tried to give it up. It would not let him: when I wished to exclude this thought altogether, lest, by busying my mind to no purpose, it should keep me from other thoughts, then more and more, though I was unwilling and shunned it, it began to force itself upon me, with a kind of importunity. So, one day, when I was exceedingly wearied with resisting its importunity, in the very conflict of my thoughts, the proof of which I had despaired offered itself. He had been fighting it off; it arrived anyway, and he received it as a gift rather than an achievement.

He first called the book Faith Seeking Understanding, and that phrase is the key to everything he did. He is not building a ladder from doubt up to belief. He is a believer trying to see what he already trusts, and he says so in the first chapter, in a sentence that has been quoted for nine hundred years:

I do not seek to understand that I may believe, but I believe in order to understand. For this also I believe, that unless I believed, I should not understand.

— Anselm, Proslogion 1

And the chapter that contains it does not read like scholarship at all. It opens with an invitation that could be printed on its own as a devotional text:

Up now, slight man! Flee, for a little while, thy occupations; hide thyself, for a time, from thy disturbing thoughts. Cast aside, now, thy burdensome cares, and put away thy toilsome business. Yield room for some little time to God; and rest for a little time in him. Enter the inner chamber of thy mind; shut out all thoughts save that of God, and such as can aid thee in seeking him; close thy door and seek him.

Then, a few lines later, the ache underneath: Lord, if thou art not here, where shall I seek thee, being absent? But if thou art everywhere, why do I not see thee present? That is not a rhetorical set-up. That is the actual question, and the argument that follows is his attempt to answer it for himself.

The kind of teacher he was

Bec under Anselm was not a severe house, and that was deliberate. Eadmer preserves an exchange with an abbot who complained that the boys in his care were incorrigible — beaten day and night, he said, and they only got worse. Anselm asked him what he supposed a young tree would look like if it were hemmed in on every side so that it could not put out a branch, and told him that souls need room in the same way. He is one of the very few people of his century on record as thinking that beating children produced worse adults.

His letters carry the same quality. They are affectionate to a degree that startles modern readers, addressed to monks and former students in language of open love, and they keep returning to the same practical counsel: do not measure yourself against others, do not despair at your own slowness, hold on. A man capable of the tightest reasoning in Europe spent a great deal of ink telling anxious people to be less hard on themselves.

Canterbury, and two exiles

In 1093, entirely against his will, he was made Archbishop of Canterbury. William Rufus had kept the see vacant for four years in order to pocket its revenues, and only filled it when he thought he was dying. The story that the bishops had to force the pastoral staff into Anselm's clenched fist comes from Eadmer, the monk who followed him for years and wrote his life; whatever the precise choreography, nobody disputes that he did not want it.

The sixteen years that followed were mostly conflict. Anselm believed the church's offices were not the king's property; Rufus, and then Henry I, believed otherwise. He went into exile twice, in 1097 and again in 1103, and spent years abroad appealing to Rome. He was not a natural fighter — his letters are full of longing for the quiet of Bec — but he did not give way, and the settlement eventually reached in England became a model for the wider investiture struggle.

The first exile produced his other great book. Cur Deus Homo, Why God Became Man, asks the question a sceptic would ask: given that God is God, why the incarnation? Why not simply forgive? Anselm's answer, worked out as a dialogue with his student Boso, is that sin is not a debt God is owed in the way a merchant is owed money, but a dishonouring of the order of things that only a human being could repay and only God could afford. It is the origin of what later theology calls the satisfaction account of the atonement, and it has been argued with ever since, which is a form of compliment.

He was also willing to be argued with, publicly and in his own book. A monk named Gaunilo wrote a rebuttal of the Proslogion's central argument, cheerfully titled In Behalf of the Fool — the fool of Psalm 14 who says in his heart there is no God. Anselm wrote a reply, and then asked that from then on Gaunilo's objection and his answer be copied together with the book itself. The standard edition still prints all three, which means that for nine centuries the most famous argument in medieval theology has travelled with its best contemporary refutation attached, at the author's own insistence.

The prayers

Alongside all this he wrote prayers and meditations, circulated to friends and to noblewomen who asked for them, and they are unlike anything before them in Latin. Earlier prayers were mostly liturgical and corporate; Anselm's are private, extravagant, emotionally naked, addressed to Christ and to the saints in the first person singular, full of self-accusation and sudden tenderness. They did more than any of his arguments to change how ordinary Western Christians prayed, and they are the reason that a great deal of later medieval devotion sounds the way it does.

He died on 21 April 1109, at Canterbury, in Holy Week. Eadmer records that he had said he would like to live a little longer because there was a question about the origin of the soul that he did not think anyone else would solve if he did not. That is Anselm exactly: dying, and still curious.

What he leaves is a demonstration that the two halves people keep separating were never separate for him. He thought hard because he loved God, and the thinking turned back into prayer as naturally as breathing. His most famous argument sits in the middle of a chapter that ends in praise, and if you take it out of that setting to test it, you have the right to — but you are no longer reading Anselm.

fields.name: Bernard of Clairvaux
fields.bio: Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153) entered a struggling new monastery at twenty-two bringing thirty companions with him, and was an abbot at twenty-five for the remaining thirty-eight years of his life. He made a pope, pursued Abelard to condemnation, preached a crusade that failed catastrophically, and in the same years wrote On Loving God and eighty-six sermons on the Song of Songs. His answer to how much God should be loved was that there is no measure.
fields.bio_html:
Bernard of Clairvaux was the most powerful man in twelfth-century Europe who held no office worth having. He was an abbot, nothing more. He made popes, unmade theologians, rebuked kings by letter, and preached a crusade that ended in catastrophe. He also wrote, in the same years, some of the tenderest prose about the love of God in any language. Both are true at once, and a biography that keeps only the warm half is not telling you about Bernard.

He was born in 1090 at Fontaines, near Dijon, the third son of a Burgundian knight. His mother Aleth died when he was in his teens and he seems never quite to have recovered from it. In 1113, aged twenty-two, he presented himself at Cîteaux — a struggling new monastery whose reformed, deliberately austere version of the Benedictine life was close to collapse for want of recruits — and he did not come alone. He had spent months persuading his brothers, his uncle, and a crowd of friends, and he arrived with about thirty men. The story that mothers hid their sons when Bernard came to town is probably a later embellishment. It is the kind of embellishment he attracted.

Two years later the abbot sent him out with twelve monks to found a daughter house in a valley in Champagne. They called it Clairvaux. He was twenty-five, and he was its abbot for the remaining thirty-eight years of his life. When he arrived there was nothing there; when he died the Cistercian order had grown from a handful of houses to some three hundred and forty, of which sixty-eight were founded from Clairvaux itself.

On loving God

His short book on the love of God opens by refusing to be complicated. A cardinal had written to ask him why God should be loved and how much, and Bernard answers in the first two sentences:

You want me to tell you why God is to be loved and how much. I answer, the reason for loving God is God Himself; and the measure of love due to Him is immeasurable love.

— Bernard of Clairvaux, On Loving God

Then, because he says he is debtor to the unwise also, he spends the rest of the book explaining it slowly. The famous part is his account of love arriving in four stages. A man begins by loving himself for his own sake, which is where everyone starts. Under pressure he learns to love God for what God gives him — a self-interested love, and Bernard does not despise it; he says plainly that this is how most people begin and that God is content to be approached this way. Then, having been carried long enough, he comes to love God for God's own sake. And then, rarely and briefly, there is a fourth:

How blessed is he who reaches the fourth degree of love, wherein one loves himself only in God! When shall my soul, rapt with divine love and altogether self-forgetting, yea, become like a broken vessel, yearn wholly for God?

— Bernard of Clairvaux, On Loving God

He is honest that he has not lived there. He calls it a rapture he would count a man blessed and holy to have known, and says that in this life it is momentary at best. A lesser writer would have implied he was describing his own address.

The whole book turns on a single refusal: that the love of God can be measured out in proportion to anything at all. Bernard's answer to how much is not a quantity but the abolition of the question — the measure of love due to Him is immeasurable love.

The public man

He should have been left in his valley, and he was not. From about 1130 the outside world took hold of him and would not let go. A disputed papal election split Europe, and Bernard's advocacy did more than anything else to make Innocent II pope. He was called to arbitrate quarrels, examine bishops, and settle disputes across France, Italy and Germany, and the letters — hundreds survive — show a man complaining bitterly about the traffic while continuing to direct it.

He pursued Peter Abelard, the age's most brilliant and most abrasive theologian, to condemnation at Sens in 1140. Bernard believed Abelard was dissolving the mysteries of the faith into logic-chopping; Abelard believed Bernard was substituting fervour for thought. Modern readers are generally on Abelard's side, and even those who are not tend to find Bernard's methods in that campaign hard to defend. He was capable of ferocity, and he did not always know when he was being ferocious in his own cause rather than God's.

Then, in 1146, at the command of Pope Eugenius III — who had been his own monk at Clairvaux before the papacy took him — he preached the Second Crusade. He was overwhelmingly persuasive: the crowds at Vézelay and through the Rhineland were enormous, and two kings took the cross. The expedition achieved nothing at vast human cost. He did not hide from it. In On Consideration, written afterwards for that same Eugenius, he faced the wreck directly rather than reaching for the easy explanation, and took the weight of it on himself. One of the things worth respecting about Bernard is that he wrote up his own worst failure and let it be published.

The Rhineland preaching had a second consequence that belongs in any honest account. A monk named Radulf had gone ahead of him whipping up massacres of Jewish communities in the Rhine cities, and Bernard travelled there to stop him — confronting him in person, sending him back to his monastery, and insisting in writing that the Jews were not to be touched. It worked, and contemporary Jewish chroniclers recorded their gratitude by name. It is also true that the crusade he had summoned created the conditions Radulf exploited. Both halves are his.

The letters show the private man the public one obscured. The very first of them is to his young kinsman Robert, who had left Clairvaux for an easier house, and it pleads rather than threatens. Writing about another man tempted the same way, he asks only that he be warned not to be induced rashly to desert the certain for the uncertain, and adds: perseverance alone is always attacked by the devil, because it is the only virtue which has the assurance of being crowned.

Writing to kings

Nothing shows the strangeness of his position better than the letters he sent to people who outranked him absolutely. Writing with the abbots of Cîteaux to Louis of France, who was persecuting the Bishop of Paris, he does not soften the address: With what confidence can we now presume to lift up our hands for you to the Spouse of the Church, while you so inconsiderately, and without the slightest cause, afflict the Church? Then, in the same breath, the reason he thinks he may say it — perhaps we have to say it with boldness, but at the same time in love.

That is the register of the whole correspondence. He is not a courtier and he is not a scold; he writes to a king exactly as he writes to a frightened novice, on the assumption that both are answerable to the same God and both can still change their minds. It made him enemies, and it made him, for thirty years, the person Europe wrote to when something had gone badly wrong.

He was not naive about what all this was doing to him. The letters return again and again to the same complaint: that he is dragged about, that his life has become other people's business, that a man who left the world at twenty-two has ended up managing it. The complaint recurs too often to be a pose, and the obvious question — whether he could have refused any of it — is one he never quite answers.

The Song of Songs

Through all of it he was preaching, in chapter at Clairvaux, a series of sermons on the Song of Songs. He gave eighty-six of them over eighteen years and reached the beginning of the third chapter of the book. They are the summit of his writing and of a whole tradition of reading that poem as the love between Christ and the soul — sensuous, exact, psychologically observant, and utterly unembarrassed. He was still working on them when he died.

He died at Clairvaux on 20 August 1153, worn out at sixty-three, having outlived his own health by years of fasting he later admitted had been foolish and had damaged him permanently. Luther, who had little patience for medieval saints, made an exception for him. Calvin quoted him. Dante gave him the last word in the Paradiso, the prayer at the summit of heaven.

What is worth taking from Bernard is not the political triumphs, which mostly turned to dust, but the thing he kept saying in the middle of them. He had every reason to believe in his own effectiveness — he had more of it than any churchman of his century — and the books he wrote in those years argue relentlessly that effectiveness is not the point, that the self is not the point, and that the only proper measure of the love of God is that there isn't one.
